SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Buddy Tate
Reel I
Interviewed by Gary Giddins

Washington, D.C.
March, 1980

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S
You ask me some questions.
Okay, let's start.
All right.
You were born when?
February 22nd, 1915, Sherman, Texas.
Tell me about your folks. Where were they born?

Well, I think they all are from -- my mother was -- I think she was raised in Oklahoma, but on my dad's side, they're all from Texas, a little town that's called Polly Grove , Texas, a small place. It's between Dallas and Sherman.
Uh-huh.

Of course, I was born in Sherman, Texas. He came to Sherman, Texas, along with his father and he was a farmer and he was very successful. He died very early. I was only two years old when he passed, but he had owned three farms and he was only 46 and I kind of admired him for that, you know, because he must have paid some dues to own three farms.

So, you know, I was raised without a father, but I had two brothers that were older. One was ten years older and one was eight years older and the sister was like seven years older. So that makes quite a difference, you know, like when
you --
They kind of helped bring you up.

They did. See, all three of them, they were like my father, you know, like my other two brothers were like my father. Of course, they've passed on and the one played saxophone, eight years older -- yeah, the one that was eight years older. He was a saxophone player and actually, he's the cause of me being in the music business because he brought me a saxophone. I wanted to be a trombone player and he left and went to Dallas and got a job earning some money and he bought me a saxophone and he brought it back to me, says, "I'm going to try to find you a teacher," said, --
Was this a tenor?
No, this was alto.
Alto.

This was alto. Alto was a popular instrument then. There weren't many tenor players, you know. It just wasn't a popular instrument at that time. Alto and C melody, like Frankie Trumbauer played C melody. That was a popular instrument then.

So he went away and as I said, he brought me this saxophone back and there was a fella there that played saxophone and trumpet by the name of Emmett Malone, He was a very advanced musician. He just had talent because he was way ahead of time, really. It's too bad he didn't pursue

it because he just went out and he passed about four or five years ago as a -- he was a streetcar driver out in San Francisco, but a fine musician. So he got me started, along with a white fellow by the name of Frank O'Bannon. He's the one that taught me how to transpose; that's the first thing he taught me. So I thought he was crazy when he was telling me to take a G and make a B out of it, you know.
(Laughter.)
You know, like transposition. So I really think my brother bought me this saxophone to keep me from bothering his, because every time he'd leave, I'd get into his case.
Did he ever play professionally?
My brother?
Yeah.
He was playing professionally. Yeah, he played professionally later. But when we were like on the --
What was his name?

His name was Herbert Tate. He played around Dallas with the bands, local, territory bands. And every time he would leave, I'd get into it and break his reeds because I didn't know what I was doing and I told him when he brought me the alto, I says, "Well, really, this isn't what I really want." I says, "I really want to play a trombone." I used to get the curtains off the wall like that and I'd put them together and I'd slide them -- maybe I was about seven,
eight, then, you know. So then -- but he quickly told me, says, "This is it." He said, "The trombone is out." He says, "I had to scuffle to get this."
(Laughter.)
Said, "If you're going to be a musician, you better learn this." And that's the way it all started. But the other brother played piano.
His name?

Marshall. But he didn't play professionally. They would -- my mother used to give parties and they would have so many people that would come out, like from the city, and stay all night, you know, stay like the weekends, and I used to see all the pretty girls that would come out there, you know, and they were so popular with the girls and things and that made me want to be a musician, too. That's another thing. Oh, there are many things, along with my auntie had a hotel in Dallas, Texas, and when I'd go -- she kept all the musicians. And when I would go to Dallas, I would meet them and I just liked the way, you know, their surroundings and everything, you know. There was a band by the name of Alfonso Trent. I thought it was just like -- Jesus, they were so ahead of time, they had about 15 uniforms. They worked at the Adolphus Hotel and half of the band stayed with my auntie. I just -- you know, there were so many things around me and then I loved music, too.
When you were growing up then, you were on this farm?
Well, yes, up until about 12. Then she also had a city house which was just about three miles from the farm.
So the farms kind of supported your mother.

Yeah. Well, see, my father was a farmer that -- well, we raised everything like we had -- she had a beautiful garden and we just had about everything we needed, like meats and calves, you know, we had cows and we had everything we really needed. So I didn't have a hard time, you know, in that respect, you know.
Do you remember the first music you heard?

First music I heard? I can remember, just about remember the first music I heard. My cousin had a vaudeville show and, well, he used to have -- he was much older, you know, and I was very small, and he used to bring that show to Sherman and he would perform like in the theater like for a week and he had Sidney Bechet.
Really?
Yeah, Sidney Bechet and comedians like Spider Bruce and I'm not sure, but I think Pigmeat was with one of his shows.
Pigmeat Markham?

Pigmeat Markham. I know he remembers him very well, because I've asked him, you know, like in later years, if they knew Bruce -- his name was Bruson or Bruce. And I remember him having a nice little sounding band, couldn't have been anymore than eight. But then -- but I don't know if that was the first or not, because I -- you know, as I said, I was listening to other bands like Alphonso Trent. But I was older though when I listened to Alphonso Trent and the Blue Devils. That's when I first met Basie. He was with the Blue Devils, Walter Page's Blue Devils. But of course, I must have been about 12, 13 then. I started playing when I was 14.
Yeah.
Professionally.
Did the kids in the neighborhood play or did you play at school?
Well, we had the farm -- see, we formed the family band and we had a trumpet, saxophone and a banjo, pianist and the bass and the drummer. Oh, by the way, they were all there.
At Sherman?
At Sherman. We took a picture.
Uh-huh.
I had them all to come up. I tried to persuade them, you know, like months before, to just be able to learn one tune. I says, -- of course, they've been out of

business so long, you know. I says, "If you could just learn one tune and that would be so great for the concert that night." So the banjo player, he's a professor over in town, about 32 miles from my hometown, and he came over with his banjo. He says, "I practiced a little and cut my hands, --"
(Recording interruption.)

I really don't. The doctor told me not to even do it anyway. I said, "Well, I don't smoke." He said, "Well, don't keep doing that because you'll get hooked," you know? So I really don't need it. Let's see, where were we?
We were talking about the Buddy Tate Day at Sherman, Texas, last week.
Oh, yeah.
And you were going to play a number.

Oh, that's right. So I tried to persuade, you know, my cousin and of course, the one that plays piano, she's still into it. She doesn't play professionally; she plays for the church, but she still can play. So the drummer says, "I doubt if I can even keep any kind of time." I said, "Well, now wait. We aren't expecting you to be -- just make some noise. People know you don't play anymore." And my cousin, the one that was the leader, I mean, like in his name -- the name of the band was Roy McCloud's Night Owls. So he let me talk and he says, "Listen," he says, "I don't want
to drag you," he says, "but I'm not thinking about -- I'm not about to let you talk me into breaking my $750.00 bridge."
(Laughter.)
So that ended that.
Uh-huh.

So I says, "Okay." But anyway, they were all there and I had them up and they all come up and people all gave them a standing ovation. So I told them, I said, "Well, this is it. This is where we all started and these are the ones. Thank God they're still hanging in there, you know?" And there was a lady by the name of Miss Callie Frost . She had a daughter by the name of Jack Frost and Dorothy Frost. She really started it all. One Christmas -- she'd heard about the band. You know, we weren't -- playing little gigs and things here and there. But around one Christmas, she came and we, you know, did an audition for her down to my cousin's house and she just flipped over the band. She just went crazy over it. She was affiliated with the colleges and we played for her and after that, we were in. We were doing like three and four gigs a week, you know, like --
What year?
This must have been about 1927.
Uh-huh.
It must have been about 1927.
And you were 12.
Yeah, about 13. I was between 12, 13, something --
And you had been playing for about --
Well, I was really trying to learn then.
Uh-huh.
See, that's when I was really getting into it.
Yeah.

Maybe nine months, maybe a year or something, you know, but it's right along in there, you know, because actually, I could take solos better than I could read then, you know. I could just -- because we would listen to all the records, Coon-Sanders -- that was a good band out of Kansas City, Coon-Sanders Nighthawks -- and we listened to Fletcher Henderson, everybody.
So you had a record player.
We had one lady -- we had a record player.
Yeah.

But we didn't have the records. We couldn't afford them. And there was a lady that -- well, our people thought it was the wrong house for us to be in. They called it like the house of ill repute, you know. The only thing she did was sold drinks because that's a dry county,

still is, and she just sold drinks. But she had every record of everybody. That's the first place, in her house, that I heard Pop's West End Blues and that's the first time I'd heard Coon-Saunders' 'Sluefoot'. They made a thing called Sluefoot, was the big thing, I loved the saxophone playing in that, you know.

So we'd go there and listen to all of her records because she had everything and until our parents found out what we were doing, see, so they just thought that was the wrong kind of house for us to be in, you know what I mean. But it really didn't stop us because, you know, we would say, 'Okay,' but we'd sneak back in there and listen to them. She ended up marrying my cousin. He wasn't a musician. And I think she's still alive. He told me that she lives in Fort Worth and she's -- well, she would be pretty old now, you know. But that's where we kept up with all the records and things.
Now your mother had a record player, too.
We had a record player, too, and she --
What kind of stuff did she have?

Well, she had some things by Bing Crosby, Bessie Smith -- she had all of Bessie Smith's records -- and she had more records by vocalists than she did bands. She had Dixie Lee, that was Bing's wife, you know.
Oh, yeah.
She was big before Bing.
I didn't know that.

Yeah, she was big before Bing and I think she gave up her career to have babies and you know, like become a housewife and she just dropped everything. I'm pretty sure, because I remember -- and Gene Austin.
How about Louie?
Lou Armstrong? That's the first place I heard Louie do 'West End Blues' was over to this house.
But your mother didn't have him.
She didn't have Louie.
No.

No, she didn't have Louie. So whoever had the bands, that's where we'd visit more, you know, because -- then I finally started buying some records by the bands, you know, and we'd turn them all down. Then you'd wind it up and you'd set your tempo where you wanted to, you know, where you wanted it to be and that's why I could learn the solos. I could learn the solos from the record because I could play it so slow and you had to learn it, you know what I mean? And I learned how to write harmony from that, just listening and listening and putting it in there and I learned how to write harmony from listening to the records, turning it down. Man, we put it so slow.
(Laughter.)

And then we -- you know, we started buying records, all of us, maybe I'd buy this one and the other one buy another record. Then, you know, we started like that. Then this fellow Malone that I told you that started me off on saxophone, the first one that taught me how to spell, I'd say, you know, "Spell it," but I couldn't read fast. My cousin trumpet player could. But the fellow Malone, we couldn't keep him. He'd been on the circuses and carnivals and everytime, anytime a carnival came to town, he'd be playing with us and everything, but anytime a carnival came to town, we didn't lock him up, when that carnival left, he was with it. So we could never depend on him.

But he started me -- like he started me off in playing one of these parties that I told you that Miss Frost arranged for us, you know, the lady that was affiliated with the colleges, a saxophone player -- they had like four theaters that had live music with like six or seven-piece bands in them, in the white theaters and I used to go in the back of the alley and listen to him because he had a beautiful tone on alto. His name was Frank O'Bannon. We -- it was segregated. I couldn't pay to go in, you know, we couldn't go to the theaters. We had to have a theater on our own.
They didn't even have the whites in the balcony, that kind of thing?
No, they didn't even have that in Sherman.

Later on, they did. But then, they didn't even have that. But they had a big alley and I'd just go back there and I would listen to them because they would play sometimes like maybe 15, 20 minutes, maybe sometimes a half an hour, then they would play sometime for the pictures. This was before talkies.
Right.
But one night -- I knew who he was -- and one night, at one of the parties, he came up to me, he says, "Gee, man," he says, "you sure can play a lot of hokum."
(Laughter.)

I said, "Oh, yeah? Thank you." He says, "I'm Frank O'Bannon." I says, "I know. I love you. I'm listening to you." He says, "Where did you hear me play?" So I says, "Well, you played the Ginn Theater." He says, "Sure." But he knew I hadn't been in the Ginn Theater. I said, "Well, look, I heard you in the alley." I says, "I was standing back there," and I says, "your sound is very beautiful." I says, "There's a lot of things I need to learn." He says, "I'll tell you what." He says, "I can't play jazz," he said, "but I can read." I said, "I know you can. You're in that theater, you got to be able to read." So he says, "I can teach you that. That ain't no problem." So he says, "Can you teach me jazz?" That's a hard thing, you know. So I said, "Yeah."
(Laughter.)
I didn't say "no," I said, "Yeah, you teach me how to read good and I'll teach you how to play jazz good."

So he had a little studio. He was teaching, too. He had students, all white students, because there weren't many black people trying to learn music, you know, which is sad now. I don't know anybody in Sherman that is learning how to play. So anyway, he says, "You come to see me." I says, "Well, I don't know if I can afford it." He says, "Can you afford 50 cents a lesson?" So I says, "Yeah, I think so." So he says, "Now, you don't have to." I says, "Well, I can."
So we started, because Malone was along with one of those carnivals and he was gone, you know. Sometimes he'd go and stay like six months, a year, something like that, and we didn't see him anymore.

So I started visiting Frank on certain days that he would have off. He played every night, but some days he didn't have to go to work until like 6:30, 7:00. So I'd go out there and the first thing he did was, you know, there was a lot of sheet music then in those days. So he says, "Can you read this?" I said, "Yeah, I can read it." He says, "But you can't play these notes now like with a piano?" I says, "Why not?" He says, "You got to transpose that now, a tone and a half below." I said, "What do you mean?"
(Laughter.)

I didn't know what I was doing, man. He says, "Transposition or transposing means that -- see, like if that's a A natural on your saxophone, on your alto, that's got to be F sharp on your horn." I says, "Oh, I don't think I can make that." He says, "Oh, yeah. You can make that." So he says, "You just start doing it at home. I'll give you some music. Instead of playing these notes," he says, "just play some low notes and I'll give you something that's got melody to it and you'll know if you're playing right." So that's the way he started me in transposing.

I had a problem, like trying to teach him how to play jazz. So he says, "Well, what do you do?" He says, "How do you feel?" I says, "Well, look, Frank, the only thing," I says, "sometime I hum a solo in my mind," and I would take like "My Blue Heaven" and I would say like what we call now scat it." So I says, "I'll try to play as close to that as I possibly can." He said, "Oh, I get it." I says, "And get that in your mind." I says, "Just hum something in your mind," I says, "and you can write." I says, "Just write out something like in your mind, how you'd like to do it." So I hipped him to that, you know, and he said, "Well, I can't write -- I get kind of tied up on my time." But you know, I'd say in six months, man, he was taking some nice solos and things and I really felt like -- he told me, he says, "You
know --" I says, "Just hum, get a tune in your mind and that you think you'd want to play variations off of and do it," I says, "and that's the only way you --"
You were how old now?
Then now I'm 13, I know I'm 13 then, 13.
So you weren't thinking in terms of chord changes?
I was doing it, but I didn't know what they were.
That phrase was not current among....
No, I didn't know what that was until -- and how to really form chord changes until I hired Earl Bostic myself in the first big band I ever worked with. I'll tell you about that.

So -- but now Malone had tried to tell me this, this other boy, but I couldn't get with that. I just didn't know -- he told me like C, E, G, C and all that kind of stuff. So he was telling me, says, "Now you got to --" He says, "You're doing it, but you don't know what you're doing with it." He says, "You don't know what key you're in, do you, half the time?" I says, "No, really." So he told me how to -- he says, "Well, whatever your last note ends on, that's just about the key it's on." He says, "Of course, there's major and there are minors and things." So when he went into that, he really lost me, you know what I mean? Because I was just
playing and I really didn't -- but I learned how to read.
Were you conscious then of trying to get a tone?

Yeah, I had a good sound because he loved my good sound, had a beautiful sound on the alto and he loved my sound. Everybody tried to get a sound in. That was very, very important and if you didn't, you wouldn't get a gig because there were a lot of -- I knew a lot of saxophone players that could play like hell, but they had -- they didn't have control of their vibrato. You know, had that nanny in there sound. So they didn't get a gig.
Was there a model that you had like for trying to get the kind of sound that you wanted?

Yeah, I wanted to get an even vibrato, but I wanted it to be pretty, you know, like there were some good saxophone players in those days that played beautiful and like Frank O'Bannon had a beautiful sound. He was a beautiful -- he would have made a beautiful first player. And like Earl has got a beautiful sound, Earl Warren, for first, you understand what I mean? And he can play those pretty things, you know. I wanted to sound like that. I was always conscious of trying to get a sound because everybody like was trying to get a sound in those days. So I think I had a good sound on the alto. He said I did and many other people said I had a good sound on the alto.

So after the band started, we started playing -- the band became so popular and we started playing other towns, like in Oklahoma and all around, you know. We'd go as far as Oklahoma City and we went to Kansas City a couple of times. We thought that was really it then, you know, we thought we really had it made.
How did you travel?
Well, we had -- in cars, touring cars, you know, we had two touring cars we used to travel --
How many guys in the band?
Well, now, by this time, we had six. We had the tenor player that really was my -- that influenced me to want to play tenor. His name was Milton Thomas, Nobody ever knew him. He had had a --
Was he the guy who started the trucks?
That's with the trucks, yeah, yeah. That's where he made his money, he got rich with trucks, you know.
Uh-huh.
He's got a lot of money now. But he still plays. He's playing with a white band now. He told me he's 75 years old. I didn't know he was that --
Is he still in Sherman?
He's in Dallas. He lived in Dallas then, but we used to bring him up there and he would stay with us

because we had a lot of gigs and -- you know, he was making money and we brought him up there. He couldn't read. Had a beautiful sound on tenor and of course, like when he left, he left, then I started playing tenor, when he left.
Let's go back to the -- you had six guys.
Uh-huh.
What was the instrumentation?
Well, let me see. Banjo, piano, drums, trumpet, alto and tenor.
No bass.
No bass. The banjo, we just had the banjo.
And who made your arrangements?

Well, we listened to the records and we'd play like the records and then we'd make head arrangements. You know, whenever -- Malone was this teacher I told you about, he would write us some arrangements, so he had written us maybe like -- we had about 15 or 20 arrangements that he had written for the band. He could write, man. He could just -- fast and write and everything, but we couldn't. And a lot of things he had written, we couldn't play. It was a little too heavy, you know. We would take us a long time, like get our introduction --
(Laughter.)
You mean you took arrangements off records?
Off records.
Which records?
Well, Coon-Saunders, Benny Moten and --
Had you heard Fletcher yet?
Yeah, we was listening to Fletcher. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers --
Uh-huh.

-- and who else? Ted Weems. Ted Weems had a good swing band during those days and we listened to all the bands, white and black. If they did something we liked, we did it. Then, as I say, we'd learn it, you know, like off the record and we'd play it for our band. One time -- another thing that helped influence me, helped me to make up our mind, Lonnie Johnson -- I know you know the name -- he'd been big many, many times up and down, up and down, he was an amazing man. I've seen Lonnie -- I want to say this before I get into how he influenced me -- I've seen Lonnie when he's riding high with a big record and the next couple of years, I'd see him a bellboy and he always would be the same. He'd be just as jolly and just as happy being the bellboy with a red jacket on as he was when he had diamonds and things on his fingers. He was really that kind of guy.

So he came to McKinney, Texas, which is between -- halfway between Sherman and Dallas and when one of his records was riding high to play in my auntie's ballroom, which we had never played for her, you know. Heavier names had played for her than we were, you know. So the band didn't show. About 6:00 -- he came early that afternoon and the band, about 6:30, 7:00, no band. So -- and he was going to start playing like from nine to twelve. At 12:00, all dances are over then. So he went to my auntie, he says, "Have you any musicians here?" He says, "I think I'm in trouble." He says, "I don't think that band's going to show from Dallas." He says, "I'm pretty sure if they were coming, they would have been here now." So she says, "No, no musicians here." He says, "Well, do you know any near here?" And I don't know why she didn't think of us right off the bat. So she says, "No. Oh," she says, "wait a minute." She says, "I've got some nephews and some cousins up the road." She was in McKinney, that's Herb's home, too, you know, Herb Ellis.
Uh-huh.

So he said -- he asked her, he said, "Well, can they play?" She said, "They say -- I understand -- people say they sound pretty good." She said, "They look good. Everytime they get some money, they buy a uniform." We got that from Trent, you know. We's sharp.
You got that from --

From Trent, Alfonso Trent's band. They had -- that was the one -- they had about 12, 14 uniforms. They used to be hanging up in my auntie's -- my other auntie's place and they were playing the Dolphus Hotel in Dallas, which was unknown. They was the only black band that played the Dolphus Hotel and they played there like a year and a half at a time and they were broadcasting from there. That really turned me on, you know, and they was sharp, man.

So anyway, we felt like if we was going to have a band, at least we'd look good. So we did. And she told him, she says, "Well, they look good." She says, "But I really haven't heard them play." He says, "Well, can you get them?" She says, "Oh, yeah." And she called us, I think it was about 25 miles. We must have made it, Gary, in 25 minutes, and when we got there, just like today, he had a line all the way around, just long, just people wanting to get in there to see him. I'll never forget, he had on a beautiful silk pongee suit and diamond about that big, man, on his fingers and had these rubber bands around his arms, you know, I don't know, this -- they used to do that, you know, pongee hat.

So he says -- we introduced ourselves. He says, "Can you guys play dance music?" And when he said that, we knew we were in. So we says, "Oh, can we? That's all we do, man." He says, "Well, if you can," he says, "I'm going to do about three or four blues for a set and I'll do two sets. Then
you play for the people to dance and you got it made." So we says, "Okay." Then we, you know, we felt a little confidence, you know, because we knew we could handle that.

So anyway, we did that and he played his guitar and we followed him. Of course, keys didn't make any difference because we didn't know what we were doing anyway. So we played in any key. I can play in any key until I started learning how to read. Then I started getting counted. That's true.

Anyway, keys didn't make any difference. So we had him, so we was playing the blues with him and then he'd do three numbers, maybe sometime -- in a couple of sets -- in one set, he did four, four tunes and that was the most he would do.
You mean singing?
Singing.
Yeah.

MR. TATE: Playing his guitar and he did four tunes. And when he finished, then we'd play and people would get back on the floor and start dancing, see? Well, he fell in love with the band. He says, "Man, this band --" he says, "that band I got can't touch this band." We did have a good one because we rehearsed everyday. We listened to all of the latest things and all the bands and we were doing things like what we'd heard as close as we could to the band, you know, the big band.
So anyway, here's the killer. When we finished

playing, he calls me over into the corner -- I don't know why he chose me -- he says -- he gave me $50.00. In those days, the dollar bills were much larger than now and fifty, it looked like you had a thousand.
(Laughter.)

And it was a lot of money then. People were working for like $50.00 a month. I remember that. So anyway, I called the five guys over -- we had five pieces -- he says, "What are you doing?" I says, "Well, I got to pay them." I says, "It's $10.00 apiece." So he says, "No, that's yours." He says, "I'm going to give them fifty." He gave us $300.00, you know, I mean, like -- $250.00. Man, when he said that, my heart stopped. I says, "Man, this man --" I says, "Are you sure?" He says, "Yeah." He says, "It's fifty for each one of them." Then that made up my mind. I says, "There's no way for me to top this in anything," so I says, "This is it." So, you know, that's the truth. This is actually the truth.

In later years, before he died, he remembered it and I used to see him in Toronto all the time and he did very good in Toronto. He was in good health and everything until somebody drove up on the sidewalk and hit him and broke both of his hips in a car and he was kind of old and he didn't get well after that. But up until then, he was doing fine. Worked all the time in Toronto and everything, loved him in Toronto. But he hasn't been dead for about seven, eight years.
But he always remembered that.
Uh-huh.
And that's one thing that really made up my mind.
To be a musician.
Yeah. I says, 'I can't beat this.' (Laughter.)

So then, you know, I really got serious. I says, 'Well, now, I got to really learn how to play so I can play with everybody, be good enough to play with everybody.' And I practiced all the time, see. Then -- now we're still in McCloud's Night Owls, aren't we? This is still the family band where we are now.
Uh-huh.

Then I think some of the boys finished school -- yeah, they did. And some of -- a couple of boys went off, like the drummer, he went to Langston, Oklahoma to college and I finished. I says, 'I don't think I'll go right now. I'm going away and play --' I had a job in Wichita Falls, Texas. It was an oil boom out there and just on the --
A what?
Oil boom. It's an oil town.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, you know. And there was money everywhere. So -- oh, yeah. Now by now, I had switched because,

yeah, we'd brought Milton up and he -- no, no. We carried him to Wichita Falls. He come up and work with us about a month, this Milton Thomas on tenor. He came up and worked with us about a month and we went to Wichita Falls to play and we went out and played a week in Wichita Falls and it was -- everybody had money out there, you know. Then there was a band out there that wanted us to join them. So Herschel [Evans] was in this band and he's playing brass alto. But I'd met him now before then, but he --
He was playing a --
Brass alto saxophone.
As opposed to --
Well, he hadn't gone to tenor. He hadn't switched to tenor then.
But I mean what kind of alto is not --

Well, it's all brass. You understand? It had a good sound, you know. It's just all brass instrument. You know -- have you seen all brass -- you've probably seen all brass. It shines. It's beautiful when it's cleaned. It's more prettier than the lacquered horns, but it's hard to keep clean. You know, it gets -- it's got a much better sound. See, that lacquer deadens the sound.
So he was playing that, had rubber bands all around it. And well, my cousin and I let them talk us into staying, this trumpet player. So then the McCloud's Night Owls, the
ones that were left, went on back to Sherman because it was -- we were on a job where we were making about $55.00 a week, and that was a lot of money, you know. So we stayed out there.

So Milton went back to Dallas. So during the time -- I had been like playing tenor anyway, switching, you know, like that month he stayed up there. So I was playing his tenor. I didn't own a tenor, but I was playing his tenor, just in case. I says, "Well, when you leave -- I know you're going to leave, so when you leave, I'm just going to switch to this tenor and get me a tenor," I said, because I liked the way he played tenor. Herschel liked the way he played tenor, too. We used to listen to him, you know. He could play, Gary.
Are you and Herschel about the same age?

No, he's -- Herschel's about three and a half years older, maybe four. Herschel and Lester and Ben and Budd-- Budd's a little older than I am, but Budd, I don't think Budd is quite as old as Herschel and Lester. They're all around the same age. They would be now about -- oh, it would be about 70 now. So, you know.

But anyway, we stayed out there with that band and I played tenor in that band. That was the St. Louis Merry-makers, that was the name of that band. Now that was like the first band that I worked with after leaving the McCloud's Night Owls. They called the band the St. Louis Merrymakers.

So then Troy Floyd was pretty -- name band then, you know. It was a bigger name than the St. Louis Merrymakers. So a friend of Herschel's had been trying to get him in that band for a long, long time and the tenor player that was playing in the band was a tenor player by the name of Funny Bagsby and he quit the band, Funny Bagsby was his name. I never forget. So Herschel joined that band. They told him they'd let him play tenor and that's when he went to Troy Floyd to play tenor. And I later played with him, you know, also, and we used to alternate. He'd play tenor some and I'd play alto, because we were both alto players.
And then all the time though, after Milton, I was listening to a tenor player, me and Herschel, also Milton, by the name of Prince Robinson. That's Harold Vick's uncle.
Oh, yeah?
Uh-huh. And he played with McKinney's Cotton Pickers. I love the way he played. He never got the recognition that was due him.
Roy Eldridge once told me that when he was coming up, the two great players were Hawkins and Prince.

That's right, that's right. Prince didn't get the recognition he deserved, he never did. He played, man, he did some -- he really swung and knew his instrument very well. He played some things that were very exciting and we used to listen to him quite a bit because actually, Prince

was smoother than Hawk at that time. He didn't have as big a sound as Hawk, but he was a little smoother than Hawk in his executions and things like that and we used to listen to him. He got over that horn. He played like, you know, and was really making it, you know. And we listened to him until Hawk -- Fletcher made "Stampede" and Hawk made "Stampede" and we forgot about everybody in the world.
(Laughter.)
He wiped out everybody in the world then after he played "Stampede." We all said, no, here's where it's at, with that big sound and everything.
What happened to Prince? Why didn't he (inaudible)?

I don't know. Sometimes it happens because -- and it was like -- now Jean Goldkette, they worked at the Greystone Ballroom and Jean Goldkette managed them, too. So they were the black band that played and whenever Jean Goldkette went out, they went out. So there was no need. I don't know why he didn't get the recognition because he was on the scene and there were people coming out of Fletcher's band like they used to go out of Whiteman's to Goldkette. They used to do that, you know. And they were doing that with Fletcher and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, same thing, and Don Redman would work with Fletcher a while and then he'd go work McKinney's Cotton Pickers, he and Benny Carter and all of them.

But he just never -- he never captured the recognition that he should have gotten and of course, you know, like in the years he started declining, styles and things change, you know, people forgot all about him. But Hawk liked him, too. He said a lot of nice things about -- I mean, even to me.
Where did Prince come from?

Well, Prince is from Norfolk, Virginia and he and Ed Cuffee and all were both with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers and of course, he died here in New York, you know. He moved here to New York after joining McKinney's Cotton Pickers. He came on here to New York. He worked around here in New York. But he -- I guess after Hawk gained such a big reputation, you know, after "Stampede," everybody was scared to even pick up a horn around Hawk.
Well, tell me about "Stampede." What was the --
Well, --
-- what was the effect?

Well, it was like -- I don't know, he was swinging so on "Stampede" and it was a terrific arrangement of Fletcher's in the first place. Everything was right there. And I'll never forget, it was in A flat and they played clarinets and it was just a hell of an arrangement, you know, absolutely fantastic arrangement and it was just made for him and he just upset everybody when he made it. He made, you
know, such a fantastic solo. I guess you could compare it to like when Lester made "Lester Leaps In," you know, one of those things, you know.
Had you been aware of Hawkins before?

Yeah. Yeah, I knew he was with Fletcher and I had listened to him, but I wasn't really -- he wasn't my idol -- Prince is like -- as much as Prince was, you know, until, of course, after that, I loved him, you know, I really did love him. And then everybody was like -- he gained the recognition as being the world's greatest saxophone player, you know, tenor player, because he really did really introduce the instrument. There's no stuff about that, you know, like even when Mamie Smith, when he was playing with Mamie Smith before Fletcher Henderson, he was playing the tenor then and he was popular, because the horn was the alto and the C melody.
Why do you think that was?
Well, let me see. Well, Frankie Trumbauer played the C Melody.
Did you ever play C Melody?
No, my brother did, the one --
It was harder, wasn't it?

Well, I don't think so. It was -- well, it's -- now, if I had played the C Melody -- I was thinking about it when he told me I was going to have to transpose because the C Melody, you can play off the same sheet, yeah,
with the same -- as the piano.
(Laughter.)

So I was thinking of the easy way out and if I had the money, I really would have been a C Melody player, too, and Frankie was a great C Melody player. Everybody dug him, you know. He was a big name. And I met him -- now I got to tell you this. I met him -- must have been about 1926 or '27 -- they played the automobile billing and Alfonso Trent, they had them to play first and Paul Whiteman had all this big band, about 45 pieces.
So Trumbauer was with Whiteman.
He was with Whiteman, he and Bix, I met Bix one time.
Uh-huh.

So I'll never forget it. And I want to tell you their reaction and how nice they were. Well, my brother says, 'You know,' he says, 'if we could just get in and hear Paul Whiteman band,' he says, 'man,' he said, 'I know there's going to be some beautiful music played.' He didn't play the jazz, the band wasn't a jazz band. But Bix and -- he broke it down like Basie used to do, the Kansas City Six and the Kansas City Seven, you understand? And they played it with Al Rinker, Mildred Bailey's brother, and the Rhythm Boys. [Bing]
Was Crosby with them then?
Yeah, uh-huh. So I says -- he says, 'I

don't know," he says, -- you couldn't have bought a ticket for a thousand dollars, because it was segregated. So they were selling in the cars and things like that. But in Texas, all of the help like that worked in the hotels are black, so -- and he just let them run it. He just tells them -- and they just run the place. They say, "Well, man, you can hear Paul Whiteman. Hell, don't worry about that. We'll see that you hear Paul Whiteman." So I says, "Well, could you --" He says, "We'll get you in, don't worry about it. Just come on and see me." And that was it.
(Laughter.)
So you know where I ended up? On the bandstand. I had a better seat --
(Laughter.)

-- than if I had been out, you know, outside. So naturally I knew about all these guys, I knew all of them, you know. I knew all the saxaphone players, I knew Ross Gorman, big names like that, Chester Hazlett; they were virtuosos, you know, those cats were technical, great saxaphone players. But Frankie and Bix played the jazz.

So I met him and my brother and well, I was kind of -- I think I talked more than my brother, you know, because I was talking to him and I says, I told him that I had their records, "Singing the Blues" he and Bix made, you know, and "The Riverboat Shuffle," and I said I had everything he'd

made. And I told him I had the things by Red Nichols and the Five Pennies, I had all of theirs. So he says, "Really?" I had on short pants -- you know Gary, in those days, you had to wear short pants, you know, until you -- you didn't hardly get a long suit, long pair of pants, until you was maybe 21 years old, until the later years, you know. So I had them on and knicker socks and my brother had on -- you know, he was eight years older. So I talked to him and I said, "I want to meet Bix, too." He says, "Well, you'll meet him." He says, "God knows where he is," he said, "but he'll be here."

So I'll never forget, when he fell in there, boy, he fell in with one of the prettiest ladies I ever seen in my life, just in time with his horn on his arm like this and he was tore up, he was higher than a kite.
Booze, yeah.

So Paul Whiteman had to announce him out and he had to get his -- he didn't go out there. So when he came on, Frankie says, "Bix, this is one of our fans," says, "he listens to all our records." So when he was saying, "Really?" He said, "Well, don't go. I got to go on." He says, "They just called me." He was apologizing because he had to go on and telling me to stay, man. You know, I was excited.
(Laughter.)
He says, "Well, look, we'll talk." He says, "Just

wait until I come back," so nice. I'll never forget it, man. So he went out and he didn't play trumpet then. He carried his trumpet out with him and put it on the piano and he played a tune called "Candlelight and Wine" and ended with "In A Mist". Then he brought Frankie out. Then -- I don't know what piano player it was then. He sat at the piano, some other piano playing, then he and Frankie played, you know, after he brought him out.

Man, then he came back there and we talked, man, we talked about everything, you know. But when I see Paul Whiteman's band and these saxophone players like opening up these books, man, I saw some music, I said, "Oh, my God, I'll never be able to make this." This is going on in my mind. I says, "I ain't going to never be able to play that." You know, because it was very technical, you know, hard music, like symphonic music, stuff like that, all the 64 notes and one bar and all this. I says, "I ain't going to be able to make it." So I said, "Frankie, just about what do you have to do to accomplish this, to be able to play like this?" I'll never forget what he said. He says, "Always remember," he says, "it's a full-time job." He says, "You hardly have any time for anything else." He says, "You got to practice and practice."
So now, I'll end this, then we'll go back where we started from. So I kept up with his career after that -- he

never was a successful band leader -- but he made nice records and things and I kept up with him like from -- this must have been about '27. I didn't see him again until I joined Basie's band in 1943. And one night, we were playing at K.U.S. -- State Kansas University and I don't know how many thousand people were listening to the band and there must have been 7 or 800 standing in front of the band and he was standing out there with his arms folded. We only had four saxophones -- Lester, Jack Washington, Earl. So Lester was on the's end, I was next to the -- so I leaned back behind him, I says, "Pres, I think I see Frankie Trumbauer out there." He says, "No, Pres, he wouldn't be down here."
(Laughter.)

You know, he -- so I didn't say anymore and I looked and the more I looked, the more I would recognize him, you know, like from pictures and things and then from back in 1926. So he says, "No." So when I leaned again, I says, "Pres, that got to be him." He says, "No, no, Tate." He always called me "Lady Tate." "No, Lady Tate, that wouldn't be --"
(Laughter.)
So I said, "Okay," don't say no more. So you know, when you get off the bandstand, you'd have to walk back and walk down -- you couldn't walk right straight out.
Uh-huh.
You know, you'd have to come to the corner, then go off the little steps.
Right.

So there were a lot of people running to the steps wanting autographs and things and things -- you know, the band was shoutin' down and everybody was so -- the band was so popular and Lester was actually -- I didn't have near the solos that he had to play and he was the big thing, you know, he was already big, you know, name and everything, featured. So Frankie let him pass. I thought sure he was going to grab Lester, you know what I mean? And man, when I came off, he walked straight up to me and this knocked me out, man. You don't know how I felt, man. He let Pres. pass and Pres. had played like 15 more solos than I had -- he listened to him -- and that's who he loved.
Yeah.
Was Frankie Trumbauer.
Yeah.

Then -- and he came up to me and he says, -- I says, 'Aren't you --' He says -- I says, 'Aren't you Frankie Trumbauer?' He says, 'Yeah.' I says, 'I know it.' I says, 'I met you --' He cut me off to let me know he remembered me. I says, 'I met you --' He says, 'With Paul Whiteman,' he said, 'in Dallas.' He said, 'You had on short pants.' So you know what he said to me? I swear to God. He

says, "I see you practiced, you have practiced." He remembered he had -- I says, "You remember you told me that?" He says, "Sure, I remember." He says, "I see you practiced." He says, "You have the prettiest subtones of anybody I've ever heard in my life," I swear to God he told me that. He says, "Because you make them. When you go down to that B natural and B flat, you don't blast them." He say, "You subtoning and it sounds just like you're playing all over your horn." He says, "Keep that in." He said -- I swear to God. And we became friends after that, you know. I says, "Well, Lester Young, I got to bring him here to meet you," I said, "because he loves you." So he says, "He plays good." Then we went on, you know, and talked and talked and everytime I'd go to Kansas City, he was here. I says, "Well, what are you doing here?" He says, "I'm in aeronautics." You running out?
No, fine.

He says, "I'm in aeronautics." He says, "I'm off everyday like 2:30." So we used to go like a couple times a year at least to play downtown at a white theater and whenever we did that theater, he would always come visit me and we'd go out and have dinner together and he spent the whole afternoon after he got off of work with me. He really liked me. Then up until he died, every Christmas, I got a Christmas card from him up -- you know, for the rest of his life until he died.
After the '20s, he never really had an impact on jazz again. He kind of just......

Just kind of -- yeah, he kind of like faded away. He never was successful. He had a band, a couple of bands, big bands. I remember the last one I heard was in New Orleans and I heard it on the air one night and it sounded good. I loved him, I loved the way he played, you know. I'll tell you who sounds more like him, Gary, than anybody in the world. That's why I believe everything has been done before, just like that song, 'Everything's Been Done Before.' You know who sounds like him? Paul Desmond.
Paul Desmond.
More than anybody. He really has the sound and everything like him. And --
Did he play C Melody to the end?

C Melody to the end. He never changed, played C Melody to the end. And he told me -- I says, 'Well, don't you play anymore?' He says, 'No,' he says, 'things have changed so,' he says, and he says, 'and I love what I'm doing. You know,' he says, 'like all the years,' he says, 'you know I flew to all of my gigs.' I said, 'Well, I heard that.' You know, like when he was with Whiteman, he flew to all his gigs then. So I says, 'Well, tell me something about your experiences, you know.' He says, 'Oh, I had many.' I says, 'Did you ever get lost?' He says, 'Well, two or three times I got

lost in storms and things," he says, "and I kind of gave up one time," he says, "because --" you know, they didn't have all that thing perfected then. He's up there in those little old planes flying by himself, you know, to his gigs, and he told me, he says, jokingly, he says, "Once the band opened at a hotel in San Francisco and," he says, "I came in too close and I almost landed on top of the hotel where we were to open at."
(Laughter.)

He broke some limbs off trees and things. He said that was his closest. And he said he's always loved that, so he just went in for aeronautics. And I understand when he died, he felt a heart attack coming on. He was a very smart man, nice man. And he made it to the desk of the hospital himself. You know, he had no history of heart trouble or anything. But he made it to the desk of the hospital and just collapsed and before they could get to him, it was too late.

I was very tight -- I felt very bad about it. Every Christmas, I got a Christmas card from him. So, you know, that and things like that, I just want to tell you that, you know what I mean, because it played a big part in my life for him to remember me and when he said -- oh, yeah, I didn't tell you. He says, "Oh, I remember him in Dallas, Texas." Then he says, "What became of your brother?"
Would it have been unusual for him to run into some young black kids who knew his records at that time?

You know, I don't think so. I think they were more turned on than today to jazz, more young black kids were turned on to jazz then because they didn't have the disco. You either liked blues singers and jazz and, you know, singers like Bessie Smith, blues singers, Mamie Smith, they were the blues singers. Then there were a lot of blacks even turned on to Gene Austin, who -- I think he sold more -- nobody's ever topped his "Blue Heaven," I don't think. I think every home in America had his "Blue Heaven." You remember that?
Oh, sure.

And then he made many songs. My mother had everything he made. And I think more black kids were turned on to jazz than they -- I don't think it would be any use because they knew about Frankie Trumbauer.
What interests me is that you were listening to whoever you liked then, it was white and black.
Yeah, yeah, that's right.
You didn't think of jazz as -- people didn't think of jazz as black music.
No, I didn't. We didn't. And -- oh, no, we never did. I mean, if it was good, we listened to it and we copied off the records, you know what I mean? Because we
copied off Coon-Saunders and Ted Weems and there was another band. I'm trying to think -- oh, Isham Jones. I loved Isham Jones' band, too. He had a good band.
Were you aware of a Morton and King Oliver?
Yeah, yeah, sure. I was -- I listened to King Oliver and I actually heard King Oliver in person.
Where?
And he came down -- when I heard -- this was after I had joined the big band, you know, the big reputation band, that was T. Holder's Twelve Clouds of Joy
Oh, yeah.
-- who was the former owner of Andy Kirk's Twelve Clouds of Joy.
Right.
And I hired Earl Bostic, myself, you know, I was like -- kind of liked the straw boss --
(Laughter.)
And Earl was in the band when I first heard -- well, we working in Seminole, Oklahoma, when I joined T. Holder's band.
This was in 1930?
That was around 1930. And Claude Williams, fiddler, he was in the band. Now he had been with the original Andy Kirk band, the one -- see, they took the first band and

gave it to Andy Kirk. They gave the band to Andy Kirk. See, T they were playing in Tulsa, he had a big reputation, you know, almost as big as Benny Moten. The only thing, he didn't record. Benny Moten recorded every week then. That's why they were so successful. Had a fella by the name of Eli Oberstein that loved their band and he recorded them all the time. They'd come to Trenton, New Jersey, and get $50.00 a side, a man, for $100.00 a record.
Yeah.
And they made a lot of hits. But Holder unfortunately didn't do any recording, but you want to know the story of how he lost that band?
Well, let's get to that. I want to hear about Oliver first.

Okay. Well, when -- this is after I joined the band. Well, King Oliver, I had listened to King Oliver's records and I would listen to Louie and he didn't move me like Louie. He could play, but this was before he developed pyorrhea and all of that. He could play, but his sound wasn't as fat and he didn't have as much punch and he didn't swing as much as Louie. And -- but of course, when I actually heard him in person, he had a big band, he was working out of an agency out of Shawnee, Oklahoma, and he came down to Oklahoma City -- we were over there playing at a ballroom -- and we went to catch him that night and he -- of course, he was declining, he wasn't playing as much as he had played, because he was sort of sick and he was having trouble with his teeth.

Then when I hear him again maybe three years later, Pres was with him, he was playing tenor with him. So I was with Victoria Spivey, she had a review, she had two million-dollar sellers, records, and she was in the first black picture that was produced by a big white production, you know, like King Vidor, and the picture was "Hallelujah" and it was ----- a pretty girl by the name of Nina Mae McKinney then, you know, she was in the picture and so was Victoria Spivey in the picture. So after she made the picture, she came to Dallas and got this revue, beautiful girls, and we were on a tour and we went to Tulsa, Oklahoma. Now we stayed at a hotel in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The name of the hotel -- it was a small hotel -- that was the best hotel in the world for blacks. He was an oil magnate and we stayed in there. And in the lobby, had a big baby grand in the lobby, and musicians would come in and jam. You know, they'd come in, this one would play hour, a half hour, and they always had some nice music in there.

So we went down there to jam and somebody told me, says, "King Oliver's here, upstairs. They just come in this morning. They got Red Young with them." They called Lester Red then, you know. So I had met Lester before when he played alto and his sister played tenor. So -- but that was back in '20s, back in Frankie Trumbauer time, when I met him, you know,

in my home town, a carnival, they came in on a carnival, like the one I told you Malone used to run over. There was a lot of those carnivals in those days. So anyway, I hadn't seen him since he had switched to tenor, but I'd heard about him, because he had made quite a reputation. So I says, "Well, I'm going to really see if this cat plays like, you know, everybody say." So I went upstairs and I found out what his room number -- he was laying up there with pads, some corn pads, two on this one, two on this one.
(Laughter.)

And it was hot. Didn't have no air conditioning then, you know, windows all up and everything. It was in the morning about 9:30, 10:00 -- we didn't go to bed, we just went ondown there and started jamming. So I says, "Lester, you remember me?" "Oh, yeah, Tate." He didn't call me "Lady Tate" then. I says, "Well, --" He says, "What are you doing here?" and so I told him and I says, "We're jamming downstairs. Would you like to join in?" "Oh, yes." Anytime there was a jam session, man, he was ready, man, and I say in ten minutes, he was dressed and came down there and Gary, I wish you could have heard him then. I never heard anybody play tenor like that in my life.
(Laughter.)
Did he have that tone then?
Smaller than it was. It developed later

because, you know, he didn't make it with Fletcher because of that light tone. He really sounded just a little bit different from an alto. He sounded between an alto and C Melody. But ideas, and he made them.
Swinging that way (inaudible)?

Oh, man, he was swinging like mad. I'll never forget it, I'll never forget the sound. So then everybody just -- could nobody play. We just stopped and just -- and he says, "Look, somebody else play something." Says, "Man, what can we play?"
(Laughter.)
All those saxophone players started putting their horns in the bag.
(Laughter.)
So they said, "Tate, you went and got him." They said, "You play something."
(Laughter.)

I said, "There ain't a damn thing I can play." But we, you know, we all listened to this cat. Man, I should never forget it. And he said, "Man, I like the way you play. Come on and play." He says, "I always did like the way you play." So he says, "Come on." So I went and played some more. But I just wanted to tell you how much he -- how well he sounded and how much he really played. He was with King Oliver and that was in '33.
Did you meet Oliver?

Yeah. Yeah, I met him. Oh, sure, I always made my business to introduce myself to these cats, man. Other people would want to and a lot of times they'd be a little shy, you know. Man, I'd go up and meet him. Sure, I met him and talked to him. I asked him about -- he knew Holder. He knew T. Holder. And Holder was -- would be about his age, see.
How did you feel about him? How did the musicians and all you guys feel about somebody like Oliver? Was he highly respected or was he --
Oh, yes.
-- (inaudible) or --
Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no. He was highly respected. I just didn't like him as good as I did Louie.
Yeah.

But everybody else -- he was kicking their behinds, you know, and everything else. But to me, he just didn't swing as much as Louie. You understand what I mean? Louie was -- Louie started -- actually, I think Louie started swinging. Louie started (HUMMING), you know, that kind of stuff, and like it's hard to explain, but King Oliver didn't gut like Louie. He just didn't swing as much as Louie.
Did you used to think of -- at this
point, did people think of musicians in terms of New Orleans style or Southwest style, Chicago?
I really didn't.
Yeah.

I really didn't. You know, I didn't think about -- well, you know, after they started talking about Midwest and Texas and New Orleans style, but I never did think that it actually all started in New Orleans. Maybe it's because when I came up, there were so many good players in Dallas.
Uh-huh.

There were good -- there were at least about four or five big bands, but good players that never got -- never left. They wouldn't leave, they just stayed right around in Dallas and played like territory bands and things like that. Then there were a lot of musicians that came up from New Orleans to be in Dallas that couldn't carry these cats' instruments and things. But I hadn't gone to New Orleans. Now, New Orleans really did have a little different style. They played more Dixieland than the cats like in Texas. The cats in Texas swung more, you know what I mean?
Did the guys in Texas play that polyphonic thing where you had the clarinet and the trombone and the trumpet, all playing lines at the same time?
Well, --
Or was it more arranged?
It was more arranged.
Yeah.
See, they played more arrangements. The bands like I heard in Texas, they were more organized like arrangements are and they'd give guys plenty of room to stretch out to take solos.
Uh-huh.

Then they'd all come back for a great ensemble all together. Now, Dixieland, I would say the New Orleans topped them on Dixieland. But for swing and more organized bands like Blue Devils and Basie and all those kind of bands, you know, I mean like Basie played with Blue Devils and Bennie Moten and T. Holder and bands like -- New Orleans didn't have those kind of bands.
What about the Morton Red Hot Peppers? Were you aware of those?
Jelly Roll Morton? No, I didn't. Listened to his records.
Yeah.

I listened to some of his records. We copied a couple of things from him, too. But actually, I didn't -- he didn't really knock me out like other bands I had really heard, you know, because they went together -- I liked that -- I kind of liked them arrangements and things

these cats was playing, you know what I mean? And the solos, like they took -- didn't impress me that much and even being unarranged, you know, I was less interested. But I'm not putting him down because he, you know, he had some nice things. But I would say the Midwest bands and the Texas bands, I thought, outswung, really, altogether. I thought they were better organized.
Which were the best ones now? Troy Floyd?
Troy was one of the best. Alphonso Trent and Bennie Moten, Blue Devils, Troy.
Was George Lee -- did he have a band?
George Lee had a good band. They had a novelty band, but it was a good band. Very good band. George Lee had nice arrangements. Jesse Stone[?] used to write for him.
Uh-huh.
And they were together.
Yeah.
And he had a good band, but he wasn't -- he didn't swing as much as Bennie.
Uh-huh. Before we get back to the chronology, I wanted -- what was the racial situation like in Sherman?
Then?
Yeah. When you were growing up.
Well, you couldn't go -- you know, like we couldn't integrate, you know, like we couldn't go to places. But they treated us very well.
The black communities and the white communities were very separate.

Yeah, but you know, in my home town, this is what I talk about today. They all, white and black, lived next door to each other. And they still do. Now, maybe I live here and two door -- next door would be a white family and there would be a black family in there. They always did that in Sherman, Texas. Of course, they had a terrible thing happen there. They burned the courthouse down there once because they brought a guy there for safekeeping and they followed him on, you know, from another town. That was a very bad mark for the town. But the town actually was a good town, really, and we always got along all right and I even used to play -- I played with a white band in Sherman right around in 1932 or 3. Not many jobs, but I went on and played some jobs with them, I came on home and I played a couple gigs with them and you know, they wasn't doing things like that then. This was back like in '33. And those guys are still my friends, some of them are lawyers and one's a lawyer -- the leader of the band's a lawyer and he's in Washington and they're all scattered out like that.
So it really wasn't too bad. You just -- you knew
you were segregated and you were used to it. But we had our own things, you know. We would own theaters, own ballrooms.
How was the schooling? Did all that touring interfere with your --

The schooling? We had the schools. I went to Fred Douglass High. That was one of our black leaders, you know, a slave. And Booker T. Washington. Now that was Booker Pitman's grandfather, who was a great saxophone player at one time. I used to play with him. He died in South America. He came up -- he left here around 1931 and went to Europe and he didn't come back until '62. Jack Paar brought him back, he and his daughter, during the time they played "Girl from Ipanema." But that was Booker T. Washington's grandson. So I played with him, Budd and I. Bud played with him -- he and Budd were raised together because --
Budd?
Budd Johnson.
Budd Johnson.

They were raised together because Budd lived in Dallas all the time. I used to go to Dallas and stay with my people and things, but I was really raised in Sherman. So we had schools named after Booker T. Washington, Frederick Douglass and hotels named Booker T. Washington Hotel, Frederick Douglass Hotel, you know, and they were nice schools. They had to be a bit inferior though, because I don't think we
had -- but we had good teachers.
Was your schooling at all interrupted by all that touring with the band?

Yeah, I did. You see, I finished. Then I didn't go to college until maybe after I'd been playing with Holder. You know, I didn't until I got a chance to -- I was playing with Holder. So when they said they'd give me a scholarship in music if I would come down and play with the band. So when I went -- that's when I went, like around 1930 -- after leaving Andy Kirk. See, I joined Andy Kirk and I went -- I says, "I think I'm going to take this up and go back home." So we went there and that's the band that Nat Toles took over, the---all of the band from the school. Nat Toles became the leader of that band and I stayed with that band. That was the band we had --
What school was this?
That was Wylie College in Marshall, Texas. So I just went there and studied music and I got a anything else I want to break, you know, anything else. That's the only --/study I could.
Before you went to college though, you were playing with Troy Floyd, 1930.
Yeah, uh-huh.
And you're 15 and then you went to T. Holder's Clouds of Joy.
Uh-huh.
And so tell me about how you got to T. Holder's (inaudible).
Well, T. Holder -- I went to T. Holder before Troy Floyd, actually.
Oh, okay.
And actually, that was the first big band. So, well, see, after T. Holder lost this -- after they gave this band to Andy Kirk, --
How did that happen?

Well, T. Holder -- they were playing in Tulsa, Oklahoma and I understand -- I know -- see, he married a girl from my home town, from Denison, Texas, which is -- we call it the same thing. It's just a few miles different. A very beautiful lady and she had a beauty parlor in Dallas, so when they were working in Tulsa -- and I understand that T. had called home like about four or five nights and nothing, could never reach her, you know, was -- like all night long, he'd call home and she wouldn't be there. So he -- on pay night, he took the whole payroll and just jumped in his Buick and drove from Tulsa down to Dallas. So the next day, they wake up and he's gone. So they -- everybody gets nervous, all the musicians get nervous, say, 'Well, man, this cat has run off with all the money,' you know what I mean? A lot of people were doing that and the promoters were doing that in

those days. So they figured he had run off with all the money. He didn't say anything. So he didn't come back until -- he stayed a whole day. So that day, they got together and they says, "Well, we'll make Andy Kirk the leader." He was playing sousaphone in the band. So Andy told me this himself. "They gave me this man's band." So when he comes back the next evening, he called a meeting, says, "Fellas, I'm sorry," he says, "but I was having a little family trouble." He says, "But everything's all right and I got the money. I'm ready to pay you. I'm sorry I ran away with your money." And he said he never felt so badly in his life. So here they done got together and fired the man and they says, "Well, T., we didn't know. We jumped the gun too quick. We acted too quick and we've given the band to Andy Kirk." He says, "But --" They says, "But we'd like you to stay on and be a," you know, "trumpet player." So he says, "No," says, "if that's the way you feel," he says, "it's quite all right." And he left, paid them, gave them the money, left and got in his car and came back to Dallas.
Now he organized another band in two weeks that was -- topped that band. He was a builder.
(Laughter.)
Now I wasn't in that band.
Yeah.
Budd was in that band. And Eddie Durham,

Eddie Tompkins, who later played with Jimmie Lunceford, Jess_e Stone[?]-- oh, had a fantastic band. I heard them, you know, but they didn't last long. He came to Kansas City and they all went but Jess Stone. So then he come back for the third time and that was the band I was in. I was in the --
He never made it really. Holder.
No, he never really made it and he was a fine trumpet player. He could play first, solo, beautiful sound, pretty and he had everything.
When did he die?
He's not dead. I just thought he was dead. You know, actually, I had heard he's dead, but my cousin came down from Muskogee to my Day .
Yeah?

He says, "Man, Holder's out there in the hospital. They've amputated his leg," say, "but he's kind of senile," says, "but he's out there." Says, "He isn't dead." I says, "Well, man, I'm going to sure write him a letter and go to see him." He'd be about 85, 87 maybe, because he and Andy are around -- you know, Andy's 85 years old.* They're around the same age.
Did he record?
Unfortunately.
Why do you think that was?
I don't know. Never did -- nobody just

never recorded him. Should have, because he's had the bands. And so I stayed with his band. We were in -- we were working in Seminole and there was a ballroom in Tulsa that we used to work like two months at a time and we'd go to Oklahoma City and work another place for a Mr. Steinberg, work two months and the name of that one, one in Tulsa, was Casa Loma Ballroom, beautiful ballroom, and the one in Tulsa was -- I mean in Oklahoma City was Spring Lake. That's where we were working when I caught King Oliver.

Anyway, but then we'd go down to Seminole -- that's between Oklahoma City and Tulsa -- a lot of money, nothing but money, oil and hustlers and everything and money. Everybody spending plenty of money. We made $75.00 a week for three days in 1930. That was a lot of money. So we got a saxophone player that loved Frankie Trumbauer, looked like Frankie Trumbauer, very light skin, looked like Frankie Trumbauer, but he was so -- could play, pretty sound and everything, and we had a lot of hard reed choruses in those days. And we'd get right in the middle of the reed chorus and he's the leader, he just might take his horn down and put it in the stand and started polishing his nails.
(Laughter.)
Who was this?
I hate to call his name, because he's still playing, you know? He lives out in California (inaudible).

And anyway, he's still alive, you know. But he was weird. So we kept saying, "We got to get a saxophone player." We didn't have but three saxophone players. So we said, "We got to find us a good first saxophone player. We got to have one because this man, you know, he lets us down." And so we go to Tulsa to play a one-nighter in the same place Louis Armstrong played when I met him. I'll tell you how that happened.

So when I get in town, I see some of the musicians. I'm on the street early in the afternoon and you know, I go to a small hotel, a lot of musicians the same hotel -- I told you about later on that I heard Lester -- and I asked a friend of mine, I says, "Look, we need an alto player." I says, "Do you know anybody -- have you got anybody that can make the band, you think?" He says, "No," he says, "everybody that can play got a job." So he says, "Oh, wait a minute." He says, "A kid up the street," says, "man, this cat makes snakes. He's all over his horn." So he says, "And by the way, he's playing this afternoon from one to four. Why don't you go up?" I says, "I will." Told me where it was and I went up. Sure enough, he was sweating and people was running, jumping all over the floor and he was playing fast and making impossible things on this saxophone. You know how Bostic plays, you know.
So I introduced myself when he took his intermission.

He says, "I know you." So he says, "That's a good band you all are playing with." I says, "Well, we want you in it." I says, "That's why I'm up here." So he says, "Well, I never played with a big band before," he says, "I don't know if I can make it." I says, "You can make it. You don't worry about that. I'll guarantee, you can make it."

So I says, "Well, why don't you come on down tonight." He says, "I know you're playing down to the Dreamland Dixie Ballroom." I says, "Yeah." I says, "Well, why don't you come on down?" He says, "Well, I'll do that." I says, "Come down and meet the fellas, anyway." So he says, "Okay." So we were playing and he was there. I looked out and I spied him out in the crowd. He wasn't dancing, he just standing and listening. So I told all the cats, I said, "That's the cat." I said, "That's the cat." I said, "Man," I says, "when we take intermission," I says, "let's everybody go and talk to him because man, he's a bitch ." I said, "He can really play."

So they says, "Okay." So sure enough, we played one of those hard things, you know, where we needed all the reed chorus for the saxophone and right in the middle of it, this saxophone player takes his horn down that particular night and puts it in the stand and started shining his nails.
(Laughter.)
So now, here's the tenor playing harmony and the

third alto player's playing and we got no lead. We only got three saxophones. So when we get off, I go off and meet him and he says, "God, that band sure sounds good." He says, -- Then I says, "Well, all the cats are coming." Everybody come on and I introduced all the cats and everything to him. So they says, "Look, why don't you come and go with us down to Seminole." He says, "Oh, no, I don't think I want to leave home." He says, "I got to stay with my mother, stay with my father." So we says, "Well, man --" He says, "But you all do need a saxophone player."
(Laughter.)
He says, "You need an alto player," he says, "you really need one."
Did anybody ask this guy why he wasn't playing the parts?
We'd always talk to him and give him hell about doing it, but he says, "Oh, man, I forgot."
Uh-huh.

They'd say, "Well, man, he was like --" "How do you forget a reed chorus, man? You're leading us." And so he would do it. He'd say, "Well, I won't do it anymore." And he'd do it again. He might do it anytime, Gary. So you never know when he's going to do it. So he wanted to go to California, anyway he wanted to move to California, and when we told Earl Bostic, he says, -- we said, "Well, man, why don't you come

with us?" says, "75 dollars a week." He says, "How much?" So we says, "75 a week." He says, "I'll go." (Laughter.) Shit, he went home and he didn't have nothing but a toothbrush and maybe a couple shirts and things. He went on and carried them on down there. So now, after we go down there the next day, we all get together, we says, "Wonder can this cat read." So now we're wondering because there's a lot of cats in those days that couldn't read at all. And we said, "Wonder can this cat read." So we says, "Well, we got to find out because we done hired him now." So we just playing light things that night in the ballroom. So King Oliver had arrangements, big sheets called "Muleface Blues" and another tune called "Louisiana Bo-Bo." And it was hard, it was very hard. Now, the way we got it, the reed section would go in the corner and we rehearsed for about an hour and the brass would go in the corner and they would rehearse, rhythm section. So then we say, "Let's see if we can put it together." (Laughter.) That's the way we did it. Hell, it took us a long time to learn that tune, man. And we couldn't play it but so fast then because it was tricky, you know. So we says, -- after we skate along -- his solos was fantastic. He was knocking everybody out in the ballroom.

People standing in front of him, listening to him and all this, you know. But he had that funny sound. He always had a bad tone, that nanny in his sound. It was much worse then than it was when he passed.

So we say, -- we didn't call it "Louisiana Bo-Bo," called that. we called it by the number, the director. So now we're going to see. This separates the men from the boys. He didn't even look at it. So we says, -- the third player reached over and said, "You better let me scuffle with this," he said, "because this got a lot of teeth in it." He says, "Am I to play it later?" So he says, "Yeah." He said, "Well, let me play it now. I might as well F it up now. If I'm going to play it, I might as well learn it."
Uh-huh.

So everybody says this cat must be crazy -- you know, everybody's all ears, you know. So he says, the director says, "Look at it and see what tempo you want it." He says, "Start it off where you been playing it," says, "that's okay." He says, "I'm learning it. I'm learning it." He just still talkin', says, "I'm learning it." So he said, "No, you stomp it off." (inaudible) That's where we made our mistake. Boy, that stomped that thing off and nobody got out of the introduction.
(Laughter.)
Bostic stomped it?
(Unintelligible). Shit, he ran through
it like (unintelligible). He didn't even look at it. Honest to God, man, he played all of that stuff. We couldn't -- he played it up here and we played it like --
(Laughter.)
That's what we did. Nobody got out the introduction, the drummer, when he finished, wasn't nobody playing but he and the drummer and he was like this. He was so damn tired.
(Laughter.)
We let him alone after that. That was the honest to God's truth. Then he wrote arrangements the next day and we couldn't play that.
Bostic must have been pretty young, too.

He was young, yeah, he was around my age. He was aroung -- yeah, he and I about the same age. But boy, he was a virtuoso on that horn, man, I mean -- and actually, what he made it big on wasn't really his style. He was in Bird vein, he played like Bird. But a lot of people didn't know that and you know, he just played like 'Flamingo'-type things and that's what they wanted to hear and that's where he made his gold. Lockjaw * told me about a -- he tells me -- well, Lockjaw was hip to him. You think you --
I'll turn it over.
Okay. I got to tell you this.
Okay.
* Tenor saxophonist Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis.
(End of Side One.)
Now, if I get nasty in here, you take that out, you know, because sometime I --
Well, this just goes into their archive. No one's going to hear this or see this besides (inaudible).
(Inaudible).
Oh, that's fine.
So -- am I on?
Yeah.

Lockjaw said one night, he and Bostick were playing a club up in the Bronx, the 8:45 Club. Well, I'm hip to him, I know how much he played. I been knowing all the time how much he played and he said Bird came in, brought his horn and he's got his name now, he's big. So he come in because Bostic was playing like the Bird style. He hadn't made the records and things like that, so Bird said, 'Let me go up and straighten this cat out and let him know who the boss is, you know?' He said Bird got his horn, boy, and Bostick started triple-tongueing on that -- he could triple-tongue. Started triple-tongueing and playing octaves and things and Jaws said, 'Buddy, he ran Bird crazy.' He says -- and Bird says -- he got off the stand, put his horn up and said -- he said, 'I really felt sorry for him because so many people saw him get his ass cut, you know, like from Bostick.' And play-
ing his thing, you know. And says, -- Lockjaw says, "I didn't have but $2.00, so I just went over to him, says, 'Come on, you can have all this because you need it worse than I do.'"
(Laughter.)
Said, "I gave him my last $2.00" He said, "Let me buy you a drink, man, because I know how you feel."
(Laughter.)

I said, "Man, I didn't know you was hip to him." He says, "Who?" He says, "I don't know anybody else." I says, "Well, man, I hired him." I says, "You know I know." I says, "I've known since 1930 how" -- he's really a virtuoso on that horn, you know." He could do anything. So we had him in that band, in the Holder band, and Claude Williams was in that band. It was a good band, but we never recorded and it was really a shame.
Then after that band broke up -- see, I worked with Troy for a short while -- they broke up, too.
Troy Floyd.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Alfonso Trent, all of them broke up at the same time.
Why?
Times were getting kind of hard with bands even then and really, I don't -- they weren't that hard

though. I don't really see why -- then Bennie Moten was scuffling because -- as big as he was namewise. That's when Basie took his band over, you see? Coleman Hawkins was -- had been hired from Jack Hilton to come to London to join his band. So, well, Fletcher's looking for some saxophone players to join his band. So in Kansas City, they had a cutting --play--- one night. I was in Little Rock. Ben, Herschel and Lester. After Fletcher finished the dance that night, they were playing the Cherry Blossom, they got Hawk down there and Fletcher came, he wanted to listen to all three of them to see which one he wanted, you know.
This is in Kansas City?
Kansas City.
Okay.
And Hawk's on his notice.
Right.
