He's going to leave and go to London. And so they get him down there that night and they tell me all three of them wiped him away. I didn't hear it, you know. They said he couldn't get straight, said he drank a quart of whiskey, right on the bandstand, trying to -- said he just -- reeds didn't work right. Just wasn't his night.
(Laughter.)
And they says all of them washed him away and says Prez washed everybody away with "Ideas" and things.

So Smack -- we called Fletcher "Smack" -- Smack chose Lester over Ben or Herschel and so when Basie, maybe about a couple of weeks later, Basie brings the Bennie Moten band to Little Rock. So I was in Little Rock and working with Ethel May's band, a woman band, you know. So --
Was she a singer?
Singer. And she had a band.
And this is 193~?

That was '33. '33. So right after -- because this was right after that Victoria Spivey thing, it's just a few months after Lester, you know, was with King Oliver. He had gone, left King Oliver and joined Basie and come down there. He had left King Oliver and joined Bennie Moten, really. Bennie Moten and George Lee merged, they had a little band together. So Lester played with them.

So Herschel said, "Well, I'm not going to follow Basie everywhere because hell, nobody don't know nothing about him." So he stayed there with Bennie Moten and he and Lester swapped jobs. So when Lester come down there, he was leaving to join Fletcher in Detroit. So they needed a tenor. So when I joined Basie's band, I replaced him then. And he didn't want to go, Gary. He didn't. He says, "Tate, I don't know." He says, "Man, in New York, they got so many cliques." He says, "I can read the charts," he says, "I'm not afraid of that." He says, "But it's more to it than that in New York, they say."

I says, "Well, he chose you. He must know who he wants." I said, "He didn't take Ben, he didn't take Herschel, so he must know who he wants." So he says, "Yeah, but --" I says, "And besides, you can always come back." So he says, "That's the part. That's the hurting part." He says, "The hurting part is to go and don't make it and come back and face the fellas when you don't make it," he says. "That's the part I'm afraid of."
(Laughter.)

So I says, "Oh, go ahead. What the hell." So I'll never forget, he left. Wasn't even drinking then. Didn't even take -- I was then. I was drinking corn whiskey out of fruit jars. I said, "Come on." He wouldn't drink. He didn't drink, smoke. He didn't do anything. He never did really smoke. So he took the job and sure enough, he said they treated him terrible-like in the band. They turned their backs to him, you know, like this and he was on the end. They wouldn't tell him the tunes. They didn't like his sound because Hawk had that big sound and his sound hadn't really developed to, you know, as it later became. And the reed section, they were pretty mean to him.
The fact that Fletcher chose him didn't carry any weight.
Didn't carry any weight. So Hilton Jefferson, God bless him, he said, "Buddy, I can't lie." He

says, "I was in the band and I was one of them." He says, "I treated him terrible, too." And he said, "Some of the notes would look like it would be G natural because Hawk wasted whiskey on him," he said, "he knew all the arrangements," and he didn't have to read them, you know, and he'd waste whiskey on him and the boy would think it was a G and it would be a B or something. So then he says, "He just had a hard time in here," said, "we really treated him cool."

So -- let me tell you -- Jeff said, "One day, Fletcher called all of us together but Lester and says, 'I want you to sit down, fellas, I want to tell you something.' He says, 'I tell you why I called you in,' he says, 'I'm going to fire this boy,' he says, 'because of you. Actually I don't want to. But I'm going to fire him because of you, because he'll never be able to play nothing in here and he'll never have any peace in here. He won't be happy.'"

And the same time, he says, "But before he go --" Fletcher was sort of friendly like Prez, you know, talking-wise, you know. He wasn't a faggot, but he -- sort of refined, you know. He says, "But before he go, I want to tell all three of you something. He can outplay you, you, you and you."
(Laughter.)
Jeff said he told us (unintelligible) and says, "One of these days," he says, "you're going to hear about him."

And sure enough, Jeff said, "Buddy, I lived to see it," he said, "but I'll never forget it." And Fletcher told me in later years, he said -- we talked about it and this is after I joined Basie. He said, "Buddy, I sure hate to do that, but he never could have had any -- he never would have been comfortable there." He said, "But I heard what he was doing," he said, "you know, he wrote all those arrangements and things," said, "I knew he could play." And he says, "He came to me and says, 'Mr. Henderson,' he says, 'thanks for giving me a chance.' He says, 'All I ask of you, would you please give me a nice recommendation?'" And he said, "That's all he asked me for."
(Laughter.)

He says, "I sure will." So he says -- you know, he always dug Prez, man. And Prez told me, he says, "Buddy," -- this is like after I joined the band -- he says, "I stayed with him." Fletcher had a nice house on 139th Street. And he says, -- Fletcher's wife would take him downstairs and put on Hawk's records. He says, "Listen to this." Says, "This is what's happening, baby." Of course, they didn't use that saying then, but, "This is the way you're supposed to sound." He said, "Can't you sound like that?" And he says, "Of course, I had to be refined. I couldn't call her the bitch as I wanted to call her."
(Laughter.)
He says, "You know, she was an ex-circus trumpet-playing bitch." You know who she was? She had been married to Fletcher's trumpet player first, to Russell.
Oh, Russell Smith?

Russell Smith. So when -- so he married Russell's wife, see? So then Russell had taught her to play trumpet, so she was a little trumpet player. Said, "I hated that bitch." Said, "She taken me downstairs every morning and put that -- you know. And I'm staying in her house," said, "I had to play my little banjo."
(Laughter.)

So they sent him back, see. And then they sent out in Kansas City and they got Ben, you know, to come. So now, all the band is breaking up and they're going back to Bennie Moten except -- well, I wasn't with Bennie Moten. But Basie was the last one to leave. So Nat Tolley is working for this man in Dallas, a gangster that owned half of Dallas -- nothing but money. Nat called me. He says, "I understand the band is breaking up." I said, "Yeah, it is." He says, "Well, who can I get out of it?" I says, "Well, I might be able to get Buster Smith," I says, "that's the main one because he's done all the writing." I said, "Buster said he didn't want to go back to Kansas City now." Buster's a -- he don't care about glory, you know. That's why nobody know about him. I says, "And I probably can get Bubble-eye." Bubble-eye was Joe Keyes.
Uh-huh.

He was a hell of a first trumpet player, Gary. He started the nanny. You know, like Basie did? I think that's Joe.

So I say, "I think I can get these two Texans." So I says, "You might have to have some money, bring them some money." He said, "Well, that's no --" he said, "Any amount they want." He said, "I can bring that." I said, "Well, you can get them. If you got some money, I know you can get them." So I just told them, I says, "Look, --" Buster said, "I don't want to go back to Bennie Moten." Lester had slipped off and Rush had gone back and I think Joe Jones had gone. No, Joe hadn't gone. Joe was one of the last. He and Basie were the last to go. The same, you know, all the guys you know, you know, Dan Minor and Lips Page was in the band, Joe Keyes and all them kind of cats. So, well, I went on to Dallas -- I went to talked to Buster. I said, "Buster, how would you like to join Nat Toles and go and write some arrangements for him?" He said, "I'd love that," said, "because I want to stay at home for a while anyway." I says, -- He says, "I may go back to Kansas City," he said, "but things are rough in Kansas City and Bennie ain't doing nothing." He said, "I'll be --" I says, "Well, you can be working in Dallas because this cat owns half of Dallas and he got clubs all over Dallas." He's a gangster.

So he says, "Well, could I get some money?" I said, "Yeah, how much you want?" He said, "I don't need but $50.00." I said, "Shit, I'll get you a hundred." So when I went and told Joe, Joe said, "Give me 25. That's all I need." Joe....
(Laughter.)

I says, "No, I'm going to get you a yard." He said, "Are you kidding?" I said, "I'll get you a yard," I said, "just be ready and I'll call Nat." I called Nat and he come over there and got us and we went back and Buster wrote that -- wrote a hell of a lot of arrangements. Man, you should have heard that band.

So he finally -- but he finally left and went on back to Bennie Moten and about time they got back -- and Basie was the last one to leave. He went on back to Bennie Moten, too, you know. Bennie started getting some jobs. They went into a club called the Harlem Club in Kansas City.

So then after that, Andy needs a tenor player. So Basie said, "Well, I got the man for you." He said, "He just left my band." So then Andy Kirk sent me a telegram to come join Twelve Clouds of Joy because Ben had gone.
You know --
That's '33, still latter part of '33. So you know, I didn't want to go because I'm having too much fun

and I'm making money, you know, at home and so I walked around with that ticket, I guess about six weeks-- send me a ticket and I wouldn't go. So he kept calling and asking me to come, asking me to come. So I says, "Well, maybe I will go." So that's when I went and joined. That's when I went and joined Andy Kirk. By that time, all the guys was back with Bennie Moten and Herschel was with Bennie Moten and I was with Andy Kirk. He and I had an apartment together. We just -- you know, we were together all the time then.
So, you know, Andy Kirk got his break before Basie.
No.

Yeah, you see, we came to New York with Mamie Smith. She came down -- she was married to a Jewish fella by the name of Bert Goldberg and they came down and got us and we played some theaters and Tim and Freddie -- Timmie Rogers and Freddie was together. We played theaters with her. She was on her -- she was declining, too. She had been a big thing. She was the first blues singer, black blues singer, they had, you know. They called them race records then, you know.

So she brought the whole band to New York. We came to New York with her and we ended up in Buffalo at a place called the Vendome and you know, the bottom started falling out of the band. So when we got back to Cincinnati, it was five bands in the hotel, Delton Syncopaters, Speed Webb -- I

don't know if Roy was with them or not. I can't remember. Zack White, that was one of the Midwest name bands. We were all at the hotel and the band broke up and that's when I left to go back to -- I had this chance to go back -- this was around '35 -- to come back, they wanted me to come down to Wylie and be with the Wylie Collegians.

So I called my mother and told her I thought I would leave the band, you know. So I went back there and joined that band and that's where I stayed until Nat Toles took the band over in the latter part of '35, maybe early '36.
So did you graduate?
From -- no, no. No, I just went that year, you know. No, I didn't. I was interested in --
Playing.
-- playing, you know. I didn't have time enough. I regret it, but --
(Laughter.)
I didn't. And anyway, we had a hell of a band. Nat Toles had a fantastic band. We had Charlie Christian, Sir Charles Thompson, Henry Coker Fred Beckett who died very young.
Yeah.
Beautiful trombone player.
Played with Harlan Leonard.
Harlan Leonard. And he later joined
Lionel Hampton and he died here in New York with tuberculosis, same as Charlie Christian.
How did Sir Charles get knighted?
I think he gave himself that name.
(Laughter.)
He said, 'There's a Count Basie and there's a --'
Duke Ellington.
'There's a Duke Ellington.'
(Laughter.)

I think he took that. Really, I don't know. But we called him -- did we call him Sir Charles then? I think we did. It must have come out of Nat Toles' band. And of course, I stayed with that band until I joined Basie in '39 and that's -- that was from Omaha, Nebraska. We had a better band at the time. You know, I've been -- this was miswritten one time. I said one time that when Basie took -- when Basie was -- John Hammond took Basie, bandwise, we were -- we had a better band.
With Nat Toles?

Nate Toles. Because we were together and he had like six pieces when John Hammond heard them coming from the Reno Club and things. But he quickly got his band together. But it was said that I said the Nat Toles band was better all throughout than Basie's band, which they weren't. You know, I didn't mean that. But we had a hell of a band.

So I -- oh, I'm a little ahead of my story. While I'm in Wylie, Andy Kirk's band, they hoboed back to Kansas City and Dick Wilson, who was a fine tenor saxaphone player, he's a stylist, actually, and he was with Zack White. But Andy called me, he sent three telegrams and says, "Look, we're going to record. The band's back together and I think we're going to make it." He says, "A guy coming down from Decca is going to record us and I want you to be on it."

So by this time, Gary, I didn't want to go through no more hard times. I was having a nice time there, you know. I just didn't go and I didn't regret it because later, I ended up with Basie, you know. But sure enough, they recorded "Until the Real Thing Comes Along." That was their big song, you know, with --
That was their first record?

That was their first record. That was the one that -- no, they had made a record before then, but actually, it didn't make any noise, you know. They made a record in -- record date in the band like maybe two years before. But "Real Thing Came Along," -- we didn't call it that. We called it "The Slave Song." But you couldn't -- the fella said, "No, I can't put this on a record." You know how they were then about titles and lyrics and things. So he says, "No, I actually can't put this on a record." So sure enough, it wasn't no time before they sold a million. And I said to
myself, I says, "Buddy Tate, you're always at the wrong place."
(Laughter.)

"You always miss the boat." But I was happy out there with Nat Toles and they used to come back out there and Andy knew what kind of band we had with Nat Toles' band. So they came back that summer to play Kansas City and we were playing near Kansas City, about 90 miles at a town, Trenton, New Jersey, with the band. So Andy called me down in Trenton, he says, "Look, there's a fella coming down and this cat's got a lot of money and he's got a lot of power and actually, he's looking for a good band." He says, "I know if he hears you all band, you'll be in." So he says, "See if you can get that band down here." So Nat and I went to the cat and he says, "No, no, no," he wouldn't let us off. So Nat and I got in the car and drove down there and that night, that's where I met John Hammond. He was out there at Fairland Park where Andy Kirk was and Andy had made it big, see, and Basie was down to Reno, scuffling with six pieces, he and Buster Smith and I think, Jack Washington, Carl Smith and Joe Jones. That was all Lips had left, see. Lips had a little band. That was all he had.
But John Hammond and Bennie liked what they heard, you know? They had heard it from the Congress Hotel, Bennie was in the Congress and they liked what they heard. So --
(Inaudible).
Uh-huh. So John just went out there. But if John would have heard our band, Gary, we would have made it. Nat Tōles' band would have made it. That's just -- the wrong thing, and you --
Had you told Hammond about the Nat Tōles -- when you drove up there?

Oh, yeah, we told him about it. We says, 'Can we take you --' We wanted to take him down to -- the next night, we wanted to take ---carry him down to Trenton, New Jersey, where we were playing, but Gatt . . . wouldn't let us off. And he says, 'I can't. I got to be at Bennie's opening tomorrow at the Palomar.' Bennie was opening at the Palomar in Los Angeles. He says, 'I got to be there.' So that night, he went down there and he signed Basie up. So we missed the boat, see, because we had -- our band was in Trenton and he didn't get -- never got a chance to hear it and when he did hear the band -- I'd gone, Sir Charles had gone, Henry Coker had gone and the band wasn't really up to par when he really did hear the band and there's another band that didn't record anything.
Was Andy Kirk's band highly regarded? The musicians?
Were they --
Highly regarded? Considered a swinging--
Yeah, yeah. But, you know, --
Despite the Pha Terrell vocal or-----

Yeah, it was more of a sweet, smooth band. Actually, it wasn't a band like the Bennie Moten band or the Basie band, but very, very clean and recorded very well because they were light and they recorded perfectly. I mean, they were beautiful for recording. And Pha was a beautiful singer and that's what really made them. Everything they did with Pha singing was a hit.
Wasn't Andy at one time associated with the same school as Whiteman in Denver?

Yeah, out in -- yeah, with Paul out in Denver. He's from Denver. Yeah, yeah, that's right. He was a -- seemed like -- I think now that he took lessons from Paul's father or something, but they were associated. They were very close together. He's from Denver. That's true.

So, you know, it didn't never worry me because I always felt that -- you know, I don't ever blame myself for something I don't know, you know. Hell, I didn't know. I went the way I felt, you know, I wasn't ready to leave then. I wanted to stay out there and I ended up -- I'm glad the way it did, because I ended up with Basie, who I would much rather prefer to be with than Andy. I loved Andy and all the guys --
Were you aware of Benny Goodman then?
Yeah, yeah, I listened to -- sure, then I was listening to Benny. We was playing some of Benny's stuff.
They would come -- you know, they'd come out on stocks and we were -- Sir Charles was writing some things.
What kind?
What was that thing? What was that thing? "Don't Be That Way." (HUMMING.)
Yeah.
And they made a thing called "Jam --" some kind of jam. Vito (Musso) did a hell of a solo on that thing. Krupa did it. And we had that arrangement.
Did you have any idea, thoughts, about why Benny's band made it so big playing some of the music that Fletcher and Chick Webb had done and they didn't make it?
Yeah, well, you know, actually, it was really hard for -- to get the recognition then that -- blacks kind of, people -- they'd dig it, but, you know, it's just -- it was really hard, you know?
Do you think it was strictly a racial thing?
I really do.
Yeah.

I really do. Because Fletcher had a fantastic band then. I mean, shit, I mean, he had Louie and all them at one time, Hawk and all of them. And I actually, I have to think so, because then I understand he didn't -- he wasn't really a good businessman himself. I don't know. I

understand he -- there's a lot of things maybe he could have been bigger had he been a better businessman, from what I heard. I don't know. But I know that's one of the things. It was just hard to get through.
Did you like the way Benny's band played then?

Yeah, I loved his band. Yeah, he has good players. I dug his band, yeah. I always did. And you know, I went to hear them one night in Omaha while I was with Nat. I -- Toles' band was out of town. I had been sick. I got up out of my sick bed and went and got me a taxi and went down there. It was cold in Omaha, Nebraska, and the doctor -- you know, I had a light touch of pneumonia, but I got up, because they played there with Krupa, Hamp, Vido, you know, his regular band. And I got up, man, and got me a taxi, man, and went down there and I went on the bandstand and met all the cats, you know. I told them that -- I told them the story, I said, 'Man, I just got out of my bed to come down and hear you cats.' They said, 'Well, we'll get you a taxi. You don't have to be outside, standing waiting,' and they did, you know, they got me a taxi and I jumped right in a hot taxi, went right on home. It didn't hurt me.
(Laughter.)
That must have been about 1930 -- I think that wasn't long before I joined Basie. Yeah, I think that was in '39 then
or late '38. It wasn't long after that I joined -- then Herschel died then.
Then how long were you with Holder?
Not Holder, Nat Toles.
Let me see. About three or four years.
Actually, let me see. Yeah, from about '35 to '39. From '36 to '39.
So you went straight from --
From Nat to Basie.
How did that come about?
Well, --
Before we get into that, what kind of places did you work with --

With Nat? Oh, well, you know, out West, there are beautiful ballrooms. They still have some of those beautiful ballrooms out there, some of the prettiest ballrooms you've ever seen in your life, Gary. And we were booked. We begged for layoffs. We had one agent had on -- he had two bands, Lawrence Welk and our band. Lawrence Welk played the polkas and we played the jazz.
(Laughter.)
And he kept us working all the time. Lawrence remembers that.
Always played "Dancing."

Yeah, always played that. And he was popular out there, you know. And we played all out in Minnesota and Iowa and you know, in Midwest. We'd come as far as Chicago with the Nat W. Toles band and we'd go back to Minnesota and Idaho and Colorado. We played all, you know, like in those places like that. He had that much of a territory and he'd book us all down South and places like that and we actually begged for days to be off and we had a sleeper bus, specially made in Sioux City, Iowa, and they had a -- you know, like the cab part up where the guy drives. It was like these buses, you know, you can turn around like that, and we'd make the seats like this and we had about as much space from here to there to hang the uniforms and our instruments and things. So we'd sit and rode in the bus and everything. It was --
How many pieces in that?
Oh, we had about 15.
And who made the arrangements?
We had five, five arrangers. Oh, we --
Among the players?
Yeah, yeah.
Who were they?
C.Q. Price, he's in Buffalo, Weldon Sneed Sir Charles Thompson, Walter Dunkins and Casey Smith, the guitar player.
And the main soloists?

Me, C.O., Bates -- these are trumpeters -- the two trumpeters -- Bates and Weldon and Sneed and all three of them played solos. Now, the trombone was like Coker, Beckett and we had a trombone player that played on a tricky sound style. He was a hell of a muted, you know, plunger trombone player.
Yeah.
And that was the brass. And Sir Charles. Then, of course, you know Charles Christian. He featured and that was it, you know?
How did he play at that time?
Charlie? He was playing his ass off at that time. Yeah, yeah.
Did he have the same style basically?
Uh-huh, same style.
And nobody else played like that.

Nobody else played like that. He was the first one. He was playing solo and he sounded like saxophone, man. He played all that stuff we played, you know. He -- we'd make something on saxophone, he says, 'Don't be mad if you hear that again,' and we heard it again.
(Laughter.)
Yeah, man, he --
Could he read?
Huh?
Could he read?

Yeah, I believe he did. Yeah, yeah, I think he could read. Yeah. You know, a lot of cats got conscious of reading and everybody wanted to try to read because there were so many cats in the earlier years that didn't read and they blew gigs because they couldn't read, you know, and the first thing them young cats, like the first thing they want to do, they want to try to learn how to read, see? I believe he did read. I think Charlie read. I'm not too sure. But I believe --
What kind of material were you playing, originals or top songs?

A lot of originals, mostly originals. Yeah, we did many or most originals and of course, we played the latest tunes like -- I'll never forget an arrangement Sir Charles made on "You Go To My Head," was one of the prettiest things. You know, songs like that that were popular in that time, you know, and "Once In a While."
Uh-huh.
Had a nice arrangement on that. "The First Time I Saw You." You know, I'll tell you though, I think Nat T'oles' band was closer to -- I would put it like the Jimmy Lunceford style.
Uh-huh. That kind of precision?
Yeah. We had that kind of precision and had a lot of salesmanship, you know. We did a lot of singing, we had sing quartets and we sang beautiful harmony because we
had people to write the harmony for us to sing. The musicians sang?

Uh-huh. And we -- you know, we had singers in the band like -- I think actually it was, you know, more of that type style. It's too bad Nat really didn't make it and neither did Milton Larkin, but there were a lot of bands in those days that didn't really make it, you know what I mean? They made territory bands, but --
How did the band fold?
Nat's band? Well, Nat really didn't fold -- he worked like -- he had moved to California and he worked up until he died with his band. He --
Which was then?
Well, Nat's been dead about eight years, eight or nine years.
He kept the band up all these decades?
Uh-huh, not a big band.
Yeah.
Small, small group.
What did he play?

He was a bass player, but he had given it up to direct and his cousin played bass with us, he was another Blanton, really. He was really ahead of his time, Gary. And he wanted to come to New York so badly until he just really lost his mind because he didn't get to New York and Nat wouldn't

come to New York. We used to beg him to come to New York. We said, 'Man, let's go. Just take a chance.' And he says, 'We'll get some work.' So he used to say, 'No, I'd rather be a big fish in a little pond than be a little fish in a big pond.' That was always what he'd always say to us, you know. And we couldn't get him to come to New York.
So even then, in the early, middle '30s, New York was a kind of --

It was -- well, actually, if you didn't come to New York, musicians used to say, 'You got to come to New York to get the New York stamp.' If you're accepted in New York, you know, and make it, then you make it anywhere in the world. That's what they used to say and all musicians wanted to come to New York to get the stamp to say, 'I come to New York and I was accepted. You know, I went over in New York and they dig me in New York,' you know.
Did the musicians take it that seriously?
Yeah, musicians took it seriously like that.
So, when Lester came back, did people think, 'Well, he didn't make it in New York,'?
Yeah, well, Lester, you know, like when he came back, he didn't come back to Kansas City right then. He went to Minneapolis and worked with a little quartet and
of course, when Basie got the thing, the break, he says, -- see, Basie started the two tenors.
Uh-huh.
He has to be given credit for that because they only had -- bands only had one tenor player in those days. So Basie says, 'Hell, I think I want two.'
Uh-huh.
He said, 'Because both of them's out of sight,' you know?
(Laughter.)
Yeah.

So he says, 'I want two of everything. I want two helluva trumpet players,' and all of them playing different styles, you know? So man, they tell me when they come to New York, -- see, I didn't come to New York with them like when they first come to New York. And they tell me when they first come to New York, cats didn't say -- cats were doing like this. They'd listen to Lester and Herschel, then run it --
(Laughter.)
They was just doing, you know, --
Back and forth.
Back and forth, you know, because see, both of these cats just come in there and just wipe them out, all these tenor players, man. I understand when they played

with Chick Webb up there -- well, Chick didn't have no soloists. He had a good band. Oh, yeah, and I meant to say, now, you know, another thing I meant to mention this a while ago when we talked about styles, but I got too carried away.
But most New York bands played up-tempos, but Bennie Moten and bands like the Western swing, they could play them things in between, which is hard to swing like that (HUMMING), like "Moten Swing."
Uh-huh.

Man, they tell me when they came in, those chorus girls went crazy because they wasn't too fast for them, you know. They said they were doing everything because the tempo was right. They said, "Where did this band come from? We ain't never heard no tempos like this." And that's another thing that made it great for them, you know. Bennie Moten took New York by storm when he came here. That's when he had -- Basie was still in the band and Ben Webster was in the band, Eddie Barefield, people like that, you know, and Eddie Durham, because they came here -- and that's why they called it the Midwestern swing because Bennie Moten would get in them tempos like that and they said all the chorus -- and when they played for the chorus show girls, man, -- and you know, like when they were whirling around they said, "We ain't never danced to no music like -- we ain't never had no tempos like they

were in," and all the bands would play like up in here. So you can't keep that up all night. If you dance one or two times with tempos up in there, you're tired. So they had a variety of tempos and I think that's another thing that had them in, you know.
One band that we haven't mentioned at all, it was Ellington. Now were you conscious of Duke?
Of Duke? Yes, yes, when he called himself the Washingtonians.
Uh-huh.

I read a write-up one time. I didn't know who they were, but I read some comments and -- I got to pull these off -- I read some comments that Paul Whiteman had given to him and I think he gave him a hundred dollars or something and that was in one of the papers. I'll never forget, I can't remember nothing except the Washingtonians, Paul Whiteman said, "Gee, that sound these cats get," and he went somewhere and he gave them a hundred-dollar tip. I don't think at that time he had six or seven pieces, maybe eight pieces or something like that. They didn't call it Duke Ellington, they just said the Washingtonian. And then I -- you know, I would listen to his records and -- but it was different from Fletcher. See, I was more turned on to Fletcher because, you know, I wasn't really realizing what he was doing, like with sounds, and what he was getting from sound. But I

dug it, you know. I mean, I dug -- and I like the way Fletcher wrote because Fletcher used to get brilliant sounds from the clarinets and things. But why he did that, I later on learned, see, he wrote in them hard keys that people don't play in, you know, like he'd write a song in F-sharp, C-sharp.
Who was this?
Fletcher.
Fletcher?
Yeah, and G-sharp. And Hawk and them was playing them solos in this key, in C-sharp and in G-sharp.
(Laughter.)
They'd learn them solos and they was playing in those keys. Nobody could play like that and that's why the band sounds so brilliant and crisp.

Then I'll tell you what Hawk told me one time. He says, -- they were playing down on Broadway and Duke was playing uptown. So, you know, wherever Duke landed, he couldn't -- Fletcher would cut him all to pieces, they tell me, you know, he wasn't popular and things like that. So Fletcher got all the credit, you know. So he said, they were playing, they weren't even listening to anybody, you know, Fletcher got a little chesty, I guess, he said they wouldn't even listen to anybody. He said he'd go home at night and they were broadcasting from the Cotton Club uptown, Duke was, you know, so he says his wife says, 'You ever listen to Duke? They got

something different. You ought to listen to him." He says, "Oh, no, I'm with Fletcher Henderson, man. Nobody like Fletcher Henderson." So he said she kept bugging him and "I had a radio in my car." He said one intermission one night, after so long of her keep bugging him -- they worked anytime they wanted to, you know, down Roseland, you know, on Broadway. So he says one night he went out and he turned the radio on and they was doing something like "Mood Indigo." He says, "I hear this moody trombone and I ain't never heard nothing like that," he said, "in my life." You know, because he says, Smack knew how to voice, but he didn't"-- Duke had come up with something different, you know, like with the clarinet and the muted trumpet and the mutes.

So he says, "Man," he says, "it scared me. It scared me to death. So I went and told Smack. I says, 'Smack, if you get a chance, come sit down in the car with me and listen. Duke got something going.' Smack said, 'Man, I don't want to play uptown. I don't want to hear nothing about it.'" He didn't want to play up in Harlem. "We're on Broadway. I don't want to hear nothing about it." He says, "I think you should listen."
(Laughter.)

He said he couldn't get him to listen. So he said one night, he finally got him to listen and he was surprised, too. Said he was, you know, really excited. So he says, "Wait a minute. What is that he got?" He was trying to see

how he had this voice, but he never did come up with it, you know how Duke had had these things voiced. So Hawk told me that somehow, they lucked up and got this break in that picture with Amos and Andy, "Check and Double Check," he said, "And after that, he wiped us completely out." He said, "He ain't looked back." You know, "Check and Double Check?" He said he was on his way. He told me that himself.
Fletcher said this.
No, Hawk.
Oh, Hawk said that.

Hawk told me, he says, "Buddy," he says, "after that," he says, "man, I started hearing, talking about this Jungle Band, he called his band the jungle music and things like that," he said, "but man, after they made that picture, 'Check and Double Check,'" he say, "we were on our way out."
(Laughter.)

Then he's the one told me Fletcher wasn't a good business manager and they never made time. You know, he hardly ever got his whole band on the bandstand at one time. Now, I understand they played at Atlantic City Steel Pier and it was hard -- see, that hadn't had no black bands in there. So they wanted Fletcher Henderson, the public kept asking, "Why don't you bring Fletcher Henderson in, man?" said, "he got a band." So the guy said he took a chance and sure enough, he'd open at

eight, nine pieces. Hawk would be in New York, get there late. And said the fella told him, said, "Mr. Henderson," he says, "you got a good band," he says, "but that's the worst conduct band I've ever seen." He says, "And I'm going to have to let you go." He says, "But I love you, really." He says, "But people come here, so and so and so and so," he says, "they got follows." Hawk had follows, Jimmy Harrison -- they tell me he was a hell of a trombone player. He had follows. And he said -- Fletcher says, "Yes, sir. You're right. I know you're right. I can't argue with you. Everything you say is right." So Smack told him, says, "But you know, when I do get them on the bandstand, when I'm lucky enough to get them all on the bandstand," he say, "I've got the baddest-ass band in the world. So I'm going to have to stick with them."
(Laughter.)
That's what Smack told him that, you know? But they did that, you know, and they -- Carney told me the same thing, he said they had terrible conduct. He never had his full band.
They must have known that they were holding the band back.
They didn't -- I don't know. Heads, I guess, you know, big heads and they'd come in. Like if he'd open at 9:00, maybe Hawk would come at ten, 10:30. Two or

three others come in, 9:30. That's when he, you know, everybody packing houses and things. He never had a full band. So that hurt. Anywhere, they did it on any job. Now, I was told this. I didn't see it, Gary, because I wasn't -- shit, I was still in Sherman. But I mean, I heard this. That hurt him, too, you know?
How did you get with Basie?
The first time? Well, you know, I replaced Lester, you know, like for the --

Oh, no, in '39, when Herschel died, they knew me. I had a -- actually, I had a better chance than anybody. Ben tried to get the gig, Chu Now they in New York and they're names, you understand what I mean. And -- but they didn't, so I get a telegram from Basie to meet the band in Kansas City and they had another boy with the band, Skippy Williams, who I did like, a very nice person. And they brought him from New York.

So actually, I was on trial. We were all on trial and so I met the band -- I meet the band in, Kansas City and you know who meets me in the lobby? Prez. Everybody's in bed because I get there about 8:00 in the morning, 8:30. So Prez meet me in the lobby of the Booker T. Washington Hotel. He says, "Gee, Tate, it's so nice to see you." I said, "Prez, didn't it's nice to see you, too." That's Lester. We/calle him Prez.

So I says, "Oh, I listen to everything you do." So he says, "Yeah," he says, "well, look like we making it." I says, "You're making it all right." So he says, "I tell you, let's go have breakfast." I says, "Okay." So he says, "You got to excuse the fellas because they were out late last night and we played a dance and this is homecoming." He says, "I just can't sleep." So we go to a place where he used to go in Kansas City. You know, he loved red beans and rice. So he ordered red beans and rice for breakfast --
(Laughter.)

-- for himself. He said, "Give him the same thing." He ordered me some. He was very sensitive. So I says, "Okay." I ate red beans and rice, too. So then he says to me, he says, "Have you been listening? Have you been keeping up on your instrument?" So I says, " Well, I've been trying," and I says, "I've been listening." I says, "Oh, yeah, I listen all the time," and I says, "I've been trying." He says, "Well," he says, "if you playing anyway like you were the last time I heard you," he said, "it will be your engagement." He says, -- then he went on to say, "There's a lot of ladies want the engagement," he said, "Lady Berry," talking about -- I says, "Who is that?" He said, "You know Chu Berry?" I says, "Namewise," I says, "Yeah." "And Ben Webster, Lady Webster." He said, "They're good players," he said, "but they don't fit." So he says, "And if you're
playing like you did the last time I heard you, it'll be your engagement."
What did he mean by that? I mean, Ben was with Moten.
Yeah.
Why did he feel that their styles (inaudible)?

Well, you know, like -- you know, Ben was better for ballads, actually, you know what I mean? When you really get into them swing things, he worked out his solos like with "Cotton Tail" and things like that. That was great. But he didn't feel like he just could stand there and Chu was playing really too many notes, he figured, for him. You know, Herschel didn't play that many notes, you know.
Right. Were you -- did they know at that time that you played Herschel ---style?

Oh, yeah, because they knew -- you see, like they knew I could play Herschel's style because they knew like even in -- that's why I'm saying I had more going for me actually than anybody, you know what, I mean? Because I could play everything Herschel played note for note, sound and everything like him. And we always had done that even when I was playing tenor. I sounded like that. This is the honest to God's truth. And he admired me, too.
Yeah.

And we used to admire each other like that. So to come in and replace him didn't mean nothing for me because I knew I could play every note, every solo he played, note for note, and that's what he wanted. That's what Basie really wanted, you know. He didn't want -- because his records was hot and everything like that. In those days, Gary, those kids was humming those solos, too. You know, those kids would hum those solos with you sitting out in the audience.
Yeah.

I'll tell you later on what happened in Philadelphia. So anyway, that night, I went down and listened to him play the colored dance and I went down and listened to that band. Boy, phew. And something says, "Well, maybe you better go on back to Nat Tole." You know, I says, "Shith --" (Laughter.)
(Laughter.)
Whee, Joe was in good shape then and Joe was terrible when he used to play good, you know what I mean? He used to push that band, boy, right on in. And then, boy, they --
Was Freddie Green with the band then?
Yeah. Freddie, Earl, Jack Washington, Buck, Sweets, Dickie Well, Shad Collins was playing his ass off.
Who was that?
Shad Collins.
Shad Collins.
Yeah, he was --
What kind of player was Washington as a soloist?
Ooh, baritone player, man, he was something. Gerry Mulligan loves him. He said that's who he really loved.
But Basie didn't feature him.
Not enough. Basie was like that. He did more -- of course, when he was with Bennie Moten, Bennie Moten featured him all the time. But Basie never featured him. Now, listen to "Dogging Around," --
Uh-huh.

-- and "Topsy," Basie's "Topsy." Listen, make a special notice to listen to his baritone playing on that. And -- oh, I can think of some more. I can't think of them all now. But those are the things where he had a chance to really stretch out. Oh, man, he's a fantastic baritone. But Basie's a kind of funny guy. He'll feature one man all night, you know, sometimes. Then the next night, he might feature the other guy all night.
Did Jack stay with Basie until the end?
No, Jack -- he went in the Army. Let's see, Jack went in the Army, he was inducted in the Army. Did he come back to the band after that? I believe he came back

to the band after his stint in the Army. Then when did he leave? I'm trying to remember if Jack was with the band when it broke up. See, I stayed with the band until the band really broke up, the first band. And then he had a quartet. Then when he went out and organized again, I couldn't make it. I stayed here in New York. I was getting my 802 card and I was recording like two and three times a day. You know, I didn't know it was so nice here in New York, you know, because I'd been on the road, you know. I'll tell you about that.
So anyway, where were we? Oh, we were talking about when I was joining now, right?
Yeah, Prez was telling you that --

Prez was telling me -- oh, yeah, he was telling me they didn't fit. So he says, "There are a lot of other ladies that don't fit." He says, "But you've got the sound and everything is there. It'll be your engagement if you're playing like you were when I heard you last." So that night, what had happened, I didn't --
Had Lester recommended you to Basie?
Yeah, well, he knew. Yeah, he had recommended me to Basie and Basie still remembered from --
From the last gig.
Yeah, like from -- which is about two and a half years later, maybe three. Let's see, '36. Yeah, about two and a half years later. And they still remembered, you
know, and he knew that I was -- like I was in Kansas City with Andy Kirk when he was with Bennie Moten before Bennie died.
Right.

So they knew about me. As I say, that's why I had more going for me in my favor. So that night, I don't think I played at the colored dance. So the next night, I'm sitting on the bandstand way back, I got my horn in a bag and the place was packed and they were breaking it up. Everything they played was -- people screaming and going on. Then there was a certain crowd of people saying, "Blue and Sentimental." He says, "I can't." "Blue / Sentimental, man." And some of them knew he was dead and then, of course, some of them don't read the papers, you know, they didn't -- hadn't read the DownBeat and things like that.
So he says, --
They didn't necessarily recognize whether Herschel was sitting --

Yeah, yeah. Some of them didn't know and some of them -- you know how a crowd can get sometime. If one starts something, it'll continue. "Blue / Sentimental, and man, Blue / Sentimental." Basie says, "I can't." The featured artist is dead." And you hear some of them say, "Yeah, you know that. He's dead. He just died." So then Basie look up at me. This was before my time to come on because Skip played up to intermission and I played the rest of the half.
Skip?
Skippy Williams.
Uh-huh.

And Basie says, "Hey, Bud, you know 'Blue and Sentimental'? Have you heard --" I say, "I heard it." So he says, "You want to try it?" It was a head arrangement, Gary, wasn't in the reeds, you know. So -- but I'd heard it, you know, I knew it. But I didn't know how well I was going to be able to play it, because I was scared to death, you know, and everybody was -- all eyes was on me, you know. Crowd, band and everything else. So man, he said, "Get your horn out." I'm trembling, trying to get my horn out, you know, shaking like that. I know I was because I'm nervous and I'm scared. And so something just kept saying, " Aw, shit. If you don't make it, go on back to Omaha. Fuck it. Try it. Come on, don't be scared." There's something in back (inaudible).
So I get my horn out and looked like that microphone was a mile and a half from that damn band and I didn't think I was ever going to get down to that thing.
(Laughter.)

(Inaudible) right down with all the people. And he made that intro, you know, like he makes that intro. Man, he made an intro and everything was right that night. My horn, the reed was right, I could play all them bottom and top notes

just so easy and subtones, wasn't no blasting, just, you know. subtone. Man, when I got through playing that damn thing, I think everybody in that hall stood up. I swear to God. And everybody in the band but Prez. Everybody in the band, "Don't look no further, he's the one," Ed Lewis and all them, "You got it, you got it."
(Laughter.)

I swear to God. And all but Prez. So I'm wondering, I said, "I wonder why he don't --" of course, then the next things they was playing "every Tub" and all them kind of -- and I knew all them, you know, I was playing those notes. So they said, "Man, he --" and this boy, God bless him, he was -- actually wanted a gig and I wanted the gig, but he says, "All the best."
Skip?

Yeah. When I'd go out there and I would say -- sincerely, as much as he wanted that gig, he wanted me to have success, too. You know, that was a funny feeling, you know, like when we were both trying out for that job. We both wanted it, you know, in the worst way. But he was sincere when he says, "All the best. Don't be nervous, go ahead, go ahead, don't be nervous." And I would say that to him. And man, of course, I won out, you know. As I said, I had more going for me than he actually did, you know.
So after about 30, 35 minutes later, everybody in

the band stood up but Prez, you know, and that was kind of bugging me. I said, "Maybe he didn't like that, you know. I wonder why." Because he'd been my friend all the time. After everybody was playing and everything, Keye looked behind the reed section and he said, --
Hm.
I said, "Okay, I'm in."
(Laughter.)

And all the way -- you know, like all during the times, he was always nice to me, you know, like he says -- when we got to New York, I had a pocketful of money and I'm standing in Grand Central Station. And I know I looked terrible. I know you could see country all over me. And these guys, they'd been out from New York for a long, long time. Everybody would run and grab cabs. Nobody said anything to me. I didn't know what the Woodside was. I didn't know nothing. That's where everybody stayed then, you know, at the Woodside Hotel. And I didn't know where to go. I looked around and there was nobody there and after a while, I -- Prez was standing over in the corner. He says, -- he called me on over, you know, he says, "You have to forgive the ladies. They haven't seen their madam queens and everybody's lonely. So that's why they leave you. They mean well."
(Laughter.)
So he carried me on up to the Woodside. So he get --
Where did that thing start with Prez with the ladies?
Prez? Prez -- I think Lady named him. Billie Holiday named him the President and he called her -- he named her Lady Day.
But how did they start calling everybody else 'Lady'?

Well, you know, he would call me Lady because he always just say, "You're so refined and you're so nice. I got to give you a Lady name because I don't ever see you mad at anybody or anything." He says, "You're just so nice and you deserve that elegant name, Lady." So that stuck. That's why he called me Lady Tate.
But he referred to the guys in the band generally as ladies.
Well, yeah, he would say that. But sometime -- he wouldn't call that to their names, he would just say, "All the ladies," and things. But he would always call me Lady Tate.
Did he pretend -- did he affect certain effeminate characteristics?
Yeah, he had feminine characteristics, but he really wasn't a faggot.
Yeah.
But you know, that hurt him because people started calling him faggot in the later years.
Uh-huh.
And he told me that, you know, like the last time I was with him. See, I was with him -- the last time I was with him, Gary, was -- we played up in -- up here for George Wein--- Newport.
Uh-huh.

That's when they were having the festival. Well, I played there the first night with Benny Goodman's big band. That was in '58. And, of course, John had made us stay over to play for Billie and me and Pee-wee and Jack T., Georgie Auld and Prez and Buck, Jo Jones. I don't remember who -- Walter Page. That was the rhythm section. I don't remember who we had on piano. So we all stayed there and played for -- I stayed -- as a matter of fact, I did two days, you know. I stayed there and did the -- after Benny's concert, I stayed there and did the next day.

So Prez was -- he was sick then. It was getting to him, you know, he was really failing. He was short-winded, he didn't have any stamina, couldn't hardly fill his horn, you know what I mean? Sound -- couldn't control his sound. So that day, we had a rehearsal, rehearsing things with Billie. So George and I was always tight, you know? Georgie always -- I'll show you, on the other hand -- he calls me Miss Tate and
I call him Mrs. Auld. We always -- "Hello, Miss Tate," right now, you know, he'd do it.
(Laughter.)

So anyway, we were there playing. So Prez couldn't find the place. The hall was really hard to find. And Prez is sincere about everything. I mean, like he didn't even want to be late, you know. We'd been playing about an hour, rehearsing about an hour and a half, just going over some things to play for her and little riffs and things we was going to play behind Billie, you know. So man, when he came in, when he found that place, he came in and he ran -- when he walked to the door, like he'd come in from that foyer there and he stops and he spies us and he got this big wide hat on and the crown's about that high. And he really looked comical, you know? And man, everybody broke down and started laughing. Said, "You finally found us, Prez." And man, it hurt his feelings, you know, because everybody was laughing at him. He says, "I don't see what's so fucking funny with you ladies." He says, "I've been looking for this fucker for two hours and a half and there ain't a damn thing funny."
(Laughter.)

He said, "Now, I don't see nothing for you all to laugh about." So we says, "Oh, Prez, we didn't mean anything like that," you know, "we just --" You know. He told me later on, he says, "Hey, Tate, you know," -- this is when he and I

were together, "you know, I was really surprised that you laughed at me." I said, "No, we weren't laughing at you. We just --" I said, "I had a hard time finding the damn place myself." I said, "George and I, he and I came in a car." George had one of those little high-powered cars then. I don't know what the hell it was, but it was one of those -- and he and I had a hell of a time finding it. So I said, "No, we didn't mean it like that." So he was all right after that. Just give you an idea of how sensitive he was, you know.
So after --
He was like this even before -- this did not start in the Army.
No, no.
He was always like that.

Yeah, he was always like that. He was always like that. And he used to tell me some stories about his father and he couldn't read and his sister played tenor. See, when I first met him, his sister played tenor and he played alto and Lee played drums. And the name of the act was Pap, Sis and Bub. They played Sherman and he was playing alto then. And that's during the time -- this must be close -- I can't pinpoint it, but it was during the time that I heard the Whiteman band and I met Bix and all of them. They played -- all those bands, all those little carnivals and

things would always come to Sherman, you know, and all the bands would come there to play and I'd catch all of them. But anyway, I was with him -- he asked me, says, "How are you going home?" It was hard to get back to New York, Gary. You had to go to Providence and wait a long time and take a bus to Providence and wait and maybe miss a train, then catch a train from Providence to New York. So he was up there, he and his lady, he had his lady and a friend that had driven him there and a Cadillac. He's sitting in the back in the middle of the seat like the way those big engines ride down in Oklahoma, you know, big hat on. So he says, "You ride with me." I said, "Well, I'd love to, Prez." He says, "You've got to. You don't go back over there. You ride with me." So I says, "Okay." He says, "And as a matter of fact, I want you to be my manager today, to take care of my business for me, pick up my money." He was playing at the Birdland. He says, "They docked me, you know. They're not going to pay me for the night." He said, "But that's all right." He says, -- I went on, he heard me play a set. So he said, "Gee, you sound good. I've been back here listening. You've got it together. You really sound good." He says, "I haven't done too well, you know." He says, "I've been down right to rock bottom." He says, "I started to call on you because I've been reading about you. I started to call on you." I used to let him have money, you know, a lot of times. He used to like to gamble,

you know, and lose his money and I'd loan him money, a hundred or something like that because I didn't have any of those habits, see. So he says -- I said, "Well, what the hell. You know if I got anything, you're part of it. Why didn't you?" I says, "You know that." He says, "I know that, but a man's got his pride. You know, a man must have his pride." He says, "I've been down to -- I've called on some others --" I won't call any names "-- that turned me down. I didn't only want like 50 or 75 dollars." He says, "You know who came to my rescue?" Says, "Miss Jones, Lady Jo Jones." Jo Jones was working with Joe Bushkin then. He was very busy, working all over New York, making good money. Jo Jones went down to the Alvin Hotel and signed his name, he said, "Let him fill it in." He says, "Whatever you fill in, it's all right." He just signed his name and put a check there, says, "Let him fill it in."

And he says, "That's who came to my rescue." And I says, "Well, I really didn't know that." And he had left home, he said he couldn't get along, he said, "I can't think no more, I can't practice because I can't get along at home." So he had moved to the Alvin Hotel.
So, you know, I tell you, when I got in the car that night with him, first thing he did, he opened his wallet like this and turned me on, you know. He lit up. He said, "Now, let's review the books."

You know, "Let's review the books." (Laughter.) So he says, "I haven't done so well, you know." I says, "What do you mean?" He says, "I never really made it on my own ." I said, "What do you mean, you haven't made it?" I says, "Man, you're a legend." I says, "You and Hawk." He says, "Yeah, but all the other ladies that they say play like me make all the money." So I says, "Well, I don't think you're a good businessman, I'll tell you that now." I says, "But you could have made it. I can even book you. All the world knows you and nobody have trouble --" I says, "But maybe you just don't take care of business," because he'd mess up at Small's , he had fallen off the stage, which wasn't like Prez. He'd gotten high and then fallen off the stage and they fired him and things like that.

So he found out that Norman GranZ was like giving him 500 and some of the others was getting 14 and Bean and them was getting 14. You see, to tell you about Prez, if you once do him a favor, he never stop paying you back. Everytime he'd think of something -- Flip told me he got nine cigarette lighters that Prez had given him, all cigarette --
Yeah.
Because he'd fix his horn, he fix his horn for him all the time. He'd come to Flip and say, "Lady

My baby ain't acting right." They'd be on a jazz -- said, "You better do something for her." And Flip said he was standing over him watching him / "Look now, Prez, if I'm going to fix it, take your ass on in the other room somewhere." He says, "I know what the fuck I'm / Leave me alone."
(Laughter.)
And you know, but I'm just giving you an idea of what kind of guy he is. So when he says--when Norman come down and get him out of the brig, they put him in the -- what is it? A brig or something?
Debilitating?

Yeah, yeah. In the barracks. And they were going to kill him because he said he couldn't get no air. He said he had a little light -- he said he would have died in there. Norman went down there and raised hell and says, "You all don't know what you're doing. You got to let this man out of here."

And they said Norman came on so strong, some of them told him, says, "Well, now, we'll put you in there." And Norman says, "Yeah, but you put me in there, you'll hear from a lot of millionaires and a lot of people," he said, "he ain't got no 'millionaires' , but I --" said, "If you put me in there, I know you all taxis, , but you're going to hear from a lot of big people." And he got him out. So then he says, "I'm starting my Jazz Philharmonic. I'll give you

$500.00 a week." And he never asked for any more. So I says, "Well, Prez --" And one of the guys, the pay-off guy, come and told him, he says, "Prez," he says, "I can lose my job for this, but you're a great cat and I know I can tell you this." He said, "You ain't getting enough money, man," and he started telling, running down the salaries to him, what this one was getting and what this cat -- he said, "Man, go and ask for some more money," says, "I know I can tell you this."

And so he told me that himself. And he says, "I never really --" I says, "Well, why in the hell didn't you go tell Norman?" I says, "You should have asked for 2,000 because they was Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins." That's the way that was then, when, you know, like he -- I said, "They come --" He says, "Well, I think the ladies come to hear me," he said, "but I don't get the money." I said, "Well, you're not a good businessman, as I said. I told you that."

So we talked all about that and he told me. We got lost and it took us nine hours to get from Newport. I'm glad, because those last nine hours was the last time I spent with him and we talked all night. So I picked up his money for him and took care of his business and everything. He told me, "Just sent my wife a hundred dollars. Just say Lester -- don't say nothing. Just --" I sent her a yard and he wanted to give the guy some money that brought him up and he wouldn't
take nothing. He got insulted. He said, "No, you're my friend, man. I don't want any money."
So anyway, he says, "I'll tell you what I'd like for you to do for me." {You think it's gone? MR. GIDDINS: No, a little farther.}
So he says, -- I said, "Prez, I want to pay you. Then he got insulted. He says, "Are you kidding?" He called me some names. He says, "But I'll tell you what I would like for you to do, if you can."
Who was this? The driver?
No, Lester.
Lester wanted to pay --
He wanted to pay me.
Oh.

And I offered to pay the driver for bringing him up there and he didn't like it. Then when I offered to pay Prez, Prez didn't like it because he cursed me out because I offered to pay him. So I said, "Well, I appreciate it." He carried me to my apartment uptown and everything. So he says, "But I'll tell you what I would like for you to do." He says, "If you know anyplace where I can get me a bottle," he said, "I'd appreciate it because there's not going to be anything, tomorrow's Sunday and I won't be able to get me a bottle until late, you know?" He said, "And I'll pay some dues." And really, that's the first thing I -- because

there's a guy walked all night right on my corner, Gary, with bottles in his pocket and he's selling them. And I says -- and she said to me -- she called me -- she said, 'If you do, the doctor done said any drink, he might start hemorrhaging to death.' She says, 'And I know he would die if you bought him a bottle and he did it,' you know, started hemorrhaging. So I wouldn't do it.

And sure enough, you know when we pulled up to that corner, the first guy I saw was that bootlegger. I could have went right to him and got it. But you know, when she told me that, I would have -- you know, I would have felt badly all my life had I bought him a bottle of whiskey and it killed him right then and there, which -- he lived about eight or nine months longer. But that's why I didn't. That's all he wanted me to do for him and I didn't. And you know, sometime that bugs me. So my wife said, 'I think you did the right thing, because if you'd had that on your conscience, if you'd had bought him whiskey and, you know, he'd take it and started hemorrhaging and died, you know,' because she told me, she said, 'The doctor said any drink might kill him, one drink. Any one drink might kill him. He might start -- that's how bad his liver -- and the condition he's in. He might start hemorrhaging anytime.'
So I wouldn't do it. So that was my last time with him, those nine hours in Newport. That was in the -- of course,
he died about six months later.
Was he a lot different after the Army than before?
Hm?
Was he a lot different after the experience in the Army?

Yeah, yeah. He was. They kind of changed him a bit. You know, actually, to me, his best recording, the two best recordings after the Army were the one he made, that 'D.B. Blues' he and Vic, and he and Buddy Rich and Nat King Cole.
(Inaudible), right.

He played his ass off in that. Oh, man, those, to me, those was the best things after. Now, the other years, I'm talking about -- this was more like the years when he was with the Basie band. He played -- to me then, he played really -- those were his last best things. I don't know. He was very sad after he came out of the Army. He was very sad.
Let's go back to the Basie years.
Uh-huh.
You joined the band, you made it that night by playing --
"Blue and Sentimental."
Uh-huh. And the guys accepted you
right away.
Right away.
Did Basie start assigning you solos?
Yeah.
Or did you just pick up Herschel's?

I played that. Then he started with the new arrangement, they started giving me solos. But never as many as he gave Prez. Well, I could understand that, you know, but actually, I thought that he should have given me more. But he didn't. So I just stayed there, you know, and I couldn't go through a thing now like I went through then, you know, in a big band, because I just couldn't -- if you don't play, you get so you can't play. You got to play all the time, you know, and I just wouldn't make a sacrifice like I made with Basie for any kind of money now. I'd rather play somewhere for just enough to get along and be able to play as often as I wanted to. As a matter of fact, I wouldn't want to work with a big band now, Gary. I like the way I do now.

But then, at the time, you know, I was glad to be with -- I was happy to be with the band and it was the big band era and we had a nice thing and I did get some things to play and I was raising a family and I needed the job.
When did you get married?
Well, in '36. See, I got married in '36 in Omaha. But I had been married before then.
Really?
Uh-huh.
How old?
I've been married all my life.
(Laughter.)
I've been married three different times. The first wife died.
How old were you then?
Well, I had to marry, you know, the first time and she was only 20.
And you?
I was about, I guess, 18. Yeah, about 17, 18. And, of course, -- a very lovely girl.
What did she die of?
