Yeah.

Well, Jerry was like -- I understand he had four or five -- he's almost had enough years to really be a doctor and Jerry said they played up in Waterbury, Connecticut and this was Herschel's last night with the band. And he told Jerry, he said, "Jerry, take this mouthpiece," he says, "I can't make it with it." And Jerry had his mouthpiece and

he gave him his. And he said he never heard anybody play like that in his life, the way he played that night, and he says, "Man, I feel terrible." Jerry was there with Benny Goodman. And they came down to listen to the band. Jerry said he carried him in the back and he laid him down on the table and said that water just -- you know how water sounds in the ocean when it hits up against a bank? He said that's the way it was sounding inside of him. And he told Basie, said, "If you don't get him to a doctor real soon, he's going to die. It's going to flood his heart."

So a friend came up and got him and carried him, brought him on back to New York, and Prez came back to New York. They had about three or four days off. Prez -- they all stayed at the Woodside and Prez said he used to go knock on his door because he wouldn't go right to the hospital. He waited about three days before he'd go. He was waiting to see his girlfriend, said he wasn't going until she showed, you know. So Prez said he'd go see him, knock on the door, said sometime it would take him so long to open the door and one day, he peeked through the hole and he was on his knees, saying his prayers. Of course, when he went to the hospital, he didn't make it. But --
Basie always had two great tenors.
Uh-huh.
He had Prez and Herschel and then
he had you and Prez. He had two great trumpet players, Buck and Sweets. Was there competition between you guys?
Well, I think there was competition. I think there was a little professional jealousy with Prez and Herschel.
How was that?

I think they were a little jealous, you know, of one another. But otherwise, it wasn't -- of course, we would always be trying to sound better than the other one when we took our solo, you know. We wanted to be the one that took the best solo, you know.
(Laughter.)

And that happens with every one of us, you know, like we'd want to do a solo that somebody -- stood out that somebody really dug, you know, and I guess they kept you on your P's and Q's and kept you trying to be sharp all the time, to keep from being made look badly, you know what I mean?
Right.
So I would say yes, I guess it really was really competition.
Yet it didn't encourage you to any kind of stylistic borrowings.
No. Oh, no.
Like Prez and Herschel had such different styles, they didn't try to play like each other.

No, no, no. No, they really didn't. I've heard a few things on some records sometimes where Herschel has played so much and Prez -- if his trumpet's in between it, sometimes I hear them do something similar. Of course, I guess that's natural. That's really natural, you know, like some glisses...brrruppp! I've heard Prez do that after Herschel had done it earlier up in the thing, you know.
Yeah.
(Laughter.)

So maybe he had that in his mind. Sometimes I know how that is because sometimes a cat can play a solo and you don't really mean to get on -- you don't really mean to -- if you're going to play a solo behind him or something, you don't really mean to do that. But if that solo has impressed you, it sounded good, you might end up using some of his notes sometime, not meaning to.
(Laughter.)

It's hard not to, you know. So I imagine that's what happened. But I understand between them, I was told that there was a little jealousy and there was a little friction, but I don't think it would be a big one, because Prez paid his doctor bill and --
Was the general feeling of the band one of camaraderie? Friendly --
With -- oh, yeah, with all -- when I got

there, yeah, all of us, you know, we would -- it was no cliques, no cliques ever and if a guy really wasn't right and was the wrong kind of guy, he stuck out like a sore thumb and finally he would come on in, you know, because there really were no cliques. Everybody hung together, maybe if you was in the band, you and I would be buddies for -- maybe we'd say this week because we got something going together, you know what I mean?
Uh-huh.

Then next week it would be you and Sweets, me and Basie -- Basie was just like all the cats. He really didn't act like a leader until -- but he got respect. He got respect and he still does. But he's just one of the guys. He's not the kind of leader that would go to a town and the band's staying here and he's over in another hotel.
Yeah.

You know, he doesn't do that. I've seen him say, -- and this would be down South when things were really rough and we had to stay in -- you know, like in the colored homes, colored families and things. We'd build up homes and things, you know, like after many tours because like two or three times a year, we'd do the same tours and we'd just go to that same house, you know. Everybody had their place where they knew they were going to stay. But I've seen when we did get in some hotels sometime when naturallythey'd have a big

room for Basie and a nice suite. He says, "No, get the boys straight and I'll take mine." He's that kind of guy. And times I remember we'd go to California and the ones that had children, if we were going to be in California like two or three months, he used to get a whole car and say we were going to play -- we'd go to Chicago maybe, play in Chicago. So maybe we're going to do four or five nighters around Chicago, Gary, Minneapolis -- what's that? Milwaukee, you know, in that area, something like that. Well, he'd derail that car and we could stay on that car and then he'd hook it up to the Silver Chief when we'd get ready to go to Los Angeles and places like that and he would tell all the guys, he says, "Now, bring your wives and babies," he said, "because I'm paying for the whole car." And you could take them and wouldn't have to pay.
I thought that was real nice, you know? And he would do that for us and I know there are some other bands that were going to California by bus in those days, big name bands.
Sure.
And he would -- you know, I can't say anything bad. He's always been nice like that. At Christmas-time, he used to give us money, watches and --
Was he a disciplinarian?
Yeah. I tell you what now. He's like

this: You can do anything you want to do. He doesn't get in your business and everything. But when you hit that band-stand, you got to play. Ain't no way in the world he would go through some things like Duke had gone through with some of his guys, no, not with Basie. He'd fire anybody if he comes on his job -- you know, he gave them a chance. But if he's going to drink and keep juicing and interfering with his work, he's not going to be there.

I saw him fire Paul Gonzales. And I told Paul, I tried to tell him, you know, because, see, Paul was the first one, first big -- he worked with us before he went with Diz, then he went with Duke. And he took Illinois' place. And he's one of the nicest persons I've ever known and I used to tell him, he started juicing a little bit heavy and he'd miss -- a couple of times, we were doing theaters and I remember once in Detroit, we got in from Chicago and we had some new acts we had to rehearse and the theater opened at 11:00 -- 11:30 for the show to go on. So that meant we didn't get in there until about one or 2:00 in the morning. That meant we had to be there around 7:30 to rehearse that act.

So Basie says 7:30 and if you go out and hang out with him just because you go out and hang out with him at a bar and get juiced and you go home and go to bed and don't make it, don't think that's going to save you, you know what I mean, because he's going to go there if he had to go sit on

the steps. He'd be there. He's not that kind of cat. He doesn't send anybody -- he makes it himself. And so I told Paul, Paul had been kind of missing little things. I said, "You know, Paul, you got to watch your cues now." I says, "He won't go for that. I've been here a long time." So I says, "He won't go for that. You're going to have to perform if you're here." Paul said, "No, no, he digs me like a son." I said, "Paul, you're not listening. I've seen them all go, man."
(Laughter.)

So he missed a couple times and I told him, I said, "Paul, I bet you one of these days he's going to let you go." So Paul says, "I don't think so because I was out with him last night." He says, "We did --" I said, "Yeah, but he made time." I says, "I know him." I said, "Listen, Paul, he fired Lester Young. Now you remember he fired Lester Young." I says, "So now, he'll fire you."

So in Detroit -- that's why I said Detroit because I remember that's where it happened -- we had a 7:30 rehearsal for some two acts we'd never played and we had to get their music down. But the other act was traveling with us -- we had two more acts and they were traveling with us. So we knew that thing, you know. He didn't make it. So when the -- he came to work that day, Basie gave him his notice. First one he came to, he came in the room to me, he says, "See here, man,
he gave me my --" I said, "I told you, man." I says, "I know."
What did he -- did he write something out?

Yeah, he wrote him notice. He said, "Two weeks from today, you're terminated -- I mean, your engagement ends with the Count Basie band. You are now on your two weeks notice." Now, if a guy -- that means like -- if I got a band, if I'm working for you, now you got to give me two weeks notice or you can pay me the salary you're paying me, you can pay me two weeks then, if you really want to get rid of me that badly. You have a choice. And so he gave him his two weeks notice. So he come to me with big crocodile tears. I said, "Well, I told you, man. I know. You cannot mess up on his gigs. That's why he keeps a good band, because he don't care what you're doing. You can ball with him all night long, but when you come on that bandstand, you got to play." That falling off the bandstand and that kind of stuff, he never put up with anything like that.
Why did he fire Lester?

You know, that's the $64 question. Everybody wondered and I've heard different things and I just don't believe it. I don't know. I really don't know because somebody said it was a Friday the 13th and Lester said his something told him not to play that day, which I don't believe.
And some people said John Hammond asked him to fire him.
Why?
I really don't know. I never -- I have never been able -- now that's one thing I really don't know. I don't think anybody knows, really.
Lester never said anything to you?

No, he never mentioned it. He never said anything to me about it, although when he came back in the band, he fired Don Byas and hired Prez again. But why he fired Don Byas, Don Byas pulled a pistol on all of us at -- Manhattan Hotel, it later became. But what was it then? Edison -- no, it wasn't Edison, it was Lincoln, Hotel Lincoln on 33rd and 8th Avenue. It was 33rd or 34. You know, right on -- it was later the Manhattan Hotel. So -- well, you know what happened there? You know, you ride to 42nd Street and you walk back and you come up and you come up in the hotel.
Uh-huh.

You know what I mean? It was like a little dungeon into -- that's where we used to work at night. You'd come right up and you'd come right into the Hotel Edison. Well, she had all the big bands there, Miss Kramer. They were called the Blue Room. Artie Shaw, Harry James, Benny and everybody played there for Mrs. Maria Kramer, was her name. But now you could go down under there, then across the street, there was a bar by the name of Martin's and they used to sell

three for one, one price, they'd sell three drinks. So Basie didn't know this bar was under there, you know, he didn't know what was going on down in this tunnel. So, you know, he would look up sometime and cats would be high on the bandstand and everything. So I know he would have a valet to go in their cases and their overcoats and things and -- but they couldn't find anything. So I knew what was going on. Then I didn't drink a drop. I would just go to work. But I'd go over there, because we had a lot of fun, you know, talking. This was like around '42, '43. This is after he'd fired Prez and Don was in the band and Don was really almost an alcoholic at that time.

But Don used to say to me, we were friendly, he says, "Look, Buddy," he says, "I know you're a friend of mine and I know you admire me and I admire you. Now look at it this way. If I'm really goofing and messing up, I'll take your advice, when you tell me I'm really goofing," he says, "I'll listen to you, because you're sober. You've got to see what's going on." So I said, "Well, that's very nice." And he really did that, until this night when he drew that gun on everybody.
Why did he draw the gun?

He got drunk. He got drunk. So he was going, like on our break, he'd go down there and go up under there and he'd drink in those two-for-ones and they didn't -- you know, like he'd buy two drinks, he had six drinks. So he was high, you know, and at this time, he could take one drink

and start -- you know, it would start -- he'd get dizzy. So Basie asked me, he says, "Where in the hell they getting that whiskey from? What's happening?" I said, "I don't know." You know, there wasn't no way I was going to tell him, you know, I couldn't tell him that. He says, "Well, man, I've looked in the cases, Henry's searched their overcoats and I looked all through the bathroom," says, "they ain't got none. What the hell they doing?" I said, "I don't know." He says, "They're damn sure getting it from somewhere." I said, "I don't know."

So what really happened this night, Ben comes down and he's working on 52nd Street and during this time, Don Byas is really playing, man. He's really playing that horn. So I don't know, he came over to our job first because we started work like 8:30 or something like that and I don't think he started until 10:30, 11:00. So Basie asked Don to get up and let Ben sit down and play some and Don did. I mean, everybody in the band just raved over Ben. Don said -- jealous, you know. Sat down in the back. Of course, he was doing some funny -- wasn't really playing, he did some funny sounds and little gimmicks and things, but actually playing, he wasn't really playing.

So the cats, "Man, I never heard nothing like that on saxophone in my life. Gee, this cat --" Man, they was talking like that and Don got stoned, you know. He just got so jealous. He went over there and he got ossified. I mean,

he couldn't hit the ground with his head. So he come back and Basie says, "You're drunk." This is after Benner had gone to work. He says, -- he didn't say anything then. So they he says, "You're drunk." He says, "Yes, and you're the cause of it. And all of you son of a bitches," you know, that's what he called all of us. "Goddamn," he says, "you're raving over him. Wasn't worth a damn thing, he was playing," you know. And one word brought on -- you know, they said -- that's what ya say something.

So, man, before we know anything, he jumped back against the wall, Gary, and pulled a little owl-head about that long. He said, "I don't want the son of a bitch to say nothing to me. I'll kill everybody." He's stoned, man. So I says, "Shit, maybe he will. He don't know what the hell he's going. He's drunk." Now he's too far to rush, you know, there's not anyplace you can grab. He's like over there, you can't rush him. So I says -- everybody says, "Oh, man, what are you talking about?" So he says, "Basie, goddamn it, you don't give a damn about nobody in the world but Lester Young, you son of a bitch, and you don't give a damn about me or him," talking about me, "either. We're just here. Lester Young is God to you." And Basie says, "I've always liked your playing, Don. I don't know why you'd say a thing like that. If you didn't, you wouldn't be here. I don't have to have you here." And he says, "Well, there's not many saxaphone players today.

Everybody's in the Army."
(Laughter.)
You know? So I says, -- I thought maybe I could talk to him. He says, "Talk to him, Bud," you know. Now we're all like hemmed up against the bandstand and we weren't playing now at this time. It was on intermission. So I said, "Come on, Don." I says, "Don't feel that way. Let me talk." He says, "You get back there with them, too." So I got back there with them. That's the first time he had ever done that to me, but I did it. I got on back there with them.

Henry Snodgrass saw what was happening and the house dick, you know, that take -- he eased up behind him and they didn't hit him. They just eased up behind him and threw their arms around him and the cat kind of hit him on the arm like that and the gun dropped. All he had to do is push him over and they got him and carried him on out and carried him home. He was living uptown. That was a swinging place called 20-40 on Seventh Avenue. All the musicians and all the chorus girls lived there. That was a wild place, you know.

So he carried him on up there. So the next day, Basie sent him his two weeks notice. And to show you how he is when he drinks, Henry knocked on the door -- Henry Snodgrass, the valet -- he says, "Yeah." He says, "Brought you something." It was in an envelope. He says, "Here it is."
He said, "Oh, that's a pay envelope." He says, "Goddamn, it's about time that son of a bitch give me a raise."
(Laughter.)

He said, "He gave you one. He done raised you out of the bed." He said, "For what?" So he looked at it and he says, "He paid you," you know, "don't come to work." You know, he fired him just then, that night, you know what I mean?

So the next day, he didn't even remember what had happened that night before. He didn't even know a damn thing about it. He'd get that Indian -- he had a lot of Indian in him. He'd get that Indian in him. He didn't know what the hell he was doing, really. And, of course, the next day -- Prez wasn't doing too good with his little band. So he was in town and I went down to Manny's. Manny's was near 6th Avenue then, all the music stores and things all around there. So I just happened to go downtown and Prez was down there getting some reeds and things and he says, "Lady Tate, it's nice to see you." He says, "You know, I'll be back with you tonight." So I says, "Well, I kind of thought so." He says, "What's the matter with them two whores? They still fucking and fighting?" Talking about Don and Basie. "What's the matter with those two bitches?" I says, "Man, I don't know." So then he came back in the band and he stayed until he went in the Army. Did I tell you about -- I told you about that.
Or do you want to know about that?
Yeah.

Well, he and Jo Jones -- what actually happened, they draftdodged for like a year. A lot of musicians were doing that because when they'd get their papers that come to the house, "Come down to the induction center on," you know, "examination --" something like that, they would say, "Well, I didn't get it. I was on the road tour." So they got by for maybe a little longer than a year. And they found out, FBI found out where we were going to be the longest time. We went to Los Angeles and we were going to be there three months and they found out about it. And this little cat comes out like a -- well, you wouldn't call him a -- yeah, I guess that's what you'd call him. They didn't call them beboppers. Yeah, beboppers. He had a chain that long --
Zoot suit.

Zoot suit, yeah, the zoot suit. He had a hat that wide. So he came on, you know, we just thought he was one of the boys, one of the hip boys. He come up and he dug Prez, me, Jo and Sweets and all night long, he sat there. We was playing a place called the Plantation, Joe Watts' Plantation out in Watts. And -- Joe Morris' Plantation, rather, out in Watts. So all night long, he sat there with us and whenever we'd take a break, we'd

go to his table. He bought Prez -- Prez was drinking heavy. Jo was drinking his Hennesey, Sweets was drinking. Do you know, at the end of the night, he pulled his coat back like this, told Prez and Jo Jones where to be at 9:00 that next morning, says, "FBI." They knew where they lived and they says, "If you aren't there, we will come after you." And Prez -- it really got to Prez, you know. He -- you know, he was kind of sensitive and man, that high voice really came out. "Man, ain't that a bitch." Now, you can take care of all of this, can't you?
Yeah, sure.

I'll say what he says, "Ain't that a bitch? Well, goddamn," he says, "little guy gained my confidence and," he says, "I liked the little son of a bitch." He says, "You know, I started to turn him on?" He started giving him some marijuana.
(Laughter.)

I said, "If you had turned him on, it probably would have been a long time before I'd seen you again." He said, "Ain't that a bitch?" He said, "He gained my confidence. He was a nice little guy, too." He says, -- he'd been buying drinks, you know, buying drinks all night. So Basie says -- Prez was featuring and Jo was the featured -- you know, they were advertised as features in the band. Basie was kind of, a little concerned. We came to town -- me, Basie and Rush

came to town. I said, "Basie, don't worry." By this time, Prez was drinking like a quart of Granddad a day. I says, "Man, they don't want Prez. His health won't allow it." I says, "I don't think he's healthy enough for the Army." I says, "And you know they don't want Jo because he's crazy." That's just what I said. Shit, two days, man, they had them in Fort Ord. That was a little old Army place right out of Los Angeles. They were mad with them and two days, they had them in Fort Ord.

So Artie Shaw had just given up the Navy band. They dropped a bomb close to him over -- they had a hell of a Navy band in the Navy. So he told them, he says, "I don't care what you do to me or how you feel about it," he says, "I'm going." He said, "Just put me in the brig," he says, "because I'm not going to play anymore." So they let him out and he was in California. We were doing command performances and he and Basie were tight. So he says, "Bill, I can play Prez' parts on clarinet." So we had him. He played the clarinet, you know, Prez' parts on clarinet and Buddy went to work -- he was working with Tommy Dorsey -- and he went to work like from five until nine. So 10:00, he --
Buddy Rich.
Buddy Rich. So by 10:00, he was there at work with us. And that went on for about six weeks.
Never recorded that.

Yes, they did. Somebody got it in in Missouri, some friend of mine got all three of our's pictures on the V-disc, You know, we made the V-disc. So I asked Basie, "Have you seen that album? Hell, no, I ain't got no money --"
(Laughter.)

All three of them, Basie, Artie Shaw and Buddy Rich on the album. This friend of mine got it in Missouri. They get everything over there and how they get it, nobody really knows. He got that -- you know, like those command performances we were playing for the soldiers and things like that, they got it.

Was there a sense of competition between the bands, other than when you were just -- I know occasionally you did a battle of the bands. But like, when you look back at the era now, the best bands that were swing-ing were the Basie band, the Duke band, Lunceford. But the bands that were making all the money and became stars were Goodman and Dorsey and Shaw.
Yeah.
Was there a kind of a jealousy among black musicians or a sense of --
Not really. They weren't really jealousy. But they wouldn't play a black band as much as they would play a white band. They just wouldn't do it. They never got a

chance to get like a camel caravan program, you know, like Benny had all of that. Even all of Duke's time, he never had a commercial, you know, like -- that's why they made a lot of money, you know, in those -- they just didn't hire black bands, like for the Chesterfields or the Camel cigarettes or -- I remember Isham Jones had the Ipana Troubadors and things like that for Ipana toothpaste, it used to be, and the black bands never got those gigs.

So they had to go in ballrooms and do one night storms, barnstorm and places like that. And all of the places weren't open to them. We were -- in many places, we were the first black band to go in, you know?
Your records sold, though.
The records sold.
What were some of the better selling records?

I would think the "One O'Clock Jump," well, you know that one, "One O'Clock Jump" and "Rockabye, Basie" sold and Basie sold good. Let me see, what's some -- "Super Chief" was a big seller and let's see, what else? "Easy Does It."
How about the ones with singers, Jimmy, and/or Helen Humes?
Yeah, Jimmy's "Going To Chicago," that was Jimmy's tune.
Was he very popular?
Yeah, he was very popular. Mr. Five By Five, they called him.
Uh-huh.
He was very popular.
Were you in the band when Billie traveled?
Holiday?
Yeah.
No.
That was before.
Uh-huh. And let me see, Helen did another thing, 'Don't Worry About Me,' that sold quite a bit. That was one of Helen's things. And they sold quite a bit.
What about Basie's piano playing? Was he playing a lot then or had he already started to....
He was playing more.
He was playing more.

Yeah, he was playing much more than now. And I always loved him. I think he's one of the best in the world to play with. He never gets in your way and he's there when you need him. If you need to hear a chord, he knows it. You know, like he feeds you and he never gets in your way. So he is really, to me, he's one of -- just about one of the -- he's definitely one of the greatest. And --
Do you think that Freddie Green's

Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. It's the flavor of the band. I've heard the band one night without Freddie and it sounds just like a well-rehearsed band. That edge, didn't have. Oh, yeah, he really needs him. People have gotten used to it, you know, because they can stride so you can hear walk and things like that. And without Freddie, it would really put a -- it really would change things and actually, only guy I know that really sounds like Freddie is Steve Jordan. I don't know if you're hip to Steve Jordan, the white guitarist. I got him on an album with me.
That's right. The Chiaroscuro.*
Yeah. He's the same -- no amplification or anything -- he's the same type thing and he would be on one that would really be the right place, in my mind.
(Recording interruption.)
Okay. Remember any other anecdotes about the Basie band, any other incidents that --

Let's see. Let me think. Oh, I remember one time, we were -- this was before the band had ever gone to Europe, it was around 1943, and we had a tour with Gypsy -- Jane Foreman, was it Gypsy Rose Lee or Gypsy Markoff or something, one of those names. I can't remember now. But we had a long tour in Europe and we were going to end up coming around through Portugal, went back to New York, and we wanted

to go, you know, we'd never been there. So all of a sudden -- we'd gotten all ready shot-wise and everything, Basie said, "I'm not going." So we says, "What are you talking about?" We thought he was kidding at first. So he said, "No, I'm serious. I'm really not going." So we said, "Well, man, we ain't never been to Europe. Why don't you want to go to Europe?" He says, "Well, --" Somebody -- he had a feeling, fortune-teller or something told him not to go. She said, "I see danger in this trip." And he was a little superstitious, I guess, then. I don't know if he still is. But anyway, he turned the trip down. So actually, what actually happened, we were in the Roxy -- that was one of the first black bands to go in there. I don't think anybody else ever went in, big band.

So we -- Miss Foster, she was like the producer of the Rockettes. So one morning, we had rehearsal about 7:30. So he had the paper in his arm. So he says -- he walked down in front of the reed section and he says, "You guys, you ain't going to say, 'Base, you was right one time,'? You're not going to compliment me or anything?" So everybody says, "What the hell is he talking about?" He said, "Well, don't you guys read the damn papers?"
(Laughter.)
So nobody had read the paper. So when he opens up the paper, it said --Jane Foreman-- the plane had fallen and killed 43 people in Portugal. That was the last stop and they were
coming home and the pilot saved she and some -- Gypsy. But the other 43 drowned. He says, "That's our tour, you know." He says, "Looked like you'd say, 'Base, you was right one time.'"
(Laughter.)

So -- but whiskey was hard to get then, you know, like Scotch. It was during the war and everything. Man, we went out and found two bottles of Scotch and we paid a hell of a price, brought him two bottles of Scotch. "You were right, boss man," you know.
(Laughter.)

I remember that and we would have been on that tour because we were going to be with them and everything. She ended up -- she probably ended up with about 43 operations, -- 42, 50 operations. She was in a wheelchair and she ended up marrying that pilot and I understand later, he finally was in a plane crash and lost his life.
What was the connection between the band and Hammond?

And John? Well, really, I think John owned the band at one time. I think, like when I first came in, because whatever he said, that's what happened, you know. And when -- because he like found the band and he did a lot for them.
Was he respected by the musicians?

Yeah. Yeah, they dug him. Everybody dug him. And he would get good spots for you. Now, he had -- he got Herschel and -- during the time when Benny had Basie, I mean, like John would put him places where they could be exposed, like on Camel Caravan. Then we went up to Savoy and I worked two months up to Savoy, so I'm straight, you know, I can work anywhere. I've got my three months in. And I worked with Lucky's band. And then he got ready to go on the road. He was going to do a tour. So I says, "Lucky, I'm going to tell you the truth. I've done about ten years of it and I'm grateful for everything, but I just can't make this road now." And I'm going to tell you what was happening.

"Swinging Like Tate." I think that would be about the best one. On the other side, I had some of the Basie-ites and you know, like Earl and Dickey and Bub and I think I had Jo Jones. Jo didn't play too good that day, though. And let me see, what else?
Was Jo very consistent during the years with Basie?
Yeah.
And then when did his --

You know, Jo, he's always been a little sick, you know, and I remember -- he'd always take a vacation whenever he wanted to. He did what he wanted to in the band. Basie would let him do it, you know, he was sort of like a pet and I think after leaving the band, you know, because all the time he was with the band, he was really something else.
Uh-huh.

But after leaving the band, I think it got to him this way, too. I think he still thinks he should be in there, you know? And he and Sonny, [Payne] Gary, remind me of each other. They always -- Sonny always walk around and said he was -- he had the band before -- Duke stole his band from him.
(Laughter.)

I think Jo really thinks Basie stole the band from him. And he says, "You know, I brought him in. I -- that was my money that brought the band from Kansas City." So I think, you know, really, after leaving the band, it kind of affected him, because I think he still loves the band. He'll walk in and look at the drummers funny and if he don't like what they're doing, when they take intermission, he'll call them. "That ain't the way that's supposed to be for that band." You know?
(Laughter.)
"Aint supposed to be like that." So I think it affected him, you know, like after leaving the band. I really do.
Well, for 21 years then your life was pretty stable.
Yeah.
The same place every night.
Yeah. You know, and --
Your home was where?
Well, I had a -- I had, this apartment up until -- see, I moved out in Massapequa in 1954. And I've been out there ever since. But I've had that apartment since 1940.
Where is the apartment?
On 146th and Amsterdam. But the neighbor-

hood is -- had really gone down, but when I moved in there, like in 1940, it was still nice, well kept, nice people, and this was before the war. Then after the war, people -- I came off the road one day and I saw people just all out on the streets and standing in the front of the apartment, so I went upstairs and I said, "Honey, what has happened?" She said, "I don't know. Looked like a plane just come over and dropped them all right here on 146th Street and Amsterdam Avenue." But before then, man, it was well kept, nice and everything. The apartment is nice inside, but outside, it's -- you know, on the streets, it looks bad. I'd be ashamed to invite anybody up there, really. But after you get inside, it's -- I went up there today and rested some. But I had a lot of memories in there, you know, since 1940 I had that.
You brought up your kids really on the Island.
Island, that's right. My wife said, "Look, let me tell you something. I don't care what you say, I'm going to get my kids off of Amsterdam Avenue."
What do you have?

I had the rest of my sons. Of course, the one that passed wasn't living with me. Then the other one was in California with my sister and one was in Chicago. There was the three boys that were away. But I had another -- I had two daughters and another son and --
With your present wife.

Uh-huh. So she says, 'Look, now, --' my daughter then was a teenager and my son next to her, he was a teenager, so she says, 'These streets in Amsterdam, on Amsterdam Avenue,' she says, 'I'm going to go out and look for a house.' I said, 'Well, go ahead.' And she went and she looked, she looked and she looked. She couldn't find anything. So we bought some property in White Plains. We thought we'd build a house in White Plains and it was a nice piece. Hazel Scott got me interested in it. When I first saw it, nobody was living on there but she and Adam Clayton Powell. So she got me to come up and look at this property and I bought it and I kept saying I'd build and I'd build and I'd build. But she went out -- I would have, but when she went out on Stone Boulevard -- now this fella was -- well, he's a big rich man -- the street, Stone Boulevard, was named after Fred Stone. He had a daughter by the -- he was an actor and so was his daughter. He had a daughter by the name of Paula Stone.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Is it gone? And --
Yeah, let me --
Uh-huh.
(End of Side One.)
-- building, you know, keep adding to it. So I says, 'Well, if you found what you want.' She said, 'I

put $1,000.00 down." I said, "Well, okay." So I said, "If you like it, okay." So she says, -- now the fella was a builder and he had started part of it inside. It was just like -- the interior was inside, but it had to be finished off like with some of the rooms and things the way you wanted it. So she says, "I just told him I wanted it as it was, because his daughter was going to live with him and he's going to fix her like another -- so they ended up -- when we ended up, we had 20 rooms in this house and of course, I added and added and added. But when I moved there, it was all woods all around me. The people hadn't even built, just woods.

So I bought 12 more lots and I gave my daughter four and she built next to me, so we got like eight more that's right on the side of her. So they're not that close to us, you know, although people -- they've built in since then. If I had had a little more money -- actually, if I had listened to my wife, I'd have been rich. I really should have listened to her. They had the log cabins -- some German people lived right next to us and so they knew Fred Stones. They were old people and they would come out in the summer and they just took a liking to -- they was joining us. They just took a liking to us and well, I didn't have much cash. I had taken just about all my cash to go in. I wasn't a G.I. or anything like that. I had to put about eight or $9,000.00 down, you know, and I really didn't have any cash. So my wife was in

with two white ladies, they had a nursing home. One wanted to buy the other two out and so my wife said -- she sold out and the other white lady sold out. So now right next to us are 17 lots, Gary, with two log cabins, beautiful log cabin houses on them, and the lady says, "Oh, it would be so nice for you all." She said, "Because we're old and it's --" she says, "It's a problem for us to come from Brooklyn out here and to keep it clean." And they kept it spotless, you know?

So they were going to give us that property, really. You know, when you think about it now, they were really going to give it to us. So what they were going to do was to give them the down payment and just pay them. We wouldn't have to go through the bank or nothing. It was less than $10,000.00 for 17 lots. You know what they sell for now? $4500.00 a lot and I would have had 17. That's what they sell for. And the lady wanted to give me the lots. But I had bought the other 12, you know, and I was just -- I says, "I can't stand it no more." I was scuffling, you know, but I'm making money. But I just didn't want to go too far over my head and I thought I had plenty of time. But my wife sold out her business and at Christmas, she says, "You know what I'm going to do? I'm going to give those people $1,000.00 and I'm going to buy those lots." I said, "Well, we got plenty of time for that. Put that money in the bank. I don't have any in the bank." She

says, "You got some money in the bank." I tell you how I got some money in the bank, because I took all I had. And I says, "No, put it away. We need some cash." But that Christmas, she went out and spent $1500.00 for furniture and stuff. I says, "Hell, if I had known you was going to do that, I would have let you go on and buy it." I said, "We got the house. We can just sleep on the floor." We had some furniture. But she wanted to buy a decorator. I says, "You can wait for that." But anyway, that's why I don't have those lots.

I went away to Europe -- oh, she didn't sell them for maybe five, six years later. I went to Europe and made a successful tour and came back and I called them. They said, "Mr. Tate, we sold it last week." They says, "Oh, gee, how badly we feel. We wanted you all to have it because you all come right in and you all went right to work and you made this such a beautiful home," she said, "that we really wanted you all to have it." She says, "We're going to look at the contract and see if there's any loopholes and things and try to take it back." So I'm so sorry that they sold it because the guy who's bought it never done nothing. He just let it deteriorate and he's never done anything to it.
Your daughters are married now?
Huh?
Your daughters are married now?
Yeah, yeah, they're both married. I got
a three-month old grandson.
And your son?
I got one that isn't married and he's at home with us. But all the rest of them are married.
How old is he?
He's -- October the 15th, I think, he was 32 years old.
Is he into music?
He went a little mental, little -- what would you call it?
Retarded?

Yeah, he had a -- well, he's not retarded. He had like a little nervous breakdown. Fantastic, he's a clarinet player, he would have been fantastic clarinet player. You know, Gary, he goes sometimes like a year and don't pick up his horn and do you know we go through some duets and things and he doesn't get hung up? He just runs through them. And the horn's dry, no chops. Man, there wouldn't have been no end if he hadn't gotten sick. So when he got sick, he wanted -- then he wanted to be a rock and roll singer, you know, he came along up in that time. So he -- but he had a good teacher and he's the only one. But my other son just made an album last week with -- for Capitol, beautiful singer. His name is Paul Tate and they're going to -- he wrote the "Christmas Song." So they're hoping it to break big.
He wrote the "Christmas --"
He wrote a Christmas song.
Uh-huh.
And one of his originals and he had -- hell, he must have had about 14 violins, he got all the works and everything. It's really a beautiful piece, piece of thing.
How old is he?

He's 41. Well, D'Angelo. I don't know, his man, he wrote all the arrangements for him and wrote for the entire section and everything. So they're tight. They're just like that. And it's going to be on Capitol. So --
Have you taught much at all?

Not really much. I have. I tell you what I did and a lot of people come to me and ask me for -- to teach, but I really didn't have the time and really didn't have the patience, but Ben, my saxophone player, is really a great teacher. So --
Ben Richardson?

Ben Richardson. So he's really a great teacher. I mean, he knows how to teach it correctly and all of that and I would always give them to him. I would give him a lot of -- they would come to me, like you know, like they'd see me being a band leader and everything. They says, "Have you got time to teach me?" I'd tell them I would like to, but I really don't have the time, you know? And that's
why I really haven't gotten into it. I really can't teach my children. They taken lessons over in the schools, you know. I guy them the instruments and they take lessons with the school.
What's it been like then since '71 when you left the Celebrity Club?

Well, since I left the Celebrity Club, I've been free to -- although I was -- the whole time I was in Celebrity Club, I was always free to take off to do a European tour alone or go away with somebody and Eli Robinson and -- they just ran the band while I was away. They'd get a saxophone player and put in my place. Tubby used to play in my band. You know Tubby Hayes?
Yeah.
He died --
Englishman?

Yeah, when he was here, you know, I kept Tubby busy all the time because I'd be on the road and he'd always sit in in my place, you know. And everybody's worked Out of that in my band. 21 years with -- including the (unintelligible). you know, I had a -- and I don't know any musician hardly in New York that didn't have -- at least worked one or two nights and, and, you know, for a gig with me, you know, something like that. And -- but since I left, I've been -- I've still been busy, like working with Benny.
How did that start?
With Benny?
Yeah.

Well, actually, I worked with Benny -- it really started around -- in the early '50s. Maybe -- you know, I could have joined Benny's band when I was with Basie's band. I started to. Later then, after Cootie {Williams} had joined the band, he asked me if I wanted to join the band. And maybe through John, John might have -- but he always dug me, you know, because I remember one time, I told Benny this, too, we broadcast from the Hotel Sherman. I think it was the Panther Room. and Benny heard the broadcast. He said, "Oh, that new tenor player," he says, "man, I like that new tenor player." And he told Basie. So Basie said Benny said, "That's it," said, "you the tenor player. So that seals that."
So when I told Benny, Benny said, "Well, hell, you wasn't working for me, you was working for him." I said, "But you said I was a good tenor player." He said, "That's it."
Well, actually, I don't know, my first engagement with him, it must have been with a big band. Maybe around '55 or '56 or something. I almost got in the Benny Goodman Story.
Yeah.
You know? I was surprised he didn't have
Vido. But I think they fell out. They had a falling out somewhere. But he had Stan and I almost was in that. Buck was in it.
Buck?

Uh-huh. And I had a gig -- I think I would have been -- I probably wouldn't have got a chance to play a solo or anything, but I would have at least been in the band. But I had to go away somewhere, I don't remember, but I couldn't get it. But everytime he had a chance, he'd always call me and get me a gig.
What kind of guy was he to work for?
Well, I never had any problem with him. And -- oh, I got to go.
(Recording interruption.)

Frankly, I really like Benny. I love to hear him play, he inspires me. I like to play with him. He said I inspire him. And I really like working with him. He's kind of moody, he's changeable and you know, today he's friendly and tomorrow he's a loner, you know, like that. But sometimes he doesn't really feel well because of back operation he had many years ago, slipped disc, and they didn't -- I don't think the operation was too successful and I know so many times, he plays in pain. He can hardly get off of the stool. I know when it's hurting him, you know.
But he apparently still likes to play.
He still loves to play. Yeah, he still
loves to play. And so I know lots of times, he plays in pain and naturally, that could maybe sometimes make you be a little moody, you know, a little cross.
Why do you think Benny and Basie, for that matter, are still out there? Certainly they don't have to be.
No, I don't --
They're in their 70s.
I really -- I know Benny doesn't have to be.
(Laughter.)

Because I know he's got plenty of loot, you know, that -- he had 75 million in 1941, the Hammonds. And maybe I shouldn't be saying this, but all this is -- I can say anything, can't I? And so -- and Benny made, you know, he was a millionaire. So I don't know. But he just wants to play. You know, after so long. So now then, he lost his wife last year and now -- and I imagine that makes him much more lonelier because he's in that big mansion up there in Stamford and by himself except the help. I don't think they live there. A lot of times, he'd just rather be out, I think, rather be out on the road playing.
He's not a talkative --
Not too much. And he's pretty nice at times. Sometimes he can be so nice to people, like with
autographs and things? And he might just -- next time, he might say, "Not now. Not now, Pops." You know, something like that. But I think he's a nice guy. I really think he's a nice guy.
How did you get started with the Gibson party?

Dick? I was asked a couple of times that I couldn't make it, of commitments, and I always wanted to. So when I says, "Next year," you know, the last time I was asked, I said, "Next year, I'm going to make damn sure I don't take anything, because I'm going to be ready for this." So when he asked me the next time, I was ready. And I don't know, Dick was pretty tight with me. He was going to be on my day, you know, in Sherman. And because the night before, we played in Corpus Christi, some oil magnates, dons, every year, we go down and play. The band was called--Carl Fontana and {Hamilton} Joe Wilder, Joe Newman, Gus Johnson, Scott and who else? John Collins and a bass player from -- first time I worked with bass -- Italian fella from Las Vegas.
Chuck Delmonico?

I believe that's his name. I believe he was. Yeah, that's his name, Chuck Delmonico. But I can only play, you know, that Friday night, because the Saturday was my day and Dick had planned to go because at first, Dick had asked Klney, the lady that runs the fair, she says

-- he asked her, says, "Now, are you sure you only want one night? Because the guys, they have to know now." He said, "Because you can't wait until the last minute and decide you want them to play that next night." So she says, "No, one night's all right." So in the middle of the stream at his party, she decides she wants them to stay two nights, you know. And they all had planned to go with me on my day. But he couldn't go because he had to be there with them. They had to play like from five to seven that Saturday.
How many years have you been going out there?
Maybe about seven. Probably six or seven.
Why are you -- does it seem as special to you as it does to me and the non-musicians?

Yeah, yeah, you know, because festivals like that, to go in his place like that and the Newport Festival like in Nice and places like that, you get to see guys that we admire, that I admire, and sometimes you get a chance to play with them. You know, like -- was it -- where did I play with Stan? And I love Stan, you know. And --
Stan Getz.

Yeah, I love his playing. And I think it was somewhere we played and you know, things like that, you know, you get a chance to be around them, you know, like for ten days or 12 days or something like that and it's nice that way.
How did you get Scott working with Scott?
With Scott? Well, when Shirley first brought me the tape of Scott, Shirley Seltzer,
Seltzer.

Uh-huh. She brought me the tape of Scott. So I says, 'Who's this?' She said, 'You ain't going to believe this. This is a young kid I found up in Providence.' I said, 'What?' So I says, 'Yes, yeah, he sounds beautiful.' So I'm trying to remember our first gig. I can't remember the first gig we had together, because she handles him, too, you know. She books him. And I'm trying to remember the first gig we did together. Anyway, I can't remember the gig, the first gig. But there was -- I'd been hearing a lot of nice things about him and I had met him and I worked with Sue, his old lady, before I worked -- I think before he and I worked together because she was like singing with Benny, too, you know, for a short while. And we came back from -- when we came back from Warsaw and Poland and Budapest, Hungary and all those places, Benny asked me had I heard him play, because he had about eight or ten days I couldn't do. They had booked me somewhere else, you know. So he asked me had I heard him play. I said, 'Benny, I only heard a tape.' I said, 'It sounded very, very good.' So he says, 'Well, I'm going to call him to do some things with me since you can't make these dates.'

So I said, 'Well, I think you'd be satisfied with him.' When did I meet him now? I can't remember. They booked us somewhere together and we just meld together -- man, we can do a lot of things together. We got another -- we got to do another album for Carl Jefferson real soon. They took off the 19th and went to -- he's in Europe now. I'll see him in Europe. They're going to be over there. He went to Copenhagen. Not Copenhagen, but Stockholm. And he's going to Warsaw and he's got George Messel and Warren Vaché. And they're going to Warsaw.
Does Shirley do all your booking?

Not all of it. Max books me, too, you know, Max Govalli..... You know Max Govalli? He's blind. He books a lot of -- he's got a lot of people he books. Then I have an agent in Sussex, Robert Masters. He books me like all through Europe. But he's got a tour, like he wants to book me in November, but I can't do these winter tours anymore and -- you know, those heating facilities in Europe, man, I nearly froze in April.
(Laughter.)
In Wales and, you know, some places in England. I can't take it anymore. But he's a good agent. He books Peanuts and who else? Barney Kessel. And Herb Ellis. He's got some nice people he books.
So you've been freelancing?

Yeah, uh-huh, but I stay busy, you know? Somebody calls me -- I'm supposed to go to Spain after Ronny's. I'm going to Ronny's on the fourth for two and a half weeks, three weeks, maybe three. But I got to be back on the 30th because Dick is having something out there on the 30th and the first. It's like a jazz party.
Uh-huh.

It's like -- I don't know what it is, really, and it's the first time and he's having it, so I'm committed the 30th and the first of December. I'm going out there Friday, too, you know, for the Denver Jazz Club.
Uh-huh.
And they're bringing in quite a few people. I don't know, Jay McShann will be on it and --
When did you first hear about McShann?
Well, actually, after I was with Basie and they came to New York.
You didn't know him in Kansas City.

No. I didn't know Jay. Actually, Jay is from Muskogee and he's a little younger. So when I was around Kansas City, Jay hadn't come to Kansas City. Then my cousin wrote me, he wanted to come to New York. There's a trumpet player that played Jay and he asked me if he could come to New York, could I help him get into the union. So I told him, you know, he had to pay his dues that come into the six -- you know, had to actually do the six months just like everybody
else. So -- but he told me about this band, Jay McShann, and we started listening to a record. I think the record -- Bird was on it, called "Swingtism," something.
"Swingmatism."

"Swingmatism." And I think that's the first one I heard. Then I started listening Walter, had a cat named Walter Brown, blues singer. And I says, -- then they came to New York to Savoy and I caught them while they were in Savoy. But Bird had been to New York before then, before he joined Jay. He'd been --
When you were playing with the territory bands and then with Basie --
Uh-huh.
-- how seriously did you take yourselves as artists?
The bands?
Yeah.
You mean the band as a whole?
Did you think that 30 years later, the Smithsonian Institution would put your story on tape or --

I'd always hoped that something like this would happen and you know, I always feel that something good's going to happen. I really do. I don't know what, but I just always feel like -- I don't worry about if I miss the boat, just like with the Andy Kirk thing. Like, you know,

I could have made it maybe two years before like before I joined Basie. See, that was my thing and that was really my gig that I -- and I just turned down. So that didn't even bother me. So then it ended up I got with Basie's band, which I would prefer, you know, and I always feel like something's going -- I always think like that, Gary.
You felt that what you were doing -- the music that you were creating was important.
I really did, because we had a good band.
Yeah.

And we really -- we rehearsed hard and we had nice arrangers and we rehearsed and tried to get the nice intonation and nice balance and everything and they were -- always been like a pretty nice band.
How do you feel about the music---?

Would change? Well, sometimes they lose me, you know, in some things. I don't say I dislike anything, but sometimes a lot of things cease to swing for me and it gets kind of way out and I don't think it's jazz.
Have you listened to Coltrane and Sonny Rollins?
Yeah, well, you know, I like early Trane better, personally.
Yeah.

I'm not taking the knowledge -- I'm not trying to take his knowledge or anything. But to me, I don't think public-wise people want to know about knowledge. I think they want to feel you more. This is just a personal feeling. I don't -- you know, I'm not saying anything's wrong -- and so his earlier things impress me more than the later ones because -- and I know Sonny can play. And he played up in -- he played with us. He followed Benny and it must have been about June the 24th, we played at Carnegie, because we had the violinist from France was the guest for Benny.
Stefan Grapelli?

Uh-huh. Then Marion followed, then Sonny followed it later, different crowd, you know, turned everybody out and he had a good crowd. He asked me to stay to listen to his band, you know, listen to his band. You know what makes me feel good about things like that? He always comes up and say, "Man, I used to listen to Prez and you, man, I used to -- and man, you did a lot. You've influenced me, although I'm playing a different thing," he said, "but I remember how you all used to sound." Well, that's a good feeling, you know, because he's big, big name and things like that and he doesn't really have to come up and say that to me, you know what I mean? He really didn't. So when he asked me, he says, "And I wish you'd stay and catch my group after you're finished," and I did. I stayed there and
made his rehearsal with him and everything and I caught his group and -- did you catch the group that night?
Oh, yeah.
Was you there that night?
Uh-huh.
They went over well, didn't they? People dug them. So I was glad I stayed and caught his group because I promised him I would and I went upstairs and talked to him.
Have there been any players that particularly impressed you that have come up since you --
Yeah. Let me see. So many, let me see, more than one.
(Laughter.)
Well, I love, as I said, you know, I love Stan. I love everything he plays because he's -- I understand, he's so lyrical and his mind is -- and he does what he goes out to do.
Uh-huh.

And -- well, like, he came up since me, [Stanley] Turrentine you know, and let's see, who else? I used to like when he swung more and I dig Zoo -- these are all younger players, you know, like to me, you know, and I dig all of those guys. And Scott, I dig Scott. I just hope he takes care of himself better because, you see, when you work -- you know, there are a lot of musicians that they got certain pets,
maybe ten songs, that nobody can beat them playing.
Uh-huh.

But then, when you work with a guy all night long, four or five hours, and you both calling songs that neither one of you ever played, then you -- that's when you can really spy a cat, you understand what I'm talking about? I'm not talking about a cat that's got his pets, but man, this cat can play, man. Scott can play his horn. He can't read.
He can't read?

He can't read. But he's got the biggest ears you've ever seen -- and he can play harmony to anything. He can play harmony so close until you'd swear it was written. And under the most difficult songs. And I just -- you know, when I talk to him, I says, Now, you just got to take care of yourself, because --" like he's only 25. But when I was 25, I was like playing with name bands. But the point was, I didn't dissipate like he did. I says, "You've made it now, 25 years old," I says, "and you got all your life before you." I says, "Look at you. Taking a band to Europe and you're doing this and you're doing that and everybody know about you. You're on the airlines and, you know, you've been lucky." Says, "You've got to leave that booze --" so he got -- it registered because like we'd be on a job out of town or something like that and I'd catch him and he'd say, "This is only
the third one. I'm not going to drink but four." So --
Has he had this problem for a long time?

Yeah, I think he had that problem when he came in and it's really getting to him. It's getting to him and I really hate to see it because he's got a lot of talent. He says, "You know," he says, "Buddy, I'm a little afraid to learn to read now." So I said, "Oh, I can teach you in a day." You know, I said -- he says, "I'm a little afraid." So I -- then I don't know what to tell him, you know, because like now keys don't mean anything to him. He can play in any key. He can play the harmony to anything and he can play the melody to anything. Just sing the song, if he knows it, he can just go right and play it and keys don't make any difference. Now, that can kind of slow you up, because it did me and before I could read.
Uh-huh.

And I'd just grab -- whatever I heard, a song, I'd just play it. I didn't find a key for it. It just -- any key I started going with would do the job. I was just as comfortable as anywhere I started, you understand what I mean? You follow me, Gary?
How did you get to that point? Did you practice scales?
You mean playing -- you mean reading or just playing or what?
How did you get to the point where you could hear the key and then you could function _______?

I just grabbed the horn and I -- no, I didn't. This was before I went into scales, see? It's only when I went into scales and things, that's when it kind of changed me down. It kind of slowed. Then you get a little conscious of what you do. I think it can kind of pull you back. It did me, I know it did, because I used to play in any key. It didn't make any difference and hear all the changes, never played any bad ones. But I didn't know what I was playing. I didn't, I just played. Herschel was sort of like that. He never did get too cool on reading, you know.
Uh-huh. You're an efficient reader now.

Well, yeah, I can read now. I'm not -- I don't say I read as great as anybody or fast as anybody, but I know what to do, you know, and I know what's happening. Nobody wouldn't have to wait on me like that, you know. I wouldn't say I could read. I know I wouldn't be able to read as fast as Benny, but I can read just about average, like if we're in a recording studio, they just hand up some music and they hand me my part and I just look it over. I ain't going to make no mistakes. I can just play it down at sight, you know, like with the band.
Today, if you can't read well, you got to make it as a soloist.

That's the only thing. You got to be a soloist, that's what I told him. I says, "Now, if you -- you got to understand this." I says, "You got to always have your own band or you got to be a soloist." So I says, "Because when they put some music up, you can't read it." So they wrote him some arrangements and things, so he have to learn him his part. It's a handicap, it's really a handicap. So then like a lot of times, Benny wanted to use him, like with the Basie band, have us both -- but he can't read. So Benny -- and Benny gets down on people that can't read. That's why he's kind of down on Vido. He says, "Man, I heard Vido taking Hymie Schertzer these solos and / rehearsed him all evening when he's coming in the band, and he hardly got one tune and a half down. (Unintelligible.) Man, this cat can't read nothing." But he could take some Bostons, he could take some solos and have that big sound and everything.
Where does that phrase come from, "Bostons"?

Well, the first guy I heard say "Boston" was Basie. No, Earl Bostic.. Earl Bostic. Then I heard, the next guy I heard say it was Basie as a joke. Basie says, "Man, he can sure take a Boston." Well, Earl used to write arrangement and he used to say, "Right here, I want a trumpet here. So," he would say, "Teddy, you take the Boston here and Buddy, you take a Boston down here, I said,
"What?" But they would be, you know, like referring to solos. Earl Bostic was the first one I heard say Boston and Basie was the next one.
Do you know what it means?
I don't know how the name came about, but it means take a solo, yeah. I don't know who started it.
How do you feel -- have you been conscious of critics over the years when they write about you?

Well, I've never been mad with any, I really haven't. I've been -- critics have been pretty nice to me, really. I haven't had -- ever had one to really put me down. I'll tell you, when I first joined the band once, I thought one was going to put me down. His name was George Frazier He used to be up in Boston. I think George has passed and George didn't have a pleasant face anyway, you know? He looked like this all the time, mean, you know. So this night, we just -- I'd been in the band, I guess, maybe two or three weeks and really, I didn't know the arrangements too well. I had to read just about everything, but I could see George because he was sitting right in front.
(Laughter.)

So Prez told me, says, before we went on, he says, "That's a critic out there." I says, "Oh, shit, why did you tell me?" I says, "Now I ain't going to do nothing." I said, "I wished I hadn't known it," you know? So, you know, every-

body's seeing who took Herschel's place, because it was a big thing, when I took -- it was bigger than joining Basie's band today. It was the band era and the world knew that he had died and they were wondering how I was going to -- who was going to be able to fill his shoes, you know.

So it was really a big thing. So we were in Boston playing the Southland, a nightclub there, and George didn't smile at me all night. He looked at me. I said, 'Shit, this man look like he want to fight me.'
(Laughter.)

He stood right in front and he kept looking. So I said, 'Oh, shit.' So I said, 'Prez, I don't think he likes me.' I said, 'But I know he digs you. But I don't think he's going to say anything good --' He said, 'You never know, Lady Tate.' I said, 'No, shit, it look like he's going to kill me. It looks like he's mad because I got the gig.'
(Laughter.)

Man, when we got through the next day, he wrote me up that long, man, saying there's no way that Basie could have found a better replacement anywhere, regardless if -- and he named names. He said, 'Chu Berry wouldn't have fit like him, Herschel --' He said the same thing that Prez had said and he said Basie should be thankful that he got me. He said the intonation was fine and I was fantastic. And I said, 'Well, I'm a son of a bitch, boy, and I'm just going to show -- you

never know what a man's going to say, man." And I looked on his face and I just knew he looked like he was going to kill me. But that's what he -- so I've never really -- I like critics. I always like to see what they're going to say.
When you -- what kind of critic are you of your own work? When you finish a record, do you say, "Well, this one's good, but this one didn't come off too --"?
Yeah.
Do you find --
I don't like many I do.
Yeah.
Not very many, no. I really don't, man, because I says, "Oh, shit, I could have done better than that."
What happens in the recording studio? I've seen you play things in the concert hall that just scare you to death? And then when the record comes out....
You get too -- this is like -- this comes back to that not reading, too, thing, the same kind of -- the feeling, you know what I mean?
Yeah.
You get too careful.
Uh-huh.

You know, you just have to kind of let go with jazz sometimes and let it fall where it may, you know? Because then it comes out better a lot of times. But you get too -- you know, you says, "Oh, shit, I -- this is a record

and everybody in the world is going to be listening to this thing." That's in the back of your mind. So "I've really got to do my best." So there's certain things you won't take, certain chances you won't take.
When you're burning, you know it.
Yeah, you can feel it.
Did you feel it that night at Birdland with Helen ?
Yeah. Yeah, I felt good that night, man. I knew then that we was really -- that we were really swinging because actually, nobody really had been swinging to me.
No, that -- you brought the whole place to a standstill. I've never seen anything like that.

They weren't swinging. They were doing other things. Big names, I mean, they're big names and things like that. But wasn't nobody really cooking. So I says, "Hell, come on, let's swing some shit. Just do our thing, you know, our way, you know?" I says, "I think we got the kind of people in here we can get to." She says, "I'm with you." And that's just -- I felt it, you know?
And there's nothing like that on her records ------
That's right. See, that's true. Now, we did this in Telleride, Gary, and Richard Cole and Joe Henderson -- is Joe Henderson black?
Yeah.
Wasn't Joe Henderson.
Joe Farrell?

Joe Farrell, yeah, Joe Farrell. And Frank Foster. He was just there and I called him up and Arnett and it was on the last set and we got into a thing, man, that may never happen again in life. We had everybody screaming, man, in that place and nobody was really trying to out -- really trying -- we just felt a groove and we just really swung and man, we had a standing ovation. That was the last tune that we all -- you know, like I called everybody out and I was sort of like the emcee and of course, Richie had just finished and I thanked the people for Richie and we came out and we joined him. Then I called Frank up and let him play some and of course, Joe Farrell was there. And man, we got into a damn thing. I hope somebody recorded that because that was one of the damnedest things I've ever seen.
Do you listen to your own records much?
Yeah, uh-huh, I do.
Which ones do you like?
You know, I got some things I made with -- trombone player from England.
Oh, Roy Williams?
Roy Williams on the Riff, Riff label.
I've never heard of that.

They don't have distribution, really, they don't have distribution here. And this , man, you wouldn't believe it. I'm going to bring you and let you hear it and this cat, man, whoo, he plays. Now when he goes to Dixie, he doesn't play as much as he does on this record. I think he's a little scared when he -- I asked him a couple of times, I said, "Roy, you comfortable?" "Yeah, yeah, I'm all right, I'm all right." He says, "Am I doing all right?" I say, "Yeah, you're doing all right." But man, I want you to hear him on this album. We made them in Holland, he and I together. I made some with Bobby Hackett and Ted Easton does this. He's a Dixieland band leader. He's got a Dixieland band, but he's got a club in Den Haag called New Orleans Jazz Club. So he's got a record place, a jazz club and a band. So he records a lot of people, you know, when they come over there.
What other records?

It's a Riff -- it's called the Riff label. But I understand out of Holland, some people got them over here. There are a few here, but it's not listed Riff. It's under another name and that's what loses you, you know? But over there, it's Riff. R-i-f-f.
Yeah.
And I think he gave me a couple. Two or three. But I want you to hear. Now it's some ballads, Roy and

I, doing this. Now, you know, like we did -- Monesta did some midnight ---six with Black and Blues, the midnight ---first. Well, Milton and I did the first. Nobody's never topped ours. He records everybody that comes over there. You know, they bring him over there and do a tour and he records them. But nobody has come up to Milton and I. We were the first in '67.
I got an idea.
Uh-huh.
(Recording interruption.)
Okay, I just handed you a bunch of your records and just go through and tell me what you think, first impressions only.
Well, this one's good.
Give the names. You holding the mike?

This is -- oh, yeah. This is "Bud and His Buddies." It could have been better and unbroken, I think I would -- musically-wise, I think it would be -- I think it's better together than the unbroken one. We had Dickie Wells, kind of goofed up with us that day and we didn't have a trombone and it was written for trombone, a lot of the arrangements and things, and we just missed -- soundwise, we needed the trombone.
For the "Buddy and His Buddies," did you choose Roy and Illinois?

Yeah, uh-huh. And that was my choice. And this unbroken, why this was unbroken, we had some bad instruments. They tore them up on the plane going over and actually, the first night, we played in Antwerp, Belgium, and we left there and it was storming and the instruments wouldn't play. And we came to -- we did this in the Black Forest, they called it, in Villigen, Germany, and we were tired and it was just a bad thing. But actually, I like this one better than I do unbroken. It came off better.
Yeah.

You know, I got to tell you something about this. When we went there, we had this German promoter and he did all the translating. He says, "Now, all of these fellas are Germans and they don't speak any English. But they all are finished concert pianists." So if you notice, they love piano. You know how many records they got of Oscar Peterson. And they are good piano players. He said, "They're hip music-wise, but they can't talk." So he says, "I'll do all the translating." We say, "Okay." So we were going (HUMMING) and Ben's horn had rubber bands on it because they torn it up on the plane, as I said before. So after we'd gone over it about three or four times, without his horn -- his horn would squeak every time. But after we got one through -- we didn't hear it squeak, but one of the guys heard it in the control room. So now they ain't said nothing all day, you
know, just -- so when we get through and we run through it, he say, "Wait a minute, wait a minute." It was such a surprise. Everybody says, "I thought he couldn't talk."
(Laughter.)

"We can't let that through." So I says, "You've been jiving all day," you know what I mean? That was a joke, you know, and it cracked up everybody, even them. They fell out in the control rooms. So they said, "Well, I'm going to bring everybody a drink down --" So that was on this "Unbroken."
Now, let me see, now this "West Coast," well, naturally, I loved that one. But I thought it could be better and I liked the one -- I liked this one here; "Bobby and I."
"Sherman Shuffle."

But I would have preferred to have had piano. I would have liked it better with a piano. We just had a bass and drums and -- what did we have? Just bass and drums, that's all. And Walter Scott and I ------- pretty much. Let me see now, if I had a choice, "Texas Twister." There's my choice.
That's your favorite?
No.
Oh, you don't like (inaudible).
Yeah, I like it, but I don't like it any better than --
Yeah.
I believe my favorite would be 'Swinging Like Tate.' I believe it would be all around. I believe that would be my favorite one and Scott and I the next. We --
What about the Dollar Brand?
Oh, yeah, I like that one. I like the one with Dollar Brand. Now, that was something that I kind of wondered about.
Whose idea was that?
[Hank O'Neal]
Hank's. And Dollar Brand wanted to do it. You see, you know -- all right, this record here, this record here, would you believe this record is a hit in South Africa?
Uh-huh.
(Laughter.)
I guess so. It's a hit in South (Africa)
(Inaudible).

Yeah, and Dollar Brand had listened to it in South Africa and he said, 'Man, your record selling in South Africa. You got a hit record in South Africa.' I said, 'Well, I can't follow it up, you know, that.'
(Laughter.)

'You know, I can't go to do any gigs.' He said, 'No, you can't do that, but you got a hit record in South Africa.' So he had told Hank that he would like to do some -- he thought it would be nice if we could do something together because he's

from South Africa and, you know, by me having a little name in South Africa, together with the both names, he thought it would sell good and I think it did, you know. So I was playing up to the Crawdaddy and Hank, he came up to see me. He says, "Got an idea. How would you like to work with Dollar Brand?" I says, "Who?" He says, "With Dollar Brand." I says -- he brought him with him. So he says, "He would like to make an album with you." So I says, "Yeah, it's all right with me, but you know, it's two different worlds, so maybe." So he says, "No, not really." So he says, "We think we can get together and if you're for it." I says, "Yeah, I'm for it," because I always did feel like I think there's room for everybody to play their own styles and that's why I like to go to these parties and things. You can play with the way-outs, just play your thing, you know what I mean? And if you got an ensemble, you get together on, everybody go out together and open together like that. But solo-wise, I don't have to try to play like him. Just play your thing and I think there's room enough for that.
How did the session go?

Fine, went fine. I got a little -- the only thing, you know, like some of their songs, one of his originals, like -- you know, like I'm accustomed to an ending. Like you play 32 bars or maybe it's 40, but there's an ending. But some of his songs, they don't end. They just go on and on

and on and on. They don't finish. So that kind of hung me up, you know, like you'd say, "Well, okay, now, I know I'm in the last eight. I done played the middle, so this is my last eight, so I'm going to start over again if I'm going to do two or three solos. I know I'm going to start over." But not with some of his songs. They don't end. They just go on and on. You just end when you want to, as long as you're with the chord changes and things.
So for a little while, -- it didn't take me too long to find out what was happening, you know, and so I just started playing some blues and it came out all right. He dug it.
All right, one last question.
Uh-huh.
A lot of people talk about the sound of the Texas saxophone players honking and this kind of affects sort of started there.
Uh-huh.
How did that start and where does it come from?
Well, actually, I think Illinois started that.
Well, Prez does a lot of that riding on one note stuff.
Oh, yeah, well, Prez. Yeah, Prez did
that. Now, Prez could do more with one note than anybody I've seen, you know, like (HUMMING) and all that kind of stuff. Well, now, that's Prez.
Uh-huh.
But the other things like you would {[Illinois]} say -- you know, like Jacquet's 'Flying Home?'
Yeah.

(HUMMING). I thought that's what they were referring to when they said honking, with the -- you know, with the one note, the same note. Well, actually, I think he was about the first one that I heard do that from Texas, but Paul Bascomb did that back with a thing called 'Nona.'
Who?

Erskine Hawkins. It didn't catch on as much as Jacquet's did, but he did that and a cat asked me once, why did Texas players have the big sounds, most of them? So I told him once, the way I could answer, I said, 'Well, there's a big stage. You got to play loud to be heard.' (Laughter.) And it stuck. You know, they made a joke out of it. But actually, I don't know. I think it's guys being impressed by some -- like a guy leaves from Texas and he makes it. Well, everybody, you know, they -- I think it's from things like that, just like --
Did Lester influence you?

Yeah, he really did. Actually, he did a lot of things -- he made me always -- made me want to play. But Jacquet- I got more Jacquet - playing with Jacq', I got more vibes for one to play when he was in the band than I did with Prez. Because when Jacq' came in the band, man, he was really -- he was cooking.
"Huttonleg"?

Yeah, when he'd take away from that -- you know, that other thing, you know like he did that reed squeaking. But I mean, just actually playing, man. When he came in that band, shit, he was really burning, man. And he made you want to play, you know, and I think he inspired me more wanting to play, of having desire -- now, Scott does, too, and whenever he and I play together, I don't ever get tired. I feel like playing all night because he plays interesting things all night.
Are you going to be gigging together?
Yeah, we're going -- now, in London, I think I finish --
In New York.
Yeah, we always -- whenever we can get together, we always do Condon's, because we always do a fantastic business. Next time we do it, I want you to come up.
Yeah, I will.
I wish you'd come and be our guest, man, because he'd love that. But --
Are you going to do Crawdaddy again?

I don't know if they're doing that now. Somebody told me that they weren't doing that. I don't know of anybody's in there now. I think Warren Vaché said that, back in the summer, they had been using a piano and he didn't think they were going to do it again. So I hadn't had a call from the agent and I know nobody's in there. So I don't know if they're going to be doing that.

I probably going in the Vanguard. I don't know. They asked me to go in January, but I've got to go to Blues Alley in January. So I don't know how Shirley's going to maneuver that, because these two weeks are right together in Annapolis at the Maryland Inn and then to Blues Alley and --
Do you still look for material at all?
Yeah.
And do you find yourself adding new things to the book?

Yeah, sure. You know, but when I play with local rhythm sections, you know, I carry some music and things sometimes because there's certain things I want, like I got a little thing, a nice little thing, on 'Shiny Stockings' like Basie played it and it really sells with a quartet, you know, the way I do it and 'Georgia Brown' and things like that.

So I got those things written out for the -- as a matter of fact, I had to write out a piano part while I was in Orlando, Florida at Disneyworld for a fella. But it's effective. And so I got a pretty nice little repertoire.
What horn do you take?
When I go out on the road? I take the tenor and the flute --
I mean what style, make?
Oh, I got a Conn Conqueror. They gave me a Yamaha flute in Japan and the clarinet is a Penzamula. That's American-made clarinet.
