You don't play that much clarinet.
Yeah, when I'm by myself. I like to, but --
I remember the records you made with Buck for Prestige.
"Blue Creek?"
Yeah.

Yeah, that's my tune. I wrote that, those tunes. I do one on here, I do a solo on here I like, on "Unbroken." I think it's "Blues for Johnny." I want you to listen to that. Play that tonight and I take a clarinet solo on that that I like.
All right.
And Ben -- this is Nat's tune, I think it's "Blues for Johnny." "Moten Swing," "Candy," "Ben's "Early Autumn," Broken Saxophone," (inaudible). "One For Johnny," I think that's

it, "One For Johnny." Now I play a clarinet solo on there I like, but, you know, most of the things, recordings, I always find there's something I should have done. But occasionally you find things. I like the ones I made with Roy Williams and the "Midnight Slows." I like just about every one of them because Milt Buckner played so damn good with that organ and man, I could hear so many things. I got to bring you -- I got to give you -- I'll bring it over next week. I got two of them I'll bring you, "Midnight Slows." I want you to hear this. They're really nice. I'll bring that over. And I'll bring the Roy Williams ones over, but I don't have but one of those. But the ones like with Milt, I'm going to give to you, the one with me and the one with Milt, I'll bring it to you next week.
Any last words you want to add?
Well, it's really been nice and --
(Laughter.)

-- I certainly enjoyed this. Let me see, what can I add now? Well, I'm going -- when Scott comes back, I want you to come up, I'll let you know, and I want you to come up and hang out with us up there. Do you ever go by there, by the way?
Haven't been there in a long time.
Really?
But I'd like to, yeah.
Yeah, well, Scott, he has a guest every

segments.title: Copyright notice and Smithsonian Reel I opening
segments.summary: Archive copyright warning and title page: Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project, Buddy Tate interviewed by Gary Giddins in Washington, March 1980.

segments.title: Birth in Sherman, Texas, and his farmer father
segments.summary: Tate gives his birth date and place, his parents' origins, his father's three farms and early death, and being raised by older siblings.

segments.title: Brother's saxophone and first teachers Malone and O'Bannon
segments.summary: His older brother brings home an alto, and Emmett Malone and Frank O'Bannon start him on the instrument and on transposing.

segments.title: Brother Herbert and the trombone he wanted
segments.summary: Herbert played in Dallas territory bands; young Tate wanted a trombone, and his brother insisted on the saxophone.

segments.title: Brother Marshall, family parties and the aunt's Dallas hotel
segments.summary: His pianist brother, his mother's parties and the musicians at his aunt's hotel, including Alfonso Trent's band, make him want to be a musician.

segments.title: Farm life and the city house
segments.summary: They lived on the farm until he was about 12, and the family had all it needed.

segments.title: First music: cousin's vaudeville show, Sidney Bechet and the Blue Devils
segments.summary: The first music he remembers is his cousin's vaudeville show with Bechet, and he first met Basie with Walter Page's Blue Devils; he began playing professionally at 14.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: The family band and its reunion at Buddy Tate Day in Sherman
segments.summary: He describes the family band, McCloud's Night Owls, and getting them to appear at the Buddy Tate Day concert in Sherman.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Miss Callie Frost's audition and a busy schedule, about 1927
segments.summary: A college-connected patron hears the family band, and the group gets three or four gigs a week; Tate is 12 or 13.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Listening to records at the neighbourhood house
segments.summary: They learn from records at a woman's house that sold drinks, hearing Coon-Sanders and Armstrong's West End Blues.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: His mother's records and learning solos by slowing the turntable
segments.summary: His mother had Bing Crosby, Bessie Smith and Gene Austin records; he learned solos and harmony by playing records slowly.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Malone, the carnival musician who taught them
segments.summary: Malone taught them to spell and wrote arrangements but kept leaving with the carnivals.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Hearing Frank O'Bannon from the alley of the white theater
segments.summary: Segregated theaters, listening to O'Bannon in the alley, and their first meeting at a party.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Lessons from O'Bannon at fifty cents and learning to transpose
segments.summary: O'Bannon offers to teach him to read in exchange for jazz lessons, and teaches transposition.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Teaching O'Bannon to play jazz by humming and scatting
segments.summary: Tate explains to O'Bannon how to improvise by humming a solo; he played changes without knowing the theory.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: The importance of a good tone on alto
segments.summary: Tate says everyone chased a good sound, with an even vibrato; he names O'Bannon and Earl Warren as models.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Touring Oklahoma and Kansas City; tenor player Milton Thomas
segments.summary: The band grows popular, travels in touring cars, and Milton Thomas, a tenor player who made money in trucks, influences Tate to take up tenor.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Instrumentation and arrangements copied from records
segments.summary: The six-piece band had no bass and made head arrangements from records of Coon-Sanders, Moten and Fletcher.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Lonnie Johnson comes to McKinney and needs a band
segments.summary: Tate describes Lonnie Johnson's ups and downs and the night his band failed to show at his aunt's ballroom in McKinney, Texas.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Alfonso Trent's band and its uniforms at the Adolphus
segments.summary: Tate explains where the family band got its uniform habit: Trent's band at the Adolphus Hotel in Dallas.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Playing dance sets behind Lonnie Johnson
segments.summary: The Night Owls reach the ballroom in 25 minutes and back Johnson on blues and play for dancing.

segments.chapter: Family band and learning to play
segments.title: Lonnie Johnson pays $50 each, which settles Tate on music
segments.summary: Johnson pays each player fifty dollars, which convinces Tate to become a musician; he later saw Johnson in Toronto.

segments.title: Leaving the Night Owls for Wichita Falls and meeting Herschel Evans
segments.summary: After some of the band go to college, Tate takes a job in the oil-boom town of Wichita Falls and meets Herschel Evans.

segments.title: The St. Louis Merrymakers; Herschel Evans joins Troy Floyd
segments.summary: Tate switches to tenor in the St. Louis Merrymakers, and Herschel Evans leaves for Troy Floyd's band.

segments.title: Prince Robinson, the underrated tenor player
segments.summary: Tate admires Prince Robinson of McKinney's Cotton Pickers and explains why he never got his due.

segments.title: Coleman Hawkins and the effect of Stampede
segments.summary: The Hawkins solo on Fletcher Henderson's Stampede eclipsed all other tenor players for Tate's generation.

segments.title: Alto and C melody as the popular saxophones
segments.summary: Why alto and C melody came before tenor, and whether Tate played the C melody.

segments.title: Getting into the Paul Whiteman concert in Dallas
segments.summary: As teenagers in segregated Texas, Tate and his brother are sneaked in by hotel staff and end up on the bandstand.

segments.title: Meeting Frankie Trumbauer as a boy
segments.summary: Tate tells Trumbauer he owns his records with Bix; he is wearing short pants.

segments.title: Meeting Bix Beiderbecke and Trumbauer's advice to practice
segments.summary: Bix arrives drunk, plays piano, and Trumbauer tells Tate that music is a full-time job.

segments.title: Spotting Trumbauer in the crowd at Kansas University, 1943
segments.summary: With the Basie band, Tate sees Trumbauer in the audience, and Lester Young refuses to believe it.

segments.title: Trumbauer remembers the boy in short pants
segments.summary: Trumbauer passes Lester Young to greet Tate and praises his subtones.

segments.title: Friendship with Trumbauer, now in aeronautics
segments.summary: They meet at Kansas City theater dates, and he sends Christmas cards until his death.

segments.title: Trumbauer's later career, flying and death; Paul Desmond
segments.summary: Trumbauer faded after the 1920s, played C melody to the end, flew to gigs, and died at a hospital desk.

segments.title: Young black listeners and the mixed white and black record collection
segments.summary: Tate says black kids of the 1920s listened to Bessie Smith and white bands alike and never thought of jazz as only black music.

segments.title: Joining T. Holder's Clouds of Joy in Oklahoma, about 1930
segments.summary: Asked about Oliver and Morton, Tate says he first heard Oliver after joining Holder's band, where he hired Earl Bostic and worked with Claude Williams; Holder's band was never recorded.

segments.title: Hearing King Oliver in Oklahoma City
segments.summary: Tate compares Oliver's records with Armstrong's, and hears him declining in person at a ballroom with a big band.

segments.title: On tour with Victoria Spivey's revue and the Tulsa hotel
segments.summary: Tate toured with the Spivey revue, who had made the film Hallelujah, and describes the Tulsa hotel with a lobby piano where musicians jammed.

segments.title: Finding Lester Young upstairs in the Tulsa hotel
segments.summary: Tate learns Oliver's band is in the hotel, finds Lester Young resting with corn pads, and invites him to the jam.

segments.title: Lester Young's tenor at the jam session
segments.summary: Lester's playing at the jam drives the other saxophonists to put their horns away; Tate describes his light tone.

segments.title: Meeting King Oliver; why Armstrong swung more
segments.summary: Tate introduces himself to Oliver, who knew Holder, and explains why he preferred Armstrong.

segments.title: New Orleans style versus Texas and Midwest swing bands
segments.summary: Tate says Texas bands were more arranged and swung more than New Orleans Dixieland.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton's records
segments.summary: Tate copied a few things from Morton but preferred Midwest and Texas bands.

segments.title: The best territory bands: Troy Floyd, Trent, Moten, George Lee
segments.summary: Tate ranks the Texas and Midwest bands and says George Lee's novelty band was good but swung less than Moten's.

segments.title: Race relations in Sherman while he was growing up
segments.summary: Segregated but friendly neighbours; he played with a white band in Sherman about 1933.

segments.title: Schools in Sherman and Booker Pitman
segments.summary: He attended Frederick Douglass High; he discusses Booker Pitman and Budd Johnson.

segments.title: Wiley College scholarship and the order of his early bands
segments.summary: Tate went to Wiley College on a music scholarship; Giddins sorts out the sequence of his early big bands.

segments.title: How T. Holder lost his band to Andy Kirk
segments.summary: Holder drove to Dallas with the payroll, the band gave his job to Andy Kirk, and Holder started another band.

segments.title: Holder's later bands and what became of him
segments.summary: Holder's later bands had Budd Johnson and Eddie Durham; Tate joined the third version; Holder never recorded.

segments.title: Seminole, Oklahoma, and the lead alto who polished his nails
segments.summary: The Holder band worked ballrooms for oil-boom money, and its lead alto would stop playing to polish his nails.

segments.title: Finding Earl Bostic in Tulsa
segments.summary: Tate hears Earl Bostic play and persuades him to join the Holder band at $75 a week.

segments.title: Bostic sight-reads the hard Oliver arrangements
segments.summary: Bostic plays a difficult part cold and outplays the band.

segments.title: Bostic's virtuosity and the Bird story from Lockjaw Davis
segments.summary: Tate describes Bostic's real style; Davis's story of Bostic out-playing Charlie Parker at a Bronx club.

segments.chapter: Henderson, Lester and the bands breaking up
segments.title: The territory bands break up; Fletcher Henderson's Kansas City audition
segments.summary: With the bands breaking up, Henderson hears Ben, Herschel and Lester in Kansas City to replace Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Henderson, Lester and the bands breaking up
segments.title: Ethel Mays's band in Little Rock
segments.summary: Tate is in Little Rock with Ethel Mays's women's band when Basie brings the Moten band.

segments.chapter: Henderson, Lester and the bands breaking up
segments.title: Lester Young afraid to join Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Herschel stays with Moten, Lester leaves for Henderson, and Tate counsels him.

segments.chapter: Henderson, Lester and the bands breaking up
segments.title: How the Henderson band mistreated Lester Young
segments.summary: The saxophone section turned its back on Lester; Hilton Jefferson tells how Henderson fired him.

segments.chapter: Henderson, Lester and the bands breaking up
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's wife playing Hawkins records for Lester
segments.summary: Lester recalls having to listen to Hawkins records at the Hendersons' house.

segments.title: Recruiting Buster Smith and Joe Keyes for Nat Towles
segments.summary: Tate gets Buster Smith and Joe Keyes to join Nat Towles' band in Dallas and Smith writes arrangements.

segments.title: Andy Kirk sends for him; the Mamie Smith tour
segments.summary: Tate finally joins Kirk's Clouds of Joy and travels to New York with Mamie Smith.

segments.title: The band folds in Cincinnati; back to Wiley College
segments.summary: After the Kirk band's breakup in Cincinnati, Tate returns to Wiley and Nat Towles takes over the college band.

segments.title: Nat Towles' band with Charlie Christian and Fred Beckett
segments.summary: Tate did not graduate; he lists the band members including Charlie Christian and Fred Beckett.

segments.title: Sir Charles Thompson's name; Towles band versus Basie's
segments.summary: Tate recounts the joke about Sir Charles Thompson's title, and how his remark about the Towles band was misquoted.

segments.title: Missing Andy Kirk's Decca recording of Until the Real Thing Comes Along
segments.summary: Tate declines Kirk's telegrams to record, and the song became a hit.

segments.title: Missing John Hammond: Towles in Trenton while Hammond signed Basie
segments.summary: Hammond hears Kirk's band, but misses the Towles band, and signs Basie.

segments.title: Andy Kirk's band: smooth, clean and Pha Terrell's singing
segments.summary: Tate calls the Kirk band sweet and recorded well; Kirk's Denver connection with Whiteman.

segments.title: Benny Goodman and why white bands broke through first
segments.summary: The Towles band played Goodman arrangements; Tate thinks racial barriers, and Fletcher Henderson's weak business sense, kept black bands back.

segments.title: Getting up from a sickbed in Omaha to hear Goodman's band
segments.summary: Tate, ill with a touch of pneumonia, takes a taxi to hear Goodman, Krupa and Hampton in Omaha.

segments.title: Nat Towles' territory: ballrooms, Lawrence Welk's agent and the sleeper bus
segments.summary: The Towles band worked the Midwest and West on the same agent as Lawrence Welk, traveling in a custom sleeper bus.

segments.title: Towles band arrangers and soloists
segments.summary: Tate names the five arranging players and the main trumpet, trombone and sax soloists.

segments.title: Charlie Christian in the Towles band
segments.summary: Tate says Christian already had his mature style, playing saxophone-like lines, and talks about whether he could read.

segments.title: Towles band repertoire, precision and singing like Lunceford
segments.summary: They played originals and current songs; Tate compares the band with Lunceford's precision and showmanship.

segments.title: What became of Nat Towles and his refusal to go to New York
segments.summary: Towles moved to California and kept a small group; he would not bring the band to New York.

segments.title: The New York stamp of approval
segments.summary: Tate says musicians believed you had to be accepted in New York to make it anywhere.

segments.title: Basie's two tenors and Lester and Herschel in New York
segments.summary: Lester came back after Henderson; Basie started two tenors, and New York players reacted to Lester and Herschel.

segments.title: Moten Swing tempos that wowed New York chorus lines
segments.summary: Tate says Western bands played in-between tempos that dancers loved.

segments.title: Hearing Ellington as the Washingtonians
segments.summary: Tate remembers a clipping about Paul Whiteman tipping Duke's band and why he preferred Fletcher's sound at first.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's brilliant sound from hard keys
segments.summary: Henderson wrote in remote keys like F-sharp and C-sharp, which gave the band its crisp sound.

segments.title: Hawkins on Ellington's Mood Indigo and Check and Double Check
segments.summary: Hawkins tells Tate how he first heard Ellington on the car radio and how the film eclipsed Henderson's band.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's undisciplined band and the Steel Pier
segments.summary: Henderson never had a full band on the bandstand; stories of the Atlantic City Steel Pier.

segments.title: Joining Basie: the trial in Kansas City and breakfast with Prez
segments.summary: Tate receives the telegram after Herschel Evans's death and meets Lester Young in the Kansas City hotel lobby.

segments.title: Lester Young on why Chu Berry and Ben Webster did not fit
segments.summary: Over red beans and rice, Lester says the engagement will be his if he plays as before.

segments.title: Why Tate fit Herschel Evans's chair note for note
segments.summary: Tate explains why Berry and Webster were wrong for the Basie book and he could play Herschel's solos exactly.

segments.title: Hearing the Basie band, its members and Jack Washington
segments.summary: Tate hears the band play a dance and discusses Freddie Green, Shad Collins and Jack Washington.

segments.title: Lester had recommended him; waiting on the bandstand
segments.summary: Basie remembers Tate from 1936; Tate sits at the back with his horn in its bag.

segments.title: Playing Blue and Sentimental to win the Basie job
segments.summary: The crowd calls for Herschel's feature and Basie asks Tate to play it; he rises to the occasion.

segments.title: The band's reaction, Skippy Williams's good wishes, and arriving in New York
segments.summary: The band stands except Lester; Skippy Williams wishes Tate well; at Grand Central Prez takes him to the Woodside Hotel.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Why Lester called everyone Lady
segments.summary: Tate explains the nickname Lady Tate and Lester's gentle manner.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Newport 1958: rehearsing with Billie Holiday and Prez's wounded feelings
segments.summary: At Newport, Tate plays with Goodman's band and with Billie and Prez, whose feelings are hurt when the group laughs.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Lester Young's early family act, Pap, Sis and Bub
segments.summary: Tate recalls meeting Lester's family act in Sherman.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: The ride from Newport and Prez's money troubles
segments.summary: Prez rides with Tate, says Jo Jones lent him money and reviews the books.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Prez not a good businessman; Flip Phillips's lighters
segments.summary: Tate tells Prez he is a legend who does not take care of business; he repays favors.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Prez in the Army brig and the pay Norman Granz gave him
segments.summary: Granz gets Lester out of the barracks and pays him $500 a week.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Prez's last night: the bottle he did not buy
segments.summary: The nine-hour trip; Tate refuses to buy Lester whiskey after a doctor's warning.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Lester Young after the Army
segments.summary: Tate says the Army changed Lester, and names his best later records.

segments.chapter: Lester Young and the early Basie years
segments.title: Accepted by the Basie band; solos and the sacrifice of the big band
segments.summary: Tate got solos but fewer than Prez, and would not make that sacrifice again.

segments.title: His marriages: the first wife from Seminole
segments.summary: Tate married at 17 or 18 a girl from Seminole, Oklahoma, who died of tuberculosis.

segments.title: Ethel Mayes as second wife and their child
segments.summary: He married Ethel Mayes, whose band he worked in, and their child was born while he was with Basie.

segments.title: Marriage to Ethel Mayes ends; news of his son's death
segments.summary: Tate says the marriage to Ethel Mayes lasted under a year; their son died the night of his Billie Holiday tribute concert.

segments.title: His son's cancer and death in Silver Spring
segments.summary: The son, a health-conscious engineer, is found to have cancer of the lung and liver and dies within weeks; Tate carries on playing in Europe.

segments.title: His present wife, five children, and his son's mother in Little Rock
segments.summary: Tate has been married since 1936 and has five children; he worries about the failing mother of his late son.

segments.title: His doctor on cancer risk among black men
segments.summary: Tate relays his doctor's remark on prostate cancer rates and the talk drifts to sickle cell.

segments.title: End of the first cassette and the Reel II header
segments.summary: Tape side ends; a new Smithsonian title page for Reel II, same interview in Washington, March 1980.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Meeting Louis Armstrong on a Coca-Cola box in Tulsa
segments.summary: At the small hotel Tate sits with Armstrong in the alley and is told he will make it in New York.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Holder's $5 fine and the night off to hear Armstrong
segments.summary: The band skips work to hear Armstrong; the ballroom owner gets a local band so Holder's men can go.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Billie Love at Armstrong's dance and her death
segments.summary: A young woman throws her undergarment onto Armstrong's horn during Body and Soul and dies hours later; Armstrong remembers it later.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: What Armstrong told him: practice, and New York players can't all play
segments.summary: Tate and Armstrong talked for hours about jazz; Armstrong told him to practice.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Practicing then and now
segments.summary: Tate says he practised all day when young, less with Basie, and now nearly as much as ever.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Why he is called Buddy: George Holmes Tate
segments.summary: He was named George after Washington; his sister who died of typhoid called him Buddy.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Charlie Parker in Kansas City and New York; Tate tries to get him into Basie's band
segments.summary: Tate knew Parker as a student of Buster Smith in 1934 and later tried to place him with Basie.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Why many older musicians put bebop down
segments.summary: Tate liked the bebop players, but did not try to play that way, and cannot see why others put it down.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Kids humming the solos at the Earle Theater in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Fans knew the Basie records note for note, and noticed when Tate played a different solo on Rockabye, Basie.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Playing record solos versus new ones; Lester never repeated a solo
segments.summary: Basie bandsmen would extend a hit solo; Lester Young would not repeat solos except on records.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: How head arrangements came about in the studio
segments.summary: Basie starts a riff, the sections find their harmony, and the casual flip side often turns out to be the hit.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Song pluggers and paying for radio time at the Hotel Lincoln
segments.summary: Basie played tunes by Nick Kenny on coast-to-coast broadcasts, and shared the cost of air time with the hotel.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Herschel Evans's last night and death
segments.summary: Jerry Jerome tells of Evans' final night in Waterbury, Connecticut, and Prez's visits at the Woodside.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Competition between the tenors and trumpets in the Basie band
segments.summary: Tate says there was professional rivalry but no borrowing of style between Prez and Herschel, and he describes the unintended borrowing.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie as a leader: no cliques, shared hardships and the train car for families
segments.summary: Basie stays in the same lodging as the men and paid for a rail car so wives and children could travel.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie the disciplinarian
segments.summary: Tate describes Basie's rule that you can do what you like but must play on the bandstand, and he introduces Paul Gonsalves.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie fires Paul Gonsalves in Detroit
segments.summary: Gonsalves misses a morning rehearsal in Detroit and Basie gives him two weeks' written notice.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Why Basie fired Lester Young
segments.summary: Tate offers rumors about the Friday the 13th and John Hammond, but says nobody knows.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: The Hotel Lincoln bar tunnel and Byas's drinking
segments.summary: Basie's men drink at Martin's bar beneath the Hotel Lincoln, and Byas, close to alcoholic, relies on Tate for advice.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Don Byas pulls a gun on the band when Ben Webster sits in
segments.summary: Byas, jealous when Ben Webster sits in, draws a pistol on the band; the house detective and Snodgrass disarm him.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Byas fired by pay envelope; Lester Young returns
segments.summary: Basie fires Byas, who does not remember the night, and Lester rejoins.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: An FBI agent in a zoot suit catches Lester Young and Jo Jones
segments.summary: Young and Jones dodge the draft until an undercover agent in Los Angeles arrests them.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Artie Shaw and Buddy Rich fill in for Lester and Jo Jones
segments.summary: With Prez and Jo in the Army, Shaw plays Lester's parts on clarinet and Buddy Rich sits in on drums; a V-disc results.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Why white bands got the radio sponsors
segments.summary: Black bands were not hired for commercial programs, so they had to barnstorm and often broke color barriers.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Best-selling Basie records and the singers Jimmy Rushing and Helen Humes
segments.summary: Tate lists top sellers such as One O'Clock Jump and Rushing's Going to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie's piano and Freddie Green's guitar in the rhythm section
segments.summary: Tate praises Basie as an accompanist who never gets in the way, says Freddie Green is the flavor of the band, and names Steve Jordan as the only player like him.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie's premonition and the cancelled Gypsy tour of Europe
segments.summary: Basie refused a planned overseas tour after a fortune-teller's warning, and the plane carrying the tour crashed in Portugal.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: John Hammond's role with the Basie band
segments.summary: Tate says Hammond practically ran the band's early career and got it exposure on Camel Caravan.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Bands Tate admired; Benny Carter's band and Marie Cole
segments.summary: He loved Lunceford's reed section and Ellington, James and Dorsey; he discusses why Benny Carter's bands never took off.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Ten years with Basie and how the band changed
segments.summary: Tate was in the band 1939 to about 1950, as the Army took players such as Buck Clayton and Illinois Jacquet came in.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: The big band breaks up: package tours and the rise of rock
segments.summary: Tate recalls the first Basie band breaking up, and says agents' bird-group packages and rock killed the big bands.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie's arrangers: Mundy, Gibson, Clayton, Dameron
segments.summary: Tate lists those who wrote for the band, including Buster Harding's boogies and Skip Martin.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: How Tate avoided the draft
segments.summary: A friend on the draft board kept postponing his induction until he was classified 4-F.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Basie got out of the Army too; Tate offers money and is refused
segments.summary: Tate says Basie also avoided service, and the sympathetic draft officer refused any payment.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Musicians' draft tricks: Don Byas, Billy Eckstine and Sweets Edison
segments.summary: Musicians faked heart trouble with benzedrine or acted effeminate to be rejected.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: Why the Army wanted Lester Young and Jo Jones, and how they passed
segments.summary: Draft officials wanted to make an example of the pair; Prez's hip talk amused the examiners.

segments.chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
segments.title: His first recording date: the 1947 Los Angeles session with Witherspoon
segments.summary: Tate leads his first date before the recording ban, with C.Q. Price singing blues, Jimmy Witherspoon, and the Supreme label.

segments.title: Leaving Basie in 1950; Lucky Millinder and the Local 802 transfer rule
segments.summary: Tate, waiting out the three-month union rule, is put to work by Millinder.

segments.title: Studio dates in New York and sitting out the road; Hot Lips Page and Rushing at the Savoy
segments.summary: Tate prefers New York recording work and staying home, and plays with Hot Lips Page and Jimmy Rushing.

segments.title: The Savannah Club with Lucille Dixon and the Celebrity Club offer
segments.summary: Tate plays Lucille Dixon's show band downtown, and the Celebrity Club owner asks him to form a band.

segments.title: The Celebrity Club's drinking house band and the offer to replace it
segments.summary: The owner has a band of alcoholics he is willing to replace, and Tate decides to take the job.

segments.title: Forming the Celebrity Club band and leaving the Savannah Club
segments.summary: Tate chooses Pat Jenkins, Eli Robinson and Skip Hall and gives up Lucille Dixon's show band.

segments.title: The Celebrity Club in Harlem and its first European-bound records
segments.summary: The 125th Street club drew a mixed crowd and Europeans; first records were for Larry Newton at Derby, with five or six tours.

segments.title: Twenty-one years at the Celebrity Club, 1950 to 1971
segments.summary: Tate describes the size of the band, the book, and how rock and disco ended the job.

segments.title: What the Celebrity Club looked like
segments.summary: Upstairs and downstairs, Polynesian-style decor, intimate dance room.

segments.title: Celebrity Club records: Nat Pierce, Black and Blue, Batan, Swinging Like Tate
segments.summary: Tate lists his recordings including a 1954 album with Inez Washington and Swinging Like Tate with Stanley Dance.

segments.title: Jo Jones after leaving Basie
segments.summary: Tate says Jo Jones did as he pleased in the band and still thinks he should be in it.

segments.title: Home: the Amsterdam Avenue apartment since 1940
segments.summary: Tate has kept an apartment on West 146th Street since 1940 and describes the neighborhood decline.

segments.title: Buying a house on Long Island to raise the children
segments.summary: His wife insisted on moving the kids off Amsterdam Avenue; they bought a partly built house on a street named after Fred Stone.

segments.title: The 17 lots that got away
segments.summary: Neighbors would have sold them seventeen lots cheaply, but they spent the money elsewhere and the chance was lost.

segments.title: His children: a clarinetist son and singer son Paul Tate
segments.summary: Tate talks about his daughters, a son with mental illness who plays clarinet, and Paul Tate's Capitol album.

segments.title: Why he has not taught, and Ben Richardson as teacher
segments.summary: Tate says he lacks time and patience to teach and refers students to his saxophonist Ben Richardson.

segments.title: Freedom to tour from the Celebrity Club; Tubby Hayes and since 1971
segments.summary: While at the club he could go to Europe, with Eli Robinson and Tubby Hayes covering for him.

segments.title: Working for Benny Goodman: how it started and the Goodman Story near miss
segments.summary: Goodman liked him on a Basie broadcast, he first worked with Goodman's big band in the mid-1950s, and nearly appeared in the Benny Goodman Story.

segments.title: Benny Goodman as a boss: moody, in pain and still playing
segments.summary: Tate likes working with Goodman, notes his back pain, wealth, loneliness after his wife's death and his moods.

segments.title: Dick Gibson's jazz party and other festivals
segments.summary: Tate explains how he came to play the Gibson party, the Corpus Christi gig and why festivals matter to him.

segments.title: Working with Scott Hamilton
segments.summary: Shirley Seltzer brought Tate a tape of Scott Hamilton, and Goodman used him when Tate was unavailable.

segments.title: Booking agents and his freelance schedule
segments.summary: Tate names the agents who book him in Europe and the US and lists upcoming jazz parties.

segments.title: Jay McShann's band and first hearing Charlie Parker on record
segments.summary: Tate learned of McShann's band from a cousin and heard Swingmatism, then caught them at the Savoy.

segments.title: Taking the music seriously and the Smithsonian interview
segments.summary: Tate says he always hoped for recognition, felt the bands' music mattered, and does not regret missing opportunities.

segments.title: Modern jazz, Coltrane and Sonny Rollins at Carnegie
segments.summary: Tate prefers early Coltrane, and recalls Rollins thanking him at a Carnegie Hall bill.

segments.title: Younger players he admires, and Scott Hamilton's ears and drinking
segments.summary: Tate admires Getz and Turrentine, and praises Hamilton's playing by ear while urging him to drink less.

segments.title: Playing in any key by ear, and learning to read
segments.summary: Tate says he played in any key before learning scales; reading is a handicap if lacking.

segments.title: The word Boston meaning a solo
segments.summary: Tate says Earl Bostic first used the term for a solo, and Basie picked it up.

segments.title: Critics: George Frazier's review of his first Basie nights
segments.summary: Critic George Frazier at the Southland in Boston turns out to praise Tate as Herschel Evans's replacement.

segments.title: Judging his own records and being too careful in the studio
segments.summary: Tate says he is critical of his own records and that jazz needs letting go.

segments.title: The night at Birdland with Helen Humes
segments.summary: Tate recalls a night when he and Helen Humes made the place swing.

segments.title: A jam-session finale at Telluride
segments.summary: At the Telluride festival, Tate called players up to a last set that brought a standing ovation.

segments.title: Records he likes: Roy Williams on Riff and the Midnight Slows with Milt Buckner
segments.summary: Tate talks about records made in Holland with Roy Williams and an organ album for Black and Blue.

segments.title: Bud and His Buddies and Unbroken
segments.summary: Giddins hands him his records; Tate reviews the missing trombone on one and the damaged instruments on the Unbroken session.

segments.title: The German engineers who spoke English at the Unbroken session
segments.summary: The German promoter said the engineers could not speak English, but they stopped a take for a squeaking horn.

segments.title: Rating his albums: Sherman Shuffle, Texas Twister, Swinging Like Tate
segments.summary: Tate picks Swinging Like Tate as his favorite, then the Scott Hamilton album.

segments.title: Recording with Dollar Brand
segments.summary: Hank O'Neal's idea to pair Tate with Dollar Brand, whose songs had no set endings.

segments.title: The Texas honking tenor sound
segments.summary: Tate says Illinois Jacquet started the single-note honking style, and jokes that Texas stages were big.

segments.title: Influence of Lester Young, Illinois Jacquet and Scott Hamilton
segments.summary: Tate says Jacquet inspired him to play more than Prez, and that Hamilton does too.

segments.title: Upcoming gigs with Scott Hamilton: Condon's, Crawdaddy, Blues Alley
segments.summary: Tate lists club dates and mentions the agent's scheduling problems.

segments.title: New material, charts and his instruments
segments.summary: He keeps adding to his repertoire, writes out charts such as Shiny Stockings, and names his Conn tenor, flute and clarinet.

segments.title: His Prestige records with Buck Clayton and clarinet solos
segments.summary: Tate points to tunes he wrote and a clarinet solo he likes, and promises Giddins records.

segments.title: Closing remarks and invitation to hear Scott Hamilton
segments.summary: Giddins asks for last words; Tate thanks him and invites him to the club.
